Measure the third variable and control for it, or compare within subgroups






An experiment settles both problems at once. When you set \(X\) yourself, \(X\) came first, which settles directionality. Random assignment to groups balances every third variable, measured or not, which settles confounding.

title: 2  Correlation
text:
2.6 Chapter Summary
Why it matters. Correlation is how we quantify whether two variables move together. We use it to describe patterns (e.g., chocolate and happiness, water and plant growth) and to decide whether a relationship is worth modeling or acting on. Chapter 9 returns to the best-fit line and tests its slope.
Core ideas

Variance and standard deviation. Deviations from the mean always sum to zero, so we square them. The variance is the mean of the squared deviations, and the standard deviation is its square root, back in the units of the data.
Plot the scatter before computing \(r\). A scatter plot shows the direction of a relationship (up, down, none), whether it is straight or curved, and any outliers. If the pattern is curved, fit a suitable model (for example, add a squared term) or transform a variable instead of stopping at \(r\).
Pearson’s \(r\) is covariance rescaled. Covariance measures whether deviations from each mean tend to align. Pearson’s \(r\) rescales covariance by the standard deviations so the result is unitless and bounded ([-1, 1]).
Interpreting \(r\). The sign of \(r\) gives the direction, and its magnitude gives the strength of a linear relationship.
Regression link. The best-fit line summarizes the average relationship. Residuals are the vertical gaps between data and the line. The line is chosen to minimize the sum of squared residuals.
Chance alone can manufacture a correlation. Small samples can produce large |\(r\)| by accident, and larger samples shrink the “chance window” toward 0. A large \(r\) from a large sample is much harder to attribute to chance.
Nonlinearity hides real effects. Curved relationships (e.g., too little or too much water harming plant growth) can yield \(r\) ≈ 0 even when the underlying effect is strong.
Confounding. A third variable can create or inflate a correlation (e.g., sunlight affecting both watering patterns and plant growth, or age affecting both shoe size and reading). An experiment, which sets \(X\) and assigns units at random, settles both confounding and causal direction.





Anscombe, F. J. 1973. “Graphs in Statistical Analysis.” American Statistician 27: 17–21.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.1 From description to inference
Download this chapter (PDF)
Chapter 1 covered study design and describing a single variable with graphs and averages, and Chapter 2 described the relationship between two variables with correlation and a best-fit line. Statistics also lets us do inference. Inference uses data from a sample to draw conclusions about the broader population the sample came from. Inference relies on two foundations: probability theory and the behavior of samples from distributions. This chapter covers probability rules and distributions first, then how samples behave: the law of large numbers, the sampling distribution of the mean and its standard error, and the central limit theorem. It ends with \(z\)-scores, estimating a population’s standard deviation, and the confidence interval.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.2 Probability vs. statistics
Probability and statistics reason in opposite directions between a model and data.
Probability starts with a known model of the world and asks what kinds of data are likely. A model here is a description of the process that produces the data, such as a fair coin or a well-shuffled deck.

Example: What is the chance of flipping 10 heads in a row with a fair coin?
Example: What is the chance of drawing five hearts from a shuffled deck?

Here, the model is known. Data are imagined.
Statistics starts with data and asks: what model of the world generated these data?

Example: If a coin comes up heads 10 times in a row, is it fair?
Example: If five cards in a row are hearts, was the deck shuffled?

Here, the data are known. The model is what we want to learn about.






NoteNote: Which direction?



Probability goes model → data.
Statistics goes data → model.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.3 What does probability mean?
Statisticians agree on the rules of probability but not always on what the word itself means. In everyday life we’re comfortable saying something is “likely” or “unlikely,” but the formal meaning varies.
Imagine a soccer game between Arsenal and West Ham. You say Arsenal has an 80% chance of winning. That could mean:

Long-run frequency: if the teams played many times, Arsenal would win ~8 out of 10.
Betting odds: you’d only take a wager if payoffs reflected an 80/20 split.
Subjective belief: your confidence that Arsenal wins is four times your confidence that it doesn’t.

All three interpretations follow the same rules, so the math works the same whichever one you hold. The frequentist view defines probability as the long-run proportion of times an event would occur if the process were repeated many times. This is interpretation 1 above, and it is the view this course uses.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.4 Basic probability theory
The core idea of probability theory is the probability distribution. Section 1.8 used distribution for the pattern of values in a dataset. A probability distribution assigns probabilities to all the outcomes a process can produce, and the Probability distributions section below defines it formally.
Suppose each customer picks one ice cream flavor: chocolate, vanilla, or strawberry. If we record how often each flavor is chosen, we might estimate the probabilities in Table 3.1.



Table 3.1: Ice cream flavor probabilities.





Flavor
Probability




Chocolate
\(P(\text{chocolate})=0.5\)


Vanilla
\(P(\text{vanilla})=0.3\)


Strawberry
\(P(\text{strawberry})=0.2\)






These probabilities form a distribution, plotted in Figure 3.1. Each value lies between 0 and 1, and together they sum to 1: \(0.5 + 0.3 + 0.2 = 1\).








Figure 3.1: A simple probability distribution: the probabilities for three flavors must add to 1.





A probability can also be about a group of outcomes. For example, let \(A=\) “not chocolate.” Then:
\[P(A) = P(\text{vanilla}) + P(\text{strawberry}) = 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5\]
Expected value
The expected value of a probability distribution is its mean, the long-run average of the outcomes if the random process were repeated forever.
A random variable is any quantity whose value is not settled in advance, such as the face a die will show or the number of rainy days next month. A random variable is discrete when its possible values are separate and countable, such as the faces of a die (see Probability distributions, below). For a discrete random variable \(X\) with outcomes \(x_i\) and probabilities \(P(X=x_i)\), the expected value is a probability-weighted average:
\[\mu = E[X] = \sum_i x_i \, P(X=x_i)\]
The symbol \(\mu\) is used because the expected value is the mean of the distribution. Later in this chapter the same symbol names the population mean.
Each outcome is weighted by its probability, so likely outcomes count more toward the expected value than unlikely ones.
Worked example: a fair die. Roll a fair six-sided die. Each face, 1 through 6, is equally likely, \(P(X=x_i)=1/6\) for every face:
\[E[X] = (1)(1/6) + (2)(1/6) + (3)(1/6) + (4)(1/6) + (5)(1/6) + (6)(1/6) = 21/6 = 3.5\]
The expected value, 3.5, is not itself a possible outcome. You can never roll a 3.5. The expected value is a long-run average across many rolls, not a prediction for any single roll. The average of the rolls in one sample is a sample mean, \(\bar{x}\), and it varies from sample to sample around the expected value.
Change the probabilities and the expected value moves. Take a die manufactured with a defect: two faces show 2, and no face shows 3, so the faces are 1, 2, 2, 4, 5, 6. The outcomes 1, 4, 5, and 6 each have probability \(1/6\), and the outcome 2 has probability \(2/6\):
\[E[X] = (1)(1/6) + (2)(2/6) + (4)(1/6) + (5)(1/6) + (6)(1/6) = \frac{1+4+4+5+6}{6} = \frac{20}{6} \approx 3.33\]
Replacing the 3 with a second 2 lowers the expected value from 3.5 to about 3.33, because a low outcome now has more of the probability.
Expected value comes back twice. Later in this chapter it defines “unbiased”: an estimator is unbiased when its expected value equals the true population parameter. In Section 7.4.1, a chi-square test’s “expected count” uses the same probability-weighted logic, applied to counts instead of individual outcomes.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.5 Conditional probability and independence
This course needs two of probability’s formal rules for combining events, conditional probability and independence. An introductory probability course would work through the full set.

3.5.1 Conditional probability
A conditional probability is the probability of one thing given that something else has already happened. Instead of asking how likely an event is among all outcomes, you count only the outcomes where the condition already holds and ask how likely the event is among those. A stream might exceed a nutrient threshold on 20% of all days, but on 60% of days following heavy rain. The stream is the same in both cases. The second probability is different because it only counts days after heavy rain.
We write the second one as \(P(\text{exceed} \mid \text{heavy rain}) = 0.60\), read “the probability of exceeding the threshold given heavy rain.” The event you are asking about goes to the left of the bar, and the condition you already know goes to the right.
The order matters. Suppose heavy rain comes before 10% of days. Then 6% of all days are rainy days that exceed the threshold (60% of 10%). This 6% is the probability that both things happen on a day, counted among all days. The conditional probabilities count among a smaller group of days. Among the 20% of days that exceed it, those 6% give \(P(\text{heavy rain} \mid \text{exceed}) = 0.06/0.20 = 0.30\). The division follows the general rule for a conditional probability, \(P(A \mid B) = P(A \text{ and } B)/P(B)\), which keeps only the days where the condition holds. Flipping the two sides of the bar turned 0.60 into 0.30, because each version counts within a different group of days.
The step from 60% of 10% to 6% is the multiplication rule. The probability that two events both happen is the probability of the first times the conditional probability of the second given the first:
\[P(\text{both}) = P(\text{first}) \times P(\text{second} \mid \text{first})\]
Here, \(P(\text{heavy rain and exceed}) = 0.10 \times 0.60 = 0.06\).
Every inference from here on uses a conditional probability. A \(p\)-value, which Chapter 4 introduces, is a conditional probability. It is the probability of data at least this extreme given that the null hypothesis, introduced in Section 4.3.1, is true.


3.5.2 Independence
Two events are independent when knowing that one occurred tells you nothing about whether the other did. In symbols, \(P(\text{first} \mid \text{second}) = P(\text{first})\).
Independence simplifies the multiplication rule. When two events are independent, \(P(\text{second} \mid \text{first}) = P(\text{second})\), so the probability that both happen is the product of their separate probabilities:
\[P(\text{both}) = P(\text{first}) \times P(\text{second})\]
Two coin flips are independent. A head on the first flip does not change the probability of a head on the second. Two soil samples taken a meter apart usually are not, because nearby soil tends to be alike, so knowing one sample’s nitrogen content tells you something about its neighbor’s.
Every test in this book requires independent observations. Section 6.3.5 states this assumption once, and later chapters refer back to it.
Independence also gives a result used in Section 8.1.1. Run \(m\) independent tests, each with a 5% chance of a false positive, a test result that signals an effect when there is none (Section 5.1 calls this a Type I error). By the multiplication rule applied \(m\) times, the chance that none of them gives a false positive is \((1-0.05)^m\), so the chance of at least one false positive is \(1-(1-0.05)^m\). For 5 and 10 tests:
\[\begin{aligned}
m = 5: \quad 1 - 0.95^5 &= 1 - 0.77 = 0.23 \\
m = 10: \quad 1 - 0.95^{10} &= 1 - 0.60 = 0.40
\end{aligned}\]

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.6 Probability distributions
A probability distribution is a rule that assigns probabilities to all possible outcomes of a random variable. Many distributions exist, but this book mostly uses five: binomial, normal, \(t\), \(\chi^2\) (“chi-square”), and \(F\). We focus on the binomial and the normal here. The others appear when we get to inference.
The binomial and the normal represent two kinds of distributions: discrete and continuous.

Discrete distributions assign a probability to each of a set of separate, countable values, such as 0, 1, 2, … heads.
Continuous distributions apply to variables that can take any value in a range, such as temperature. Probabilities for them are measured as areas under a curve, explained in What’s probability density? below.


3.6.1 The binomial distribution (discrete)
The binomial distribution models the number of “successes” in a fixed number of independent trials.

A trial is a single attempt with two possible outcomes. One outcome is labeled the success, which is only a name for the outcome you are counting and carries no good or bad meaning. An exceedance day is a success if exceedances are what you count. The other outcome is the failure.
The success probability is the chance of success on any one trial, usually written as \(\theta\).
The size parameter \(n\) is the number of trials.
The random variable \(X\) is the number of successes observed in those \(n\) trials.

We write this as:
\(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n, \theta)\)
For example, if you flip a fair coin 20 times (\(n=20\), \(\theta=0.5\)), the binomial distribution tells you the probability of getting 0 heads, 1 head, 2 heads … all the way up to 20 heads. The bars of the distribution in Figure 3.2 show the probability of each outcome, and the total always sums to 1.








Figure 3.2: Binomial probabilities for 20 trials, \(X \sim \text{Binomial}(n = 20, \theta)\), with \(\theta = 0.5\) (left) and \(\theta = 0.2\) (right). Bars show \(P(X = x)\).





Table 3.2 shows how \(\theta\) sets the shape of a binomial distribution. In Figure 3.2 the left panel (\(\theta = 0.5\)) is symmetric and the right panel (\(\theta = 0.2\)) is right-skewed.



Table 3.2: How the success probability sets the shape of a binomial distribution.





Success probability
Shape of \(\text{Binomial}(n, \theta)\)




\(\theta = 0.5\)
Symmetric


\(\theta < 0.5\)
Right-skewed


\(\theta > 0.5\)
Left-skewed






Two common questions

Exact probability. For example, the chance of exactly 4 heads: \(P(X=4)\)


dbinom(x = 4, size = 20, prob = 0.5)
#> [1] 0.004620552

The probability is about \(0.5\)%.

Cumulative probability, the probability of a value at or below a cutoff. For example, \(P(X \leq 4)\):


pbinom(q = 4, size = 20, prob = 0.5)
#> [1] 0.005908966

The probability is about \(0.6\)%.
This is higher than the 0.5% for exactly 4 heads because it also includes the probability of getting 3, 2, 1, or 0 heads.






NoteNote: R’s distribution helpers



Every distribution in R comes with the same four functions:

d* = exact probability for a discrete distribution, or density (the curve’s height) for a continuous one
p* = cumulative probability \(P(X \le q)\)
q* = quantile, the value with a given cumulative probability below it (p* in reverse)
r* = random draws

For binomial: dbinom, pbinom, qbinom, rbinom. For discrete distributions, some percentiles don’t exist exactly. In that case qbinom() returns the smallest \(x\) whose cumulative probability, \(P(X \le x)\), reaches at least \(p\).




3.6.2 The normal distribution (continuous)
The normal distribution describes variables that can take on a wide range of values, clustered around a central point. The normal distribution is the one this book uses most. It’s also sometimes called a Gaussian distribution or a bell curve.

The mean \(\mu\) is the center of the distribution.
The standard deviation \(\sigma\) measures spread: how tightly or widely values are clustered around the mean.
The random variable \(X\) represents the outcome, which can be any real number.

We write this as:
\(X \sim \text{Normal}(\mu, \sigma)\)
The standard normal distribution is the normal distribution with \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\). A variable with this distribution is written \(Z\), so \(Z \sim N(0, 1)\), and one value of it is a \(z\)-score (Section 3.12). Figure 3.3 shows it.








Figure 3.3: Standard normal probability density function (PDF), where \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\).











NoteNote: A single value has probability 0



For a continuous variable, the probability of any single exact point is 0, so probability is always an area under the curve.


Changing \(\mu\) shifts the curve left or right. Changing \(\sigma\) makes it wider or narrower. The total area under the curve is always 1.
Figure 3.4 shades the area between −1 and 1, which is about 0.68 of the total.
Areas under every normal curve follow the 68-95-99.7 rule, which Section 3.12 uses again.
The 68-95-99.7 rule


~68% of values fall within \(1\sigma\) of the mean

~95% fall within \(2\sigma\)

~99.7% fall within \(3\sigma\)

The 2 in the 95% line is rounded. The exact cutoff for 95% is 1.96 standard deviations.








Figure 3.4: Shaded area shows \(P(-1 \le X \le 1) \approx 0.68\) for \(X \sim \text{Normal}(0, 1)\).





Two common questions

Probability of being below a value, e.g. \(P(X \leq 1.64)\) for \(X \sim \text{Normal}(0,1)\)


pnorm(q = 1.64, mean = 0, sd = 1)
#> [1] 0.9494974

In a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1, the probability the value is less than or equal to 1.64 is about 95%.
“Less than or equal to” and “less than” give the same answer here. In general, \(P(X \ge a) = P(X > a) + P(X = a)\), and for a continuous variable that last term is zero. Setting lower.tail = FALSE tells pnorm() to return the area above the cutoff instead of below it. So pnorm(q = 1.64, mean = 0, sd = 1, lower.tail = FALSE) gives both \(P(X > 1.64)\) and \(P(X \ge 1.64)\), and R never has to decide whether the cutoff itself is included.
For a discrete variable like the binomial, \(P(X = a)\) is a bar with nonzero height, so the two are different. With 20 fair coin flips, \(P(X \le 4)\) is about 0.6%, but \(P(X < 4) = P(X \le 3)\) is about 0.1%.

Value for a percentile, e.g. the 97.5th percentile:


qnorm(p = 0.975, mean = 0, sd = 1)
#> [1] 1.959964

The 97.5th percentile of the standard normal is 1.96, so 2.5% of the area is above 1.96 and another 2.5% is below \(-1.96\). This 1.96 is the cutoff the 95% confidence interval uses at the end of this chapter.


3.6.3 What’s probability density?
For continuous distributions like the normal, probabilities belong to ranges of values instead of to single values. You cannot ask for the probability of one exact value (e.g., \(P(X = 23)\)), because the answer is zero. Instead, we calculate the probability of being in a range, such as \(22.5 \leq X \leq 23.5\).
Probability density is the height of a continuous distribution’s curve at a point, written with a lowercase \(p\), \(p(x)\), to keep it separate from a probability, \(P(X)\). The \(y\)-axis of a normal curve shows density. A density is not itself a probability. Probabilities come from the area under the curve between two values. For example, about 68% of values from a standard normal fall between −1 and 1, because the area between −1 and 1 is 0.68.
In R, functions like dnorm() return the density (the curve’s height), while pnorm() and qnorm() work with cumulative probabilities and quantiles, which are usually more useful for applied problems.
Table 3.3 sets the binomial and normal distributions side by side.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.7 Samples, populations and sampling
Descriptive statistics summarize what we do know. Inferential statistics is the branch of statistics that carries out inference, drawing conclusions from sample data about populations or about causal relationships. It aims to “learn what we do not know from what we do.” Introductory statistics typically divides inference into two big ideas, estimation and hypothesis testing. Estimation uses sample data to give a best guess of a population value, along with how uncertain that guess is. This chapter introduces estimation, and Chapter 4 introduces hypothesis testing. Estimation only makes sense once you understand how samples relate to populations, so this section covers sampling first.
To talk about making inferences, we must be clear about what we are drawing inferences from (the sample) and what we are drawing inferences about (the population).
A sample is the finite set of data points a study actually collects. In almost every study, the sample is all we have. We cannot survey every voter in a country or measure every tree in a forest.

3.7.1 Defining a population
A population is the set of all possible individuals or observations you want to draw conclusions about, and it is usually much larger than the sample. Ideally you would define the population before designing the study, because the definition shapes the design. In practice, the population is often only loosely defined. A study of “stream temperature in Indiana” may never say which streams, or which months, count. Still, the sample should represent some broader population we care about.


3.7.2 Simple random samples
The sampling method is the procedure used to choose which members of the population end up in the sample. The relationship between a sample and its population depends on it.
Suppose we have a bag with 10 chips, each uniquely labeled, some black and some white. This bag is the population. A simple random sample is a sample chosen so that every member of the population has the same chance of being selected. If we shake the bag and draw 4 chips without replacement (no chip goes back in the bag), each chip has the same chance of being selected, so the 4 chips are a simple random sample. Figure 3.5 shows three such samples.








Figure 3.5: Simple random sampling without replacement from a finite population.





Now imagine a different procedure: someone peeks inside and deliberately picks only black chips. That is a biased sample, one where some part of the design (who, where, when, or how you measure) pushes results in one direction, on purpose or not. More data does not fix it. Figure 3.6 shows three biased samples drawn this way. With a random sample, we can use statistical tools to generalize from the sample to the population. With a biased sample, we cannot. Every chip in the three biased samples is black, so they would put the proportion of black chips at 1, while in the population it is 0.4 (4 of 10).








Figure 3.6: Biased sampling without replacement from a finite population.





Another variation is to draw chips with replacement, meaning each chip is returned to the bag before the next draw. In Figure 3.7, some letters repeat within a sample for that reason. In practice, most studies are “without replacement,” but much of statistical theory assumes replacement. When the population is large, the difference is negligible. With 10 chips, removing the first chip changes each remaining chip’s chance from 1/10 to 1/9. With 10,000 items, the change is from 1/10,000 to 1/9,999.








Figure 3.7: Simple random sampling with replacement from a finite population.







3.7.3 Random and non-random samples in practice
Random samples are the ideal, and in many areas of environmental science they are common. Inventory plots, transects, and monitoring networks are usually placed at random, so that every location has a known chance of being chosen. Still, many studies rely on modified approaches:

Stratified sampling divides the population into subgroups (strata) and samples within each. This guarantees that small groups, such as rare habitat types, appear in the sample.
Opportunistic or logistically constrained sampling selects cases that are accessible or already monitored. These are not random, but they are common in practice when budgets, terrain, or historical networks limit where data can be collected.



3.7.4 How much does it matter if you don’t have a random sample?
A non-random sample matters when the way you sampled could plausibly distort the conclusions. Stratified sampling that deliberately oversamples small strata over-represents those groups. The analysis corrects for this by weighting each stratum, the same idea as the weighted mean in Section 1.9.5, so that each stratum counts in proportion to its share of the population. Opportunistic samples can be acceptable if the bias is unlikely to affect the phenomenon being studied. For example, if you want to study tree growth rates, sampling only trees on one side of a valley may or may not be problematic, depending on whether the valley side influences growth. If the north-facing side gets less sun and its trees grow more slowly, a sample from that side alone would underestimate growth for the whole valley.
When designing your own studies, choose a sampling method that reaches the whole population you want to draw conclusions about. And when critiquing others, be specific about how a sampling choice might bias results. Noting that a sample is not random does not say which way the results would be off.
Table 3.4 summarizes the four sampling methods in this section, each with an example from this chapter.



Table 3.4: Four sampling methods.










Method
What it means
Example




Simple random
Every unit has the same chance of being selected
Shake the bag and draw 4 of the 10 chips


Stratified
Divide the population into subgroups (strata) and sample within each. Small strata are over-represented, and weighting each stratum in the analysis corrects for it.
Sample within each habitat type so that rare habitat types appear in the sample


Opportunistic
Select cases that are accessible or already monitored. Acceptable if the constraint is unlikely to affect what you are measuring.
Measure tree growth on only one side of a valley


Biased
Some part of the design (who, where, when, or how you measure) pushes results in one direction, on purpose or not. More data does not fix it.
Survey adults about coffee consumption only inside coffee shops








3.7.5 Population parameters and sample statistics
So far we have talked about populations the way a scientist might: a group of people, a stand of trees, a set of rivers. Statisticians describe a population with a probability distribution. The distribution gives the probability of each value that a randomly chosen member of the population could have.
Population parameters are the numbers that describe a population distribution, such as its mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\). For example, suppose daily coffee consumption in adults follows an approximately normal distribution with mean \(\mu = 2\) cups/day and standard deviation \(\sigma = 1\) cup/day. These two numbers are the population parameters.








Figure 3.8: The population distribution of daily coffee consumption (a) and two random samples: one of size 100 (b) and one of size 10,000 (c). In panels (b) and (c), the lime-green dotted line marks the sample’s mean and the dashed orange line marks \(\mu = 2\).





Now suppose we take a random sample of 100 adults, shown as the histogram in panel (b) of Figure 3.8. The histogram follows the population’s bell shape, with bumps and gaps the population curve does not have. This sample’s mean is 2.07 cups and its standard deviation is 0.99 cups, close to \(\mu = 2\) and \(\sigma = 1\) but not equal to them.
Panel (c) shows a second random sample, this one of 10,000 adults. Its histogram follows the population curve more closely than the sample of 100 does. The next section returns to this comparison.
Sample statistics are numbers calculated from the data in a sample, such as \(\bar{x}\) and \(s\). This sample’s mean and standard deviation are sample statistics. They approximate the population parameters, which describe the entire distribution. The central problem of inference is how to use sample statistics to estimate population parameters, and how much confidence we can place in those estimates.
A statistic describes your data. An estimate is your best guess about the matching population parameter. An estimator is the formula that produces the estimate, such as “add up the values and divide by \(n\).” The estimate is the number that formula gives for one sample. For the mean, the statistic and the estimate are the same number, \(\hat\mu = \bar x\), as the table shows.








Symbol
What is it?
Do we know it?




\(\bar{x}\)
Sample mean
Yes, calculated from the raw data


\(\mu\)
True population mean
Almost never known for sure


\(\hat{\mu}\)
Estimate of the population mean
Yes, for simple random samples \(\hat\mu=\bar x\)

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.8 The law of large numbers
In the last section we compared a small sample of coffee drinkers (\(n=100\)) to a much larger sample (\(n=10{,}000\)). The larger sample produced a histogram that looked much closer to the population distribution. Its mean, 2.02 cups (shown above panel c), was also closer to the population mean, \(\mu = 2\) cups/day, than the smaller sample’s mean of 2.07 cups.
This illustrates the law of large numbers. As the sample size grows, the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) settles near the population mean \(\mu\). Symbolically:
\[n \to \infty \quad \Rightarrow \quad \bar{x} \to \mu\]
Although easiest to see with the mean, the law applies to many sample statistics: proportions, variances, correlations, and more.
Jacob Bernoulli first formalized the law of large numbers in 1713. Averaging over more observations does reduce what he called the “danger of wandering from one’s goal.”
In practice, any single sample statistic will differ somewhat from the population parameter. Even the sample of 10,000 in Figure 3.8 has a mean of 2.015 cups, not exactly 2.
The law of large numbers needs random sampling. \(\bar{x}\) settles near the mean of whatever population your sampling method actually reaches. Survey 10,000 people inside coffee shops and \(\bar{x}\) will settle, very precisely, on the average for coffee-shop customers, which is not the average for all adults.
A larger sample shrinks sampling error, the gap between a sample statistic and the population value that comes from seeing only a subset. It does nothing about bias, such as a sampling method that consistently reaches the wrong people. So a random sample of 100 adults can give a better estimate of the adult average than a sample of 10,000 coffee-shop customers. Its estimate varies more from sample to sample, but it converges on the right population mean.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.9 Sampling distributions
The law of large numbers tells us that with enough data, our sample mean will get close to the population mean. But in practice, we never have infinite data. We need a way to describe how the sample mean behaves with finite samples. The sampling distribution of the sample mean describes that behavior.

3.9.1 Sampling distribution of the sample mean

A sample mean is the average of the values in one sample.

A sampling distribution is the distribution of a statistic, such as the mean, across many samples of the same size \(n\).

The sampling distribution of the sample mean is the distribution of the means of many samples of size \(n\), as if the study were repeated many times.
The sampling distribution tells us how much the sample mean varies from sample to sample, and how close we can expect it to be to the population mean.
Three distributions come up in this section, and they are easy to confuse:










Distribution
What it contains
Center
Spread
Its shape




Population distribution
Every value in the population
\(\mu\)
\(\sigma\)
Whatever shape the population has


One sample
The \(n\) values you collected
\(\bar{x}\)
\(s\)
Roughly the population’s shape, with noise


Sampling distribution of the sample mean
One mean from each of many samples of size \(n\)
\(\mu\)
\(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\), the standard error
Close to normal once \(n\) is large enough



A bigger sample makes the second row look more like the first (Figure 3.8). It does not make your data look normal. A sample of 500 household electricity bills is still right-skewed, because the population of bills is. The central limit theorem, defined later in this chapter, is a statement about the third row only.


3.9.2 Building a sampling distribution step by step
We can build a sampling distribution in four steps:

Start with a distribution to sample from.

Draw repeated random samples of the same size \(n\).

Compute the mean of each sample.

Plot those means in a histogram.

For example, suppose we draw numbers from a uniform distribution on 1 to 10, where each whole number from 1 to 10 has the same probability, 0.1 (Figure 3.9).








Figure 3.9: A uniform distribution over the numbers 1 to 10. Each number has the same probability of being drawn, 0.1, so all ten bars are the same height.





Figure 3.10 shows three samples of 20 numbers drawn from this population. Each dot is one number drawn, and the lime-green dotted line marks that sample’s mean. The three samples look different from each other, and their means, given in the panel titles, differ too.








Figure 3.10: Three samples of 20 numbers each, drawn from the uniform distribution of the numbers 1 to 10. Each dot is one number drawn, and dots stack when a number was drawn more than once. The lime-green dotted line marks each sample’s mean.





If we repeat this 10,000 times and plot all the sample means, we get a close picture of the sampling distribution of the sample mean for samples of size 20.
This simulation uses two different numbers. The sample size, \(n = 20\), is how big each study is. The 10,000 is how many times we repeat the study. The spread of the histogram is set by \(n\). The 10,000 only controls how smooth the histogram looks. Drawing 100,000 samples of size 20 would give a smoother histogram of the same width.
Before you look. Each bar in Figure 3.11 counts sample means, and each mean comes from one sample of 20 numbers like those in Figure 3.10. The raw numbers are spread evenly from 1 to 10. Decide whether you expect the histogram of means to be flat like the population, and whether you expect the means to spread over the whole range from 1 to 10 or over a narrower range.








Figure 3.11: Sample means from 10,000 samples of size 20, drawn from the uniform distribution of numbers 1 to 10. The histogram centers on the expected value of 5.5, but individual samples scatter around it.





The histogram of means in Figure 3.11 is not flat. It is bell-shaped and centered on 5.5, the population mean. The means also spread over a much narrower range than the raw numbers. The middle 99% of them fall between 3.9 and 7.2, while the raw numbers run from 1 to 10. The histogram of sample means has its own shape and its own spread. The standard error, below, describes the spread, and the central limit theorem describes the shape.


3.9.3 Beyond the mean
Although we’ve focused on means, the same idea applies to any statistic: medians, standard deviations, maximum values, and so on. Each has its own sampling distribution, which describes how that statistic behaves across repeated samples. The sample mean is the most important case, because most of classical inference uses it. To illustrate, suppose we draw 10,000 samples of size \(n=50\) from the IQ population used later in this chapter, a normal distribution with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. For each sample we compute the mean, standard deviation, maximum, and median, then plot the histograms of these values (Figure 3.12).








Figure 3.12: Histograms of four statistics, each computed on 10,000 samples of size 50 from a normal population with mean 100 and standard deviation 15. The orange dashed line marks the population mean, 100, in the mean, maximum and median panels, and the population SD, 15, in the SD panel.





The mean and median panels center on 100. The maximum panel centers well above 100, at about 134, so the largest value in a sample is a poor estimate of the population mean. The SD panel, computed with R’s sd(), centers close to 15 at \(n = 50\). Figure 3.19, later in this chapter, shows that with small samples the SD computed by dividing by \(n\) falls well below 15 on average.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.10 The standard error
The law of large numbers gives a direction. As \(n\) grows, \(\bar{x}\) settles near \(\mu\). The standard error, named below, gives a size. For one fixed \(n\), it gives the spread of the sample means. Figure 3.13 shows both at once.
The distribution of sample means is the sampling distribution of the sample mean, defined earlier in the chapter. It also goes by the shorter name sampling distribution of the mean.
Figure 3.13 animates this idea with a normal population (orange curve) that has \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\), at four sample sizes. Each frame draws one new sample in every panel. The top row shows that sample’s values as gray points, with its mean as a lime-green dotted line. The bottom row collects the means of all the samples drawn so far, one green dot per sample. This chapter calls that collection the pile of sample means. Watch three things:

The spread of the values in one sample stays near \(\sigma = 1\) as \(n\) grows. The \(s\) shown in each panel bounces around 1. At \(n = 2\) it swings from below 0.1 to about 3 from frame to frame, and at \(n = 128\) it stays within about 0.15 of 1. A sample’s standard deviation estimates \(\sigma\), which is a fixed feature of the population, so collecting more values does not shrink it.
The spread of the sample means shrinks. The pile of means is wide at \(n = 2\) and narrow at \(n = 128\). The SE shown in each panel is \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\), the standard deviation this pile of means approaches as more samples are drawn. It halves each time \(n\) is multiplied by 4, from 0.71 at \(n = 2\) to 0.35, 0.18 and 0.09. The formula is explained below.
One sample’s mean gets closer to \(\mu\). The lime-green line jumps around at \(n = 2\) and stays near 0 at \(n = 128\). This is the law of large numbers from the previous section.

The pile is bell-shaped at every \(n\) here because the population itself is normal. The central limit theorem, below, describes the shape when the population is not normal.








Figure 3.13: One new sample per frame from a normal population (orange curve, \(\mu = 0\), \(\sigma = 1\)), at four sample sizes. Top row: the sample’s values (gray points) and its mean (lime-green dotted line). Bottom row: the means of all samples so far. The sample SD, \(s\), does not shrink as \(n\) grows, while the pile of means narrows.





So the sampling distribution of the mean is itself a distribution, with its own spread. The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of a sampling distribution. In this context, it is the standard error of the mean, written \(SE_{\bar{x}}\). The standard deviation describes how spread out the individual values are. The standard error describes how spread out the sample means are. Collecting more data does not shrink the standard deviation, but it does shrink the standard error.
Two facts about the sampling distribution of the mean hold at every sample size, for any population with a finite standard deviation:

Its mean equals the population mean, \(\mu\). This is what it means to call \(\bar{x}\) unbiased.
Its standard deviation, the standard error, equals the population \(\sigma\) divided by \(\sqrt{n}\):

\[SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
This is the standard error when \(\sigma\) is known. Usually it is not, and then the same standard error is estimated by \(s/\sqrt{n}\), as the end of this chapter shows. Both are written \(SE_{\bar{x}}\), so each time you compute one, note which SD went into it.
Neither fact needs the central limit theorem. Both come from how averages of independent values behave, and both hold even at \(n = 2\). The second fact is why the pile of means in Figure 3.13 narrows. Its spread is \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\), and \(\sqrt{n}\) grows with \(n\). The law of large numbers is about where one sample’s mean heads as \(n\) grows, and the central limit theorem is about the shape of the pile.
The law of large numbers follows from the standard error. Because \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) shrinks toward zero as \(n\) grows, a single sample’s \(\bar{x}\) becomes very likely to be close to \(\mu\). The formal argument uses Chebyshev’s inequality, but this is the idea we need.
The second fact also gives the width of Figure 3.11. The numbers 1 to 10 have mean 5.5. Their population variance is the average squared distance from 5.5, and with \(n = 20\) the formula gives the standard error:
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &= \frac{1}{10}\sum_{x=1}^{10}(x - 5.5)^2 = 82.5/10 = 8.25 \\[1.2ex]
\sigma &= \sqrt{8.25} = 2.87 \\[1.2ex]
SE_{\bar{x}} &= \sigma/\sqrt{n} = 2.87/\sqrt{20} = 2.87/4.47 = 0.64
\end{aligned}\]
The standard deviation of the 10,000 sample means in Figure 3.11 is 0.64, matching the formula.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.11 The central limit theorem
The central limit theorem (CLT) states a third fact about the sampling distribution, and the only one about shape:

As \(n\) grows, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal shape, no matter what shape the population has, as long as the population has a finite standard deviation.

The CLT is why the normal curve appears so often in statistics. It describes sample means even when the underlying data are skewed or flat. The full theorem is more general and has a complicated proof, but this is the part we need.
The next three figures show histograms of sample means drawn from populations with different shapes. These are distributions of sample means, not of individual observations.
In Figure 3.14, we are sampling from a normal distribution (orange line). The sampling distribution of the mean (green bars) is also normal.








Figure 3.14: Means of 10,000 samples of size 10 and of size 50 from a normal population (orange curve). The sample means are normal at both sample sizes, and narrower at n = 50.





Return to the uniform population of the numbers 1 to 10 from Figure 3.9. Figure 3.15 shows the means of 10,000 samples at each of two sample sizes, \(n = 10\) and \(n = 50\). The population is flat (orange line), but the sampling distribution of the mean (green bars) is bell-shaped at both sample sizes.








Figure 3.15: Means of 10,000 samples of size 10 and of size 50, drawn from the uniform distribution of the numbers 1 to 10 (orange line). Even though the population is flat, the distribution of sample means is approximately normal.





The exponential population in Figure 3.16 is right-skewed, with most values near 0 and a long right tail (orange curve).








Figure 3.16: Sampling distributions of the mean from a strongly right-skewed exponential population. At n = 10 the sample means are still somewhat right-skewed; at n = 50 they are close to normal and narrower.





At \(n = 10\) the sample means are still a little right-skewed. At \(n = 50\) their histogram is close to a bell shape.
Together, these figures show the central limit theorem at work. The sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal shape whether the population is normal, flat, or skewed. Its center and spread follow the two facts from before, at every sample size: mean \(\mu\) and standard error
\[SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.\]
This formula shows how sample size controls the precision of \(\bar{x}\), meaning how little \(\bar{x}\) varies from sample to sample. As \(n\) increases, the denominator grows and the SE falls. The SE falls with the square root of \(n\). Doubling \(n\) divides the SE by \(\sqrt{2} = 1.41\):
\[SE_\text{new} = SE/1.41 = 0.71 \times SE,\]
a cut of about 30%. Each further increase in sample size gives a smaller gain in precision. In Figure 3.13, going from \(n = 2\) to \(n = 8\), six more observations, cuts the SE from 0.71 to 0.35. Going from \(n = 32\) to \(n = 128\), 96 more observations, cuts it from 0.18 to 0.09.
The facts about sample means in this chapter fall into two groups: three facts about the pile of sample means, and the law of large numbers, which is about a single sample.
The pile of sample means is the means of every possible sample of size \(n\). It is theoretical. A simulation draws many samples (10,000 in this chapter) to approximate it. More draws make the histogram smoother, not narrower. Its width depends on \(\sigma\) and on \(n\), the size of each sample behind one \(\bar{x}\) in the pile, not on how many samples are drawn. For a random sample of \(n\) independent observations from a population with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), Table 3.5 describes the pile.



Table 3.5: The pile of sample means. Only the central limit theorem is about shape.










Question
Answer
Where you saw it




Where is the pile centered?
At \(\mu\), at every \(n\)
Figure 3.11, centered on 5.5


How spread out is the pile?
Its standard deviation is the standard error, \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\), at every \(n\)
Bottom row of Figure 3.13, and the SD of 0.64 in Figure 3.11


What shape is the pile?
Approximately normal when \(n\) is large enough (the central limit theorem). Normal at every \(n\) if the population is normal
Figure 3.15 and Figure 3.16






The law of large numbers says that as \(n\) grows, a sample’s statistics settle near the population’s values.

One sample’s \(\bar{x}\) settles near \(\mu\) (Figure 3.8, and the lime-green line in Figure 3.13). This follows from the standard error: \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) shrinks toward 0.
\(s\) settles near \(\sigma\). The spread of the values stays about the same size as \(n\) grows.
The sample’s shape settles on the population’s shape. The share of values in each range settles on the population’s share, so a sample’s histogram looks more like the population as \(n\) grows (Figure 3.8). Skewed data stay skewed. Only the pile of sample means becomes approximately normal.
This needs random sampling. With a biased method, each of these settles on the values of whatever population the method reaches, however large \(n\) is.


3.11.1 How large is large enough?
The CLT says the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normal as \(n\) grows. It does not say how fast. That depends on the shape of the population. The three populations simulated in this chapter show the range:







Population shape
What this chapter’s simulations show




Normal
Sample means are normal at every sample size (Figure 3.14)


Flat (uniform, the numbers 1 to 10)
Sample means are already bell-shaped at \(n = 10\) (Figure 3.15)


Strongly right-skewed (exponential)
Sample means are still right-skewed at \(n = 10\) and close to a bell shape by \(n = 50\) (Figure 3.16)



You will often see \(n \ge 30\) given as the sample size at which sample means become roughly normal. No single cutoff works for every population. The exponential example needs more than 30, and a population with a longer tail or extreme outliers needs more still.
The skew fades as \(n\) grows because each unusually large value gets averaged with more ordinary ones. The longer the tail, the more ordinary values it takes.
Later chapters use “once the sample is large enough” to mean a sample size from this table. With a small sample from a skewed population, the sample means may not be close to normal, and Chapter 6 comes back to this case.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.12 \(z\)-scores
A \(z\)-score is the number of standard deviations a value is above or below its mean. \(z\)-scores are useful for two reasons. Areas under the normal curve translate directly into probabilities. And by the CLT, many averages, such as sample means, are approximately normal, so \(z\)-scores give probabilities for those too.
First, recall the geometry of the normal curve. In Figure 3.17 we draw vertical lines at 0, ±1, ±2, and ±3 standard deviations for a standard normal (\(\mu=0,\sigma=1\)). The labels show familiar areas: about 34.1% between 0 and 1, 13.6% between 1 and 2, and so on. Altogether, about 68.3% of values lie between −1 and +1 SD.








Figure 3.17: A standard normal distribution. Vertical lines mark the mean and 1, 2 and 3 standard deviations on either side. Each label gives the proportion of the area between two adjacent lines, and the outermost labels give the area beyond 3 SD.





Those same proportions hold for any normal distribution, regardless of its mean or SD. In Figure 3.18 (with \(\mu=100,\ \sigma=25\)), the region from 100 to 125 (one SD above the mean) still contains about 34.1% of values.








Figure 3.18: A normal distribution with mean 100 and SD 25. The areas between the lines match Figure 3.17, so one SD on either side of the mean still covers about 68.3%.






3.12.1 What “standardized” means
Standardizing converts a raw score, the value as measured, into a \(z\)-score by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. \(z\)-scores are also called standardized scores.
Standardizing lets you compare values that come from distributions with different means and spreads, because a \(z\)-score’s unit is the standard deviation. A stream that usually runs at 12 °C, with an SD of 2 °C, reads 18 °C one afternoon. A city whose summer days average 25 °C, with an SD of 5 °C, has a 30 °C day.
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Stream: } z &= (18 - 12)/2 = 3 \\
\text{City: } z &= (30 - 25)/5 = 1
\end{aligned}\]
The city’s 30 °C is the larger number, but the stream’s 18 °C is the more unusual reading, and the \(z\)-scores of 3 and 1 show it.
There are two versions, depending on which mean and SD you have:
\[z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma} \qquad\qquad z=\frac{x-\bar{x}}{s}\]
The first uses the population mean and SD, when they are known. The second uses the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) and sample SD \(s\), which is the usual situation with real data. Keep each pair together: a population mean goes with a population SD, and a sample mean goes with a sample SD.
Interpretation is the same for both:

\(z=0\) is the mean
\(z=1\) is one SD above the mean
\(z=-2\) is two SDs below the mean



3.12.2 Calculating \(z\)-scores
Example: generate ten observations from a \(\text{Normal}(100, 25)\) distribution.
These ten scores can be standardized both ways. Using the known population values, \(z = (x - 100)/25\). Using only the sample itself, \(z = (x - \bar{x})/s\), with \(\bar{x} =\) 98.79 and \(s =\) 25.19:
