7.4.2 The chi-square test of independence
The chi-square test of independence asks whether two categorical variables measured on the same units are related. Suppose researchers classify 150 city blocks by land use and by whether each block’s peak summer surface temperature, measured from satellite images, topped 40°C. The data in this example are invented. Every block falls into exactly one cell of Figure 7.9. A cell is one combination of categories in the table, here one land use with one temperature outcome.








Figure 7.9: A test-of-independence design. Two categorical variables are crossed, and each cell holds the count of blocks that fell into that combination.





In that table, nobody assigned anything. The blocks already had their land use and their summer temperatures before the researchers looked, and the cells count how many turned out each way. That makes this an observational design. Each block’s temperature has been reduced to a yes or no, so the cells hold counts of blocks rather than temperatures.

Alternative (\(H_a\)): land use and topping 40°C are related, so the rate differs between land uses.

Assumption. Same rule as goodness-of-fit: expected counts should generally be 5 or more in every cell of the table. Unlike the goodness-of-fit test, where expected counts came from a stated proportion (25% per zone), the expected counts here come from the table’s own row and column totals. In both chi-square tests, the expected count is the count \(H_0\) predicts. In this test \(H_0\) is independence. If land use and temperature are unrelated, parkland blocks should make up the same share of the 87 blocks that did not top 40°C as they do of all 150 blocks, which is \(\frac{50}{150}\), or one third. That gives an expected count of \(87 \times \frac{50}{150} = 29\) for Parkland/No. In general, the expected count for a cell is \(\frac{\text{row total} \times \text{column total}}{\text{grand total}}\).

title: 7  Nonparametric and Categorical Data
text:
7.5 Chapter Summary
Why it matters. Environmental data often fail the assumptions a \(t\)-test needs. Samples can be small, distributions can be skewed, and some outcomes are counts in categories instead of measurements. This chapter covers the tests for those cases and how to tell when you need one. Chapter 8 compares three or more groups, with the Kruskal-Wallis test as its rank-based option.
Core ideas

Rank-based tests trade power for weaker assumptions. The Wilcoxon signed-rank and Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon tests ask the same questions as the one-sample or paired and the independent-samples \(t\)-tests, but work from ranks instead of raw magnitudes.
The sign test uses even less of the data. It looks only at the direction of each difference. On the same restoration data, the \(t\)-test, signed-rank test, and sign test gave \(p\)-values of 0.026, 0.057 and 0.508, because each one uses less of the data than the last.
Nonparametric tests have their own assumptions. The signed-rank test assumes the differences are symmetric about their median. Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon assumes the two distributions have the same shape, which is not the same as equal variance. State the assumption you are actually making.
Check assumptions before you run a test. Choosing the test after seeing its result lets the result decide the test. Both worked examples ran the parametric test first only to show how its \(p\)-value can mislead when an assumption fails.
Categorical data needs a different tool entirely. The chi-square tests handle counts: goodness-of-fit asks whether one variable’s counts match an expected pattern, and the test of independence asks whether two categorical variables are related.
The testing logic never changes. State \(H_0\) and \(H_a\), compute a statistic, and ask how surprising that statistic would be if \(H_0\) were true. Only the statistic and its null distribution differ from test to test.





Cochran, W. G. 1954. “The \(\chi^{2}\) Test of Goodness of Fit.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 23: 315–45. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177729380.


Larntz, K. 1978. “Small-Sample Comparisons of Exact Levels for Chi-Squared Goodness-of-Fit Statistics.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 73: 253–63. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1978.10481567.


Mann, H. B., and D. R. Whitney. 1947. “On a Test of Whether One of Two Random Variables Is Stochastically Larger Than the Other.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 18 (1): 50–60.


Pearson, K. 1900. “On the Criterion That a Given System of Deviations from the Probable in the Case of a Correlated System of Variables Is Such That It Can Be Reasonably Supposed to Have Arisen from Random Sampling.” Philosophical Magazine 50: 157–75.


Wilcoxon, Frank. 1945. “Individual Comparisons by Ranking Methods.” Biometrics Bulletin 1 (6): 80–83.

title: 8  Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
8.1 ANOVA is analysis of variance
Download this chapter (PDF)
ANOVA stands for analysis of variance. It tests whether the means of three or more groups differ by more than chance alone would produce. Chapters 6 and 7 compared two groups, and with two groups a \(t\)-test answers this question. Environmental studies often compare more than two, such as several sites, treatments, or time periods, and ANOVA extends the \(t\)-test’s logic to them.
This chapter starts with why running a \(t\)-test for every pair of groups goes wrong, and with the single question ANOVA asks instead. It then builds ANOVA’s test statistic, \(F\), as a ratio, shows what values \(F\) takes when there are no real differences, and computes \(F\) by hand for a small example. The full workflow on one example follows, through post-hoc comparisons and a rank-based (nonparametric) alternative, and the chapter ends with repeated-measures ANOVA.

title: 8  Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
NoteNote: Where ANOVA came from



Sir Ronald Fisher invented the ANOVA (Salsburg 2001) and wanted to publish it in the journal Biometrika. The editor at the time was Karl Pearson, of Pearson’s \(r\), and the two men disliked each other, so Pearson refused to publish the new test. Fisher published it in the Journal of Agricultural Science instead. The feud carried into the next generation. Years later, Karl Pearson’s son Egon Pearson, working with Jerzy Neyman, revamped Fisher’s ideas and re-cast them into what we now call null vs. alternative hypothesis testing. Fisher objected to that too.



8.1.1 Why not run multiple \(t\)-tests?
With three groups, A, B and C, there are three possible pairwise differences:

Group A vs. Group B
Group A vs. Group C
Group B vs. Group C

We could test each with a separate \(t\)-test, asking whether that pair’s means differ significantly.
The problem is that every test carries its own 5% chance of a false positive (a Type I error, Chapter 5), and those chances accumulate across tests. This follows from the independence multiplication rule (Section 3.5.2). Each test has a \(1-\alpha = 0.95\) chance of avoiding a false positive. If the \(m\) tests are independent, the chance that all of them avoid one is 0.95 multiplied by itself \(m\) times, or \((1-\alpha)^m\). The chance of at least one false positive is 1 minus that, so for \(m\) independent tests at \(\alpha = 0.05\),
\[P(\text{at least one false positive}) = 1-(1-\alpha)^m.\]
With three groups, that’s three tests. The familywise error rate is the chance of at least one false positive across a set of tests. For three tests it is 14%, compared with 5% for a single test:
\[1-(1-0.05)^3 = 0.14.\]
With \(k\) groups there are \(k(k-1)/2\) pairs to compare, so the number of tests grows faster than the number of groups. Four groups give \(4 \times 3/2 = 6\) tests, and five groups give \(5 \times 4/2 = 10\) (Table 8.1).



Table 8.1: Familywise error rate for independent tests at \(\alpha = 0.05\).










Number of groups (\(k\))
Pairwise tests (\(m\))
Familywise error rate




3

\(1-0.95^3=0.14\)

Even with only five groups, there’s a 40% chance of turning up at least one “significant” difference somewhere purely by chance, even if every population mean is identical. Figure 8.1 shows how the chance of at least one false positive grows as the number of independent \(t\)-tests grows.








Figure 8.1: Familywise Type I error rate as the number of independent \(t\)-tests increases, at \(\alpha = 0.05\) per test.





Pairwise \(t\)-tests that share a group are not fully independent, so for pairwise comparisons these rates run a little high. Simulating three groups of 10 with no real differences gives about 12% for three pairwise tests, 20% for four groups, and 29% for five. The rate still climbs quickly as groups are added.
ANOVA solves this by replacing the separate \(t\)-tests with one test, so the chance of a false positive stays at \(\alpha\).


8.1.2 ANOVA is an omnibus test
An omnibus test is a single test that covers several comparisons at once, and ANOVA is one. Instead of the three pairwise \(t\)-tests listed above, ANOVA asks one more general question about all three means:

Null (\(H_0\)): no differences anywhere, \(\mu_A=\mu_B=\mu_C\).
Alternative (\(H_a\)): a difference somewhere, in one of four patterns:

\(\mu_A\neq \mu_B=\mu_C\) (A differs)
\(\mu_B\neq \mu_A=\mu_C\) (B differs)
\(\mu_C\neq \mu_A=\mu_B\) (C differs)
\(\mu_A\neq \mu_B\), \(\mu_B\neq \mu_C\), and \(\mu_A\neq \mu_C\) (all three differ)


A large \(p\)-value means we don’t reject the hypothesis of no differences. Because the differences between the sample means could easily be due to chance, we have no evidence that the three population means differ. A small \(p\)-value (below \(\alpha\)) means we reject that hypothesis and conclude at least one group mean differs from the others. The omnibus test tells us whether the means differ, and a separate step tells us which ones.


8.1.3 Kinds of ANOVA
As with the \(t\)-test, different research designs call for different kinds of ANOVA.
The one-way ANOVA is the simplest version of the test. In ANOVA an independent variable is called a factor, and the groups it defines are its levels. A one-way ANOVA has one factor with two or more levels.
Table 8.2 sets the one-way ANOVA beside the two other kinds of ANOVA this book covers.

title: 8  Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
8.2 The \(F\) ratio
ANOVA’s test statistic is \(F\), named for Fisher, who invented ANOVA. Like \(z\) and \(t\), it divides a measure of effect by the variation that sampling error alone would produce (Chapter 4).
\[F = \frac{\text{measure of effect}}{\text{measure of error}}\]
The \(t\)-test puts a difference between two means over its standard error. \(F\) uses variances for both parts. It divides the variation between groups (how far the group means are from one another) by the variation within groups (how far individual scores are from their own group’s mean).
\[F = \frac{\text{Variation between groups}}{\text{Variation within groups}}\]
When the two are about the same size, \(F \approx 1\), and the group means differ no more than ordinary sampling noise would make them. When the between-group variation is much larger than the within-group variation, \(F\) climbs well above 1, which is evidence that the groups differ. When the between-group variation is smaller, \(F\) drops below 1. An \(F\) of 5 means the group means vary five times as much as within-group noise alone would make them vary, and an \(F\) of 0.6 means they vary less than that noise alone would typically produce. Both parts of \(F\) are variances, so “five times as much” compares squared distances, not raw distances.
With two groups, \(F\) is exactly the square of the pooled \(t\) (Section 6.5), \(t^2 = F\), which is why the two tests give the same \(p\)-value.
Figure 8.2 shows both situations with the same noise. Both panels are simulated, so we know the population means behind them. In the left panel all three population means are 10, so any differences among the group means are chance. In the right panel the population means are 10, 12.2 and 15. The dashed line in each panel is the grand mean, the mean of all the scores across every group.








Figure 8.2: Simulated scores with the same within-group noise. Left: all three population means are 10, so there are no real differences. Right: the population means are 10, 12.2 and 15. Three groups of 12; small points are individual scores, large dots are group means, bars are 95% confidence intervals. The blue bracket marks within-group variation, the spread of Group A’s scores. The orange arrows mark between-group variation, each group mean’s distance from the grand mean (dashed line).





The within-group variation is the same in both panels. Group A’s scores span about 9 units, the length of the blue bracket. In the “No real differences” panel (left), the three group means are all within about half a unit of the grand mean, so the between-group variation is small compared with the within-group variation, and \(F\) = 0.64. In the “Real differences” panel (right), Group C’s mean is about 3 units above the grand mean, and \(F\) = 21.4. The within-group variation did not change, so the larger \(F\) comes entirely from the larger between-group variation.

title: 8  Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
8.3 \(F\) when \(H_0\) is true
Before computing \(F\) by hand, we need to know what values it takes when the null hypothesis is true, because that is what an observed \(F\) is compared against. The \(p\)-value for \(F\) means the same thing as for every other test we’ve covered. It is the probability of an \(F\) this large or larger if the null hypothesis (no real group differences) were true.
Since \(F\) is a sample statistic, we can find out how it behaves the same way we did for \(t\), by simulating it many times under the null. Consider a monitoring study with three site types (A, B, C) and 10 sampling plots per type, 30 in all, measuring species abundance at each plot. All 30 plots are drawn from one null population distribution (population mean \(\mu = 100\), \(\sigma = 10\)), so site type has no real effect, and any differences between the group means come from sampling error alone. We repeat this study 10,000 times and compute \(F\) each time. The histogram of those 10,000 \(F\)-values, in Figure 8.3, is the null distribution of \(F\) for this design. The null population distribution describes individual abundance scores. The null distribution of \(F\) describes the \(F\)-values, one per experiment.
Before you look. Each bar in Figure 8.3 counts \(F\)-values from these null studies. Decide whether most of them will fall near 0, near 1, or well above 1.








Figure 8.3: A simulation of 10,000 studies from a null population distribution with no group differences. The histogram shows the 10,000 \(F\)-values, one per study, all produced by sampling error alone. The blue dot-dash curve is the \(F\) distribution with 2 and 27 degrees of freedom. The red line is the critical value at \(\alpha = 0.05\), and the shaded bars beyond it hold 5% of the \(F\)-values.





Most simulated \(F\)-values here fall near or below 1, because under the null the numerator and denominator of \(F\) estimate the same thing. All 30 plots come from one null population distribution with \(\sigma = 10\). The denominator of \(F\), the within-group variation, estimates \(\sigma^2\) from the spread of scores inside each group. The numerator, the between-group variation, estimates the same \(\sigma^2\) from how far the group means stray from the grand mean, since with no real effect, sampling variation is the only thing moving them. Two estimates of one variance give a ratio near 1. When the population means really differ, the numerator picks up those differences on top of \(\sigma^2\), and \(F\) grows. (Section 8.4 shows how each part is computed.)
The \(F\) of 5 from Section 8.2 is rare under the null. Values that large occur in about 1% of the simulations.
The null distribution of \(F\) never goes below 0, because \(F\) is a ratio of two variances and variances can’t be negative. It is right-skewed.
From simulation to the \(F\) distribution. The blue dot-dash curve over the histogram is the \(F\) distribution, the theoretical distribution of \(F\) when the null hypothesis is true. Its shape is set by two degrees of freedom, the numerator \(df\) (\(k - 1 = 2\) for the three site types) and the denominator \(df\) (\(N - k = 30 - 3 = 27\), where \(N\) is the total number of plots). It is worked out from theory with no simulation, and it follows the histogram closely, so from here on we use the curve. Software does the same, and the \(p\)-value it reports for \(F\) comes from the \(F\) distribution for the design’s two \(df\)s.

8.3.1 Making decisions
To decide whether a real study’s \(F\) is too large to be explained by chance:

Set \(\alpha = 0.05\).
Find the critical value of \(F\) for the design’s two \(df\)s (in R, qf(0.95, 2, 27)), the red line in Figure 8.3.
Reject \(H_0\) if the observed \(F\) is at or beyond it.

For 2 and 27 degrees of freedom the critical value is 3.35, and only 5% of the \(F\) distribution lies at or beyond it. The simulation agrees, with 4.8% of the 10,000 simulated \(F\)-values at or beyond 3.35. The \(F\)-test has one critical value, in the upper tail. Differences among the means in any direction make the numerator of \(F\) larger, so they all push \(F\) up, and a small \(F\) is consistent with \(H_0\).
If we ran the same design for real (30 plots, 10 per site type), an observed \(F\) at or beyond 3.35 would lead us to reject \(H_0\) and conclude that mean abundance differs among site types. The critical value and the \(p\)-value give the same decision. \(F\) is at or beyond the critical value exactly when its \(p\)-value is at or below \(\alpha\).


8.3.2 What group means look like when \(F\) exceeds the critical value
The 10,000 simulated studies kept only each \(F\)-value, not the group means behind it. To see those means, we reran the same null simulation and kept the first 10 studies with \(F > 3.35\), shown in Figure 8.4. Every one of them was still drawn from the same null population distribution, with no real group differences. Rejecting the null whenever \(F\) clears 3.35 is the right long-run decision rule, but every one of these particular simulations would be a Type I error if we did.








Figure 8.4: Group means from 10 null simulations in which \(F\) exceeded the critical value. Error bars are 95% confidence intervals. Every one of them is a Type I error.





In four of the ten panels in Figure 8.4, at least one pair of 95% confidence intervals doesn’t overlap, which looks like a convincing real difference. In the others, the means are still spread out enough for \(F\) to clear the critical value. When chance produces a pattern like these, the \(F\)-value is large and the \(p\)-value is small, so in the output a Type I error looks exactly like a real effect.
Studies like these ten are the 5% the critical value allows. One \(F\)-test keeps that chance at 5% for the whole set of groups, where three separate pairwise \(t\)-tests would have raised it to about 12%. The same risk returns after a significant \(F\), when post-hoc comparisons test each pair of groups, and that is why those comparisons are adjusted (Section 8.5.4).

title: 8  Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
8.4 Computing \(F\) by hand
ANOVA splits the total variation in the data into two sources: variation between groups, which group membership can explain, and variation within groups, which it can’t. If we can measure those two parts separately, we can turn them into a ratio and get an \(F\)-value.
\[\text{Total variation} = \text{Variation between groups} + \text{Variation within groups}\]
To make that precise we need an actual measure of variation. As in Chapter 2, the measure is the sum of squares.
\[SS_\text{Total} = SS_\text{Between} + SS_\text{Within}\]
The next sections compute each piece for a small example with nine scores. We find \(SS_\text{Total}\) and \(SS_\text{Between}\), get \(SS_\text{Within}\) by subtraction, and check it directly. Then we divide each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom, take the ratio to get \(F\), and compare it with its critical value.

8.4.1 Nine litter counts
Suppose a city counts the pieces of litter along nine stretches of sidewalk, three in each of three neighborhoods, A, B, and C. The counts are invented. Each count is one score. Table 8.3 lists them by neighborhood, with each neighborhood’s mean and the grand mean, the mean of all nine scores.

The deviations sum to zero, because the mean is the balancing point of the data, so their sum can’t measure spread. Squaring turns every deviation positive and, as a side effect, weights larger deviations more heavily.
Adding up the squared deviations gives the sum of squares (SS) from Table 2.3. Writing \(Y_{ij}\) for score \(i\) in group \(j\) and \(\bar{Y}_\text{grand}\) for the grand mean,
\[SS_\text{Total} = \sum (Y_{ij} - \bar{Y}_\text{grand})^2 = 302.\]
That is the first piece of the partition:
\[SS_\text{Total} = SS_\text{Between} + SS_\text{Within}, \qquad 302 = SS_\text{Between} + SS_\text{Within}.\]
We only need to compute one of the two remaining pieces directly. The other follows by subtraction.


8.4.3 SS Between
\(SS_\text{Total}\) captured all of the variation in the data. \(SS_\text{Between}\) is the part of the total variation that group membership can explain. It measures how far each group’s mean is from the grand mean.
To find it, replace every score with its own group’s mean (Table 8.5), then square and sum each group mean’s distance from the grand mean. Writing \(\bar{Y}_j\) for the mean of group \(j\) and \(n_j\) for its number of scores,
\[SS_\text{Between} = \sum_j n_j(\bar{Y}_j - \bar{Y}_\text{grand})^2.\]
The \(n_j\) is there because every score in group \(j\) is replaced by the same group mean, so each group’s squared distance counts once per score. Here every group has 3 scores. With unequal groups, larger groups count more.

The fourth column is the difference between each score and its own group mean, and the last column squares it. Summing the last column gives \(SS_\text{Within} = 230\), the same value we got by subtraction.
\(SS_\text{Within}\) has several other names. It is also called the error sum of squares, since it is the variation left over after group membership has explained what it can. R labels its row Residuals. In the next sections we divide it by its degrees of freedom to get \(MS_\text{Within}\), which some articles report as \(MSE\) (mean squared error).


8.4.5 Degrees of freedom
Degrees of freedom work the same way here as for the \(t\)-test. Every time we estimate something from the data, we use up a degree of freedom.
\(df_\text{Between} = k-1\), where \(k\) is the number of groups. With \(k=3\), \(df_\text{Between}=3-1=2\). Once we fix the grand mean, two of the three group means are free to be anything, but the third is determined by the other two.
\(df_\text{Within} = N-k\), where \(N\) is the total number of scores. With \(N=9\) and \(k=3\), \(df_\text{Within}=9-3=6\). Estimating the 3 group means uses up 3 degrees of freedom, one per group. Within each group, the deviations from the group mean must sum to zero, so only 2 of a group’s 3 deviations are free to vary. Three groups with 2 free deviations each give \(df_\text{Within} = 6\).
\(df_\text{Total} = N-1\), and it splits the same way the sums of squares do: \(df_\text{Total} = df_\text{Between} + df_\text{Within}\), here \(8 = 2 + 6\).


8.4.6 Mean squares
We’re building toward \(F=\dfrac{\text{measure of effect}}{\text{measure of error}}\), and the first idea is to divide \(SS_\text{Between}\) by \(SS_\text{Within}\) directly. The problem is that each sum of squares grows with the number of free pieces that go into it, its degrees of freedom. \(SS_\text{Between}\) comes from 3 group means, which have 2 degrees of freedom, and \(SS_\text{Within}\) comes from 9 deviations with 6 degrees of freedom. Even with no real differences, \(SS_\text{Within}\) would tend to be about three times as large as \(SS_\text{Between}\) for that reason alone. Dividing each one by its degrees of freedom turns it into an average, and two averages can be compared directly.
A mean square is a sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom. We divide by degrees of freedom rather than by \(n\), because each group mean we estimate uses up a degree of freedom, as the previous section showed.
\[MS_\text{Between} = \frac{SS_\text{Between}}{df_\text{Between}} = \frac{72}{2} = 36\]
\[MS_\text{Within} = \frac{SS_\text{Within}}{df_\text{Within}} = \frac{230}{6} = 38.33\]
Both are variances. \(MS_\text{Within}\) measures how much individual scores vary around their own group’s mean. \(MS_\text{Between}\) measures how much the group means vary, multiplied by the number of scores per group. Here the group means 11, 5 and 5 have variance
\[\frac{(11-7)^2 + (5-7)^2 + (5-7)^2}{3-1} = \frac{24}{2} = 12,\]
and \(3 \times 12 = 36\), which is \(MS_\text{Between}\). The multiplication is needed because a mean of \(n\) scores varies less than a single score does. The variance of a mean is \(\sigma^2/n\), the squared standard error from Section 3.10. Multiplying by \(n\) puts \(MS_\text{Between}\) on the same scale as \(MS_\text{Within}\).


8.4.7 Calculate \(F\)
With \(MS_\text{Between}\) and \(MS_\text{Within}\) in hand, \(F\) is their ratio:
\[F = \frac{MS_\text{Between}}{MS_\text{Within}} = \frac{36}{38.33} = 0.94\]

An ANOVA table lists the sums of squares, degrees of freedom, mean squares, and \(F\) for each source of variation. Table 8.7 gives the formulas, and Table 8.8 fills them in for the toy data.

title: 8  Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
8.5 The full ANOVA workflow
In practice, software computes the ANOVA table. We computed one by hand so that each number in the table has a meaning when we read it.
The following example applies the full ANOVA workflow, from descriptive summaries through the omnibus \(F\) test to post-hoc comparisons, to a salamander study.

8.5.1 Salamander abundance across forest types
Plethodontid salamanders are sensitive indicators of forest condition, because they depend on moist microhabitats, abundant coarse woody debris, and stable soil temperatures, all features that decline with forest disturbance. A field ecologist surveys salamander abundance across three forest types, laid out in Figure 8.6. The counts in this example are invented. We built them so that old-growth plots average about 14 salamanders, secondary forest about 7, and managed plantation about 5, with 8 plots of each type.








Figure 8.6: The salamander study as a design schematic. Structurally this is the two-group design from Chapters 4 and 6 with one more box added.





More groups mean more pairwise comparisons, which raises the familywise error rate from the start of the chapter.
The hypotheses are:

Null (\(H_0\)): mean salamander abundance is the same in all three forest types, \(\mu_\text{Old-growth} = \mu_\text{Secondary} = \mu_\text{Managed}\).
Alternative (\(H_a\)): at least one forest type’s mean differs.









Figure 8.7: Mean salamander abundance (individuals per plot) across three forest types. Points show individual plot counts, and error bars show 95% confidence intervals.





The bar graph shows a gradient. Old-growth plots have the highest mean abundance, managed plantations the lowest, and secondary forest is in between. The individual plot counts (dots) spread widely within each forest type. Old-growth plots range from 10 to 19 salamanders and secondary plots from 3 to 13, so even where a real difference exists, individual plots from different forest types overlap.


8.5.2 Checking ANOVA’s assumptions
Before running the ANOVA, check whether its assumptions hold. Section 6.3.5 introduced independence as the assumption every test in this book shares, so we do not list it again here. ANOVA adds two assumptions of its own.
The first is homogeneity of variance, which means the groups have roughly equal spread around their own means. The second is approximately normal residuals. In ANOVA the model predicts each score with its group mean, so a residual is the score minus its group mean, the same idea as the residuals in Figure 2.7. Here each residual is a plot’s count minus its forest type’s mean, the same deviations that make up \(SS_\text{Within}\), and the residuals should be roughly bell-shaped.
Both matter because the \(F\)-test pools the within-group spread of every group into one error variance, \(MS_\text{Within}\), and then compares \(F\) to a null distribution that assumes normal residuals. Pooling only makes sense when the groups have similar spread.
Levene’s test (Levene 1960; Brown and Forsythe 1974) checks homogeneity of variance. Its null hypothesis is that every group has the same variance, so a small \(p\)-value is evidence that the spreads differ. It reports its own \(F\) statistic, separate from the ANOVA’s \(F\). The Shapiro-Wilk test from Section 6.3.5 checks normality, here applied to the residuals.

car::leveneTest(abundance ~ forest_type, data = salamander_df)

The residuals come from the fitted model, so we fit the ANOVA first and set its table aside until the checks are done.

aov_out <- aov(abundance ~ forest_type, data = salamander_df)
shapiro.test(residuals(aov_out))




Shapiro-Wilk test on ANOVA residuals.


Statistic (W)
p




0.93
0.078





Levene’s test gives \(F(2, 21) = 0.52\), \(p = 0.599\), so there is no evidence of unequal variance across forest types. The Shapiro-Wilk test (Shapiro and Wilk 1965) on the model’s residuals gives \(W = 0.93\), \(p = 0.078\), so there is no evidence against normality either. Both checks agree with the individual plots in Figure 8.7, which show similar spread across groups and no outliers far from the rest.
Formal assumption tests are evidence, not a gate. Section 6.3.5 made this point about Shapiro-Wilk, and it holds for Levene’s test too. It’s tempting to treat Levene’s test as a strict gate, where significant means “stop” and not significant means “proceed.” With a small sample (exactly when a violated assumption matters most), these tests have low power and will often say “no problem” even when there is one. With a very large sample (where ANOVA is fairly robust to mild violations anyway), they have high power and will flag trivial differences as “significant.” Look at the data too, as we did with Figure 8.7 above.
In practice, one-way ANOVA’s \(p\)-values stay close to correct under mild departures from these assumptions, especially when the design is balanced, with the same number of observations in every group, as here (8 plots per forest type). Be most cautious when small, unbalanced samples come with visibly skewed data or very different spreads. For very different spreads, use Welch’s ANOVA, and for skewed residuals in a small or unbalanced sample, use the Kruskal-Wallis test. Both are described below.
Table 8.9 lists each assumption, how to check it, and what to use if it fails.

Table 8.10 gives the result. With 3 forest types and 24 plots, the degrees of freedom are \(3 - 1 = 2\) and \(24 - 3 = 21\), and the critical value at \(\alpha = 0.05\) is 3.47, a little higher than the 3.35 for 30 plots because the error term has fewer degrees of freedom. Our \(F\) of 14.60 is more than four times that cutoff. Values this large arise by chance less than 0.1% of the time, so we reject the null hypothesis that all three group means are equal.


8.5.3 Effect size: eta-squared
The \(F\)-test answers whether the group means differ by more than chance would produce. It says nothing about how much of the variation in salamander abundance forest type explains. Chapter 5 made the same distinction, where \(p\) told us whether a difference was detectable and the effect size told us how large it was, in the study’s units or, with Cohen’s \(d\), in standard deviations. ANOVA adds a third kind, the share of the total variation that the groups explain.
ANOVA’s effect size is eta-squared (\(\eta^2\)), and we already computed both of its ingredients when we partitioned the sums of squares:
\[\eta^2 = \frac{SS_\text{Between}}{SS_\text{Total}} = \frac{SS_\text{Between}}{SS_\text{Between} + SS_\text{Within}}\]
\(SS_\text{Between}\) is the variation the group means explain and \(SS_\text{Total}\) is all the variation there is. So \(\eta^2\) is the proportion of the total variation in the response that the factor explains. It runs from 0 to 1.




Table 8.11: Eta-squared for the effect of forest type on salamander abundance.






SS Between
SS Within
SS Total
Eta-squared




312.58
224.75
537.33
0.582








Here \(\eta^2 = 0.58\) (Table 8.11), so forest type explains about 58% of the variation in salamander abundance across these 24 plots. The remaining 42% is within-group variation, the plot-to-plot differences that forest type alone cannot explain.
Regression (Chapter 9, the next chapter) uses the same quantity under the name \(R^2\). It also divides the total variation into a part the model explains and a part it leaves over, and reports the explained part as a proportion of the total.
Interpreting the number. Cohen’s conventional benchmarks are \(\eta^2 = 0.01\) (small), \(0.06\) (medium), and \(0.14\) (large), so 0.58 is a large effect by these benchmarks. Treat those cutoffs as rough orientation. What counts as a large effect depends on the system you are studying. An \(\eta^2\) of 0.10 would be unremarkable in a controlled greenhouse experiment and notable in a field survey where dozens of uncontrolled factors also drive the response.
\(p\) depends on sample size, and \(\eta^2\) does not. Survey enough plots and a difference of half a salamander per plot will clear \(p < 0.05\) while explaining almost none of the variation. Reporting both keeps a statistically detectable result from being mistaken for an ecologically meaningful one.


8.5.4 Post-hoc comparisons with Tukey HSD
The omnibus \(F\) test tells us that at least one group mean differs, but not which pairs, and the ANOVA table does not report the group means at all. Post-hoc comparisons are tests run after a significant omnibus test to find which pairs of groups differ. This is a different use of “post-hoc” from post-hoc power (Section 5.4.4). To identify which forest types differ, we use Tukey’s Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) test (Tukey 1949). Tukey HSD compares every pair of groups while keeping the familywise error rate across all of the comparisons at \(\alpha\), so it is the standard choice after a significant ANOVA.

TukeyHSD(aov_out)

Reading Table 8.12, column by column. Each row is one pairwise comparison, and there are three of them because three groups make three pairs.

diff is the difference in group means, computed as the first group in the row label minus the second: Secondary-Old-growth is secondary minus old-growth.
lwr and upr are the lower and upper bounds of the 95% confidence interval for that difference.
p adj is the \(p\)-value after adjusting for the fact that you are making three comparisons at once. Because of this adjustment, the chance of at least one false positive across all three comparisons stays at 5%, compared with about 12% for three unadjusted pairwise tests.

Watch the sign. The row Secondary-Old-growth has a diff of \(-6.88\), and that negative sign does not mean secondary forest has more salamanders. It means secondary minus old-growth is negative, so old-growth is the higher of the two, by 6.88 individuals per plot. Always translate the sign back into a sentence naming which group is larger before you write anything down.
The confidence interval and the \(p\)-value say the same thing. A pair differs significantly at \(\alpha = 0.05\) exactly when its 95% interval excludes zero. Check both columns against each other as a habit: Secondary-Old-growth runs from \(-11.00\) to \(-2.75\), entirely below zero, and its \(p\) is 0.001. Managed-Secondary runs from \(-5.50\) to \(2.75\), straddling zero, and its \(p\) is 0.683. If they seem not to agree, reread that row.
So the three comparisons give:

Old-growth vs. Secondary. Old-growth is higher by 6.88 individuals/plot, \(p = 0.001\), a significant difference.
Old-growth vs. Managed. Old-growth is higher by 8.25 individuals/plot, \(p < 0.001\), a significant difference.
Secondary vs. Managed. They differ by 1.37 individuals/plot, \(p = 0.683\), not a significant difference.

A non-significant difference is one the test could not detect. Secondary and managed plantation differ by 1.37 salamanders per plot in this sample. The test says that with eight plots per group, we cannot distinguish it from sampling noise. A larger study might well separate them. Report it as “we did not detect a difference,” never as “there is no difference.”
Compact letter display. A compact letter display summarizes post-hoc results with a letter above each group. With more than three groups, a list of pairwise sentences gets long, so this is the usual summary. Groups that share a letter were not significantly different, and groups that share no letter were. Figure 8.8 puts the salamander results in that form.








Figure 8.8: Mean salamander abundance with Tukey letters. Error bars show 95% confidence intervals.





Old-growth gets its own letter because it differs from both of the others. Secondary and managed share a letter because the test could not separate them. Sometimes a group carries two letters, written “ab”. Suppose group 1 is labeled “a” and group 3 is labeled “b” because those two differ significantly. Group 2 has a mean between them. If group 2 does not differ significantly from group 1 or from group 3, it shares a letter with each, so it is labeled “ab”.
We built a difference of about 2 salamanders per plot between secondary forest and managed plantation into these invented counts, and the test could not detect it with 8 plots of each type.






ImportantResults reporting: one-way ANOVA



Report the direction in plain language, the test statistic with both degrees of freedom, \(p\), and the effect size, then which groups the post-hoc comparisons separated.

Salamander abundance differed significantly among forest types, \(F(2, 21) = 14.60\), \(p < 0.001\), \(\eta^2 = 0.58\). Tukey HSD comparisons showed more salamanders in old-growth plots than in secondary forest, by 6.88 per plot, 95% CI [2.75, 11.00], \(p = 0.001\), and than in managed plantation, by 8.25 per plot, 95% CI [4.13, 12.37], \(p < 0.001\). Secondary forest and managed plantation did not differ significantly, \(p = 0.683\).

8.5.5 Nonparametric alternative: the Kruskal-Wallis test
Our assumption checks above came back clean, so the ANOVA result stands as-is. Suppose instead the groups had visibly unequal spread. Then Welch’s ANOVA (oneway.test() in R) compares the means without assuming equal variances, the same fix Welch’s \(t\)-test makes (Table 6.4). If the residuals were clearly skewed in a small or unbalanced sample, the Kruskal-Wallis test (Kruskal and Wallis 1952) is the rank-based, nonparametric alternative to one-way ANOVA. It has the same relationship to ANOVA that the Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test has to the independent-samples \(t\)-test.
How it works, conceptually. Rank every observation across all groups together, from smallest to largest, ignoring group membership. Then check whether the average rank differs more across groups than chance alone would produce. If abundance differs among forest types, one group’s observations should occupy systematically higher or lower ranks than the others. In the salamander data, the old-growth plots have a mean rank of 19.7 out of 24, against 10.1 for secondary and 7.8 for managed. If forest type had no effect, all three mean ranks would be close to 12.5, the middle of 1 to 24.
Its assumption. Kruskal-Wallis assumes the groups’ distributions have roughly the same shape, and it does not require normality. When the shapes match, a significant result means the groups differ in location, meaning where the center of each distribution is, measured by the median, as with the Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test. If the shapes differ a lot, a significant result tells you the groups differ, but not whether that difference is in location, spread, or shape.

kruskal.test(abundance ~ forest_type, data = salamander_df)

R reports the Kruskal-Wallis statistic as \(\chi^2\) because, when the null hypothesis is true, it approximately follows a chi-square distribution with \(k - 1 = 2\) degrees of freedom. Here \(\chi^2(2) = 13.09\), \(p = 0.001\), a significant result and the same conclusion as the ANOVA (\(F(2, 21) = 14.60\), \(p < 0.001\)).
Post-hoc comparisons. Just as a significant ANOVA needs Tukey HSD to identify which groups differ, a significant Kruskal-Wallis result needs its own follow-up. We run a Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test on each pair of groups and adjust the \(p\)-values with the Holm correction (Holm 1979), which keeps the familywise error rate across the comparisons at \(\alpha\).

title: 8  Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
8.6 Repeated-measures ANOVA
Every unit in the salamander study was measured once: 24 plots, 8 per forest type. Many environmental studies instead measure the same monitoring stations in every season or the same streams before, during, and after a drought. A repeated-measures (within-subjects) design measures the same units under every condition, and it calls for a repeated-measures ANOVA.
This is ANOVA’s version of the paired \(t\)-test from Chapter 6. The paired \(t\)-test subtracted each plot’s before score from its own after score, so differences between plots dropped out and only the change was left. With three or more conditions there is no single difference to take, so repeated-measures ANOVA does the equivalent with sums of squares, measuring how much the units differ from one another and removing that variation from the error term.

8.6.1 Fine particulate matter at four monitoring stations
An air quality agency has four PM2.5 monitoring stations, ordered from the most rural (A) to the most urban (D). The concentrations in this example are invented. Table 8.16 gives each station’s mean PM2.5 concentration in winter, spring, and summer. The question is whether concentrations differ by season.

Null (\(H_0\)): mean PM2.5 is the same in every season, \(\mu_\text{Winter}=\mu_\text{Spring}=\mu_\text{Summer}\).
Alternative (\(H_a\)): at least one seasonal mean differs.

8.6.2 Splitting off the stations
A one-way ANOVA on these 12 numbers would split the variation into two pieces, as before. The grand mean is 10 and the season means are 13, 8, and 9. Each season mean counts once per station, so
\[SS_\text{Between} = 4\left[(13-10)^2 + (8-10)^2 + (9-10)^2\right] = 4(14) = 56.\]

Squaring and summing the 12 distances, one season at a time, gives
\[SS_\text{Total} = (1 + 1 + 36 + 64) + (64 + 4 + 1 + 1) + (36 + 9 + 4 + 9) = 230,\]
which leaves \(SS_\text{Within} = 230 - 56 = 174\).
A one-way ANOVA would also break the independence assumption, because each station contributes three of the 12 numbers, and readings from the same station tend to be alike.
Repeated-measures ANOVA splits \(SS_\text{Within}\) one more time. Part of it is station-to-station variation. The units measured repeatedly are called subjects, even when they are stations, so this piece is \(SS_\text{Subjects}\), computed exactly like \(SS_\text{Between}\) but from the station means instead of the season means. Each station mean counts once per season, so
\[SS_\text{Subjects} = 3\left[(5-10)^2 + (8-10)^2 + (13-10)^2 + (14-10)^2\right] = 3(54) = 162.\]
Whatever is left is the error term:
\[SS_\text{Error} = SS_\text{Within} - SS_\text{Subjects} = 174 - 162 = 12,\]
so the full split is
\[SS_\text{Total} = SS_\text{Between} + SS_\text{Subjects} + SS_\text{Error}, \qquad 230 = 56 + 162 + 12.\]
\(SS_\text{Error}\) is the part of the within-season variation that the stations’ own levels can’t explain. It measures how much each station’s seasonal pattern departs from the average seasonal pattern. Its degrees of freedom are the one-way \(df_\text{Within}\) minus the degrees of freedom the four station means use up, where \(n\) is the number of stations:
\[\begin{aligned}
df_\text{Within} &= N - k = 12 - 3 = 9 \\
df_\text{Subjects} &= n - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3 \\
df_\text{Error} &= 9 - 3 = 6 = (k-1)(n-1)
\end{aligned}\]
\(F\) uses the same numerator as before, \(MS_\text{Between} = 56/2 = 28\). Only the denominator changes:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{One-way: } F &= \frac{28}{174/9} = \frac{28}{19.33} = 1.45 \\[1.2ex]
\text{Repeated measures: } F &= \frac{28}{12/6} = \frac{28}{2} = 14.00
\end{aligned}\]

A repeated-measures design has more power than a between-subjects design with the same number of measurements when the units differ from one another, as monitoring stations usually do.

title: 8  Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
8.7 Chapter Summary
Why it matters. Comparing more than two groups with a separate \(t\)-test for each pair raises the chance of at least one false positive with every group added. ANOVA solves that by asking one omnibus question first, and its variance-partitioning logic is the same idea that reappears in regression, factorial designs, and ANCOVA.
Core ideas

Many \(t\)-tests inflate the false-positive rate. Each comparison carries its own chance of a false positive, and they accumulate. With \(m\) comparisons, the familywise error rate for independent tests is \(1-(1-\alpha)^m\), which is already 14% for three tests.
Partition the variation. Total variation splits into a piece explained by group membership (\(SS_\text{Between}\)) and unexplained residual variation (\(SS_\text{Within}\)).
\(F\) is a ratio of the two. After dividing each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom to get a mean square, \(F = MS_\text{Between} / MS_\text{Within}\). A large \(F\) means between-group differences are large relative to within-group noise.
Under \(H_0\), \(F\) is near 1. Both mean squares estimate the same \(\sigma^2\), so \(F\) follows an \(F\) distribution with \(df_\text{Between}\) and \(df_\text{Within}\). Differences in any direction make \(F\) larger, so the test has one critical value, in the upper tail.
Run the omnibus test first, then post-hoc comparisons. The omnibus test asks whether any group means differ. If it is significant, run post-hoc comparisons (Tukey HSD) to find out which pairs differ.
\(\eta^2\) is the effect size. \(SS_\text{Between}/SS_\text{Total}\) is the proportion of variation explained by the factor. It is the same quantity regression calls \(R^2\) (Chapter 9), and it does not depend on sample size the way \(p\) does, so report it alongside \(F\).
Check the assumptions. ANOVA needs approximately equal variances across groups (Levene’s test) and roughly normal residuals. Treat formal tests as evidence rather than a gate, since they have least power exactly when small samples make violations matter most.
When assumptions fail. Welch’s ANOVA handles unequal spread. The Kruskal-Wallis test is the rank-based alternative for skewed residuals in small samples, with pairwise.wilcox.test() as its post-hoc counterpart.
Repeated measures. When the same units are measured under every condition, repeated-measures ANOVA splits \(SS_\text{Within}\) into \(SS_\text{Subjects}\) and a smaller \(SS_\text{Error}\). The smaller error term is why it has more power, the same reason the paired \(t\)-test does.





Brown, M. B., and A. B. Forsythe. 1974. “Robust Tests for Equality of Variances.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 69: 364–67.


Holm, S. 1979. “A Simple Sequentially Rejective Multiple Test Procedure.” Scandinavian Journal of Statistics 6: 65–70.


Kruskal, W. H., and W. A. Wallis. 1952. “Use of Ranks in One-Criterion Variance Analysis.” Journal of the American Statistical Association 47: 583–621. https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1952.10483441.


Levene, H. 1960. “Robust Tests for Equality of Variances.” In Contributions to Probability and Statistics: Essays in Honor of Harold Hotelling, edited by I. Olkin et al. Stanford University Press.


Salsburg, David. 2001. The Lady Tasting Tea: How Statistics Revolutionized Science in the Twentieth Century. Macmillan.


Shapiro, S. S., and M. B. Wilk. 1965. “An Analysis of Variance Test for Normality (Complete Samples).” Biometrika 52: 591–611.


Tukey, John W. 1949. “Comparing Individual Means in the Analysis of Variance.” Biometrics 5 (2): 99–114.

title: 9  Simple Linear Regression
text:
9.1 Regression basics
Download this chapter (PDF)
Back in Chapter 2, we used the covariance between two variables to quantify the strength and direction of a relationship (Pearson’s \(r\)), fit a best-fit line through a scatterplot, and judged \(r\) against a simulated chance window. Chapter 2 gave no formal test of the question every other test in this book has asked:
Could chance alone plausibly have produced our result?
Now that we’ve learned hypothesis testing, sampling distributions, and the logic of comparing an observed statistic to a null distribution, we can apply that same logic to the regression line and test whether a given slope is evidence of a real relationship.
The equation for a linear regression is one of the most heavily used equations in applied science:
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon\]
Here \(y\) is the dependent variable (DV) and \(x\) is the predictor, the independent variable (IV) (Section 1.4). \(\beta_1\) is the slope, the change in \(y\) for each one-unit increase in \(x\). \(\beta_0\) is the intercept, the value of \(y\) when \(x = 0\). The intercept and slope are the regression coefficients. These subscripted \(\beta\)s have no connection to \(\beta\), the Type II error rate from Section 5.1.
A statistical model is an equation that describes how the DV changes with a predictor, plus a term for the variation the equation leaves out. A linear equation fit to data is one example. Real data do not fall exactly on a line, and the error term \(\varepsilon\) is the part of the DV that the population line does not explain. We never observe \(\beta_0\), \(\beta_1\), or \(\varepsilon\) directly, because they describe the population, and we have only a sample.

title: 9  Simple Linear Regression
text:
9.1.1 Computing the best-fit line by hand
In practice, we let software find the line with the smallest sum of squared residuals (the least-squares line from Section 2.4.1), but working through one example by hand shows where that line comes from. We write the intercept and slope calculated from a sample as \(b_0\) and \(b_1\), to keep them apart from the population values \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). Here are the formulas for \(b_0\) and \(b_1\), calculated straight from the data:
\[\text{intercept} = b_0 = \frac{\sum{y}\sum{x^2}-\sum{x}\sum{xy}}{n\sum{x^2}-(\sum{x})^2}\]
\[\text{slope} = b_1 = \frac{n\sum{xy}-\sum{x}\sum{y}}{n\sum{x^2}-(\sum{x})^2}\]
Here \(x\) and \(y\) are the individual scores, \(n\) is the number of \((x, y)\) pairs, and \(\sum\) means add up that column over all pairs. This is the same line from Figure 2.10. To find its slope and intercept, we start with this table:

&= \frac{39 \times 200 - 34 \times 231}{7 \times 200-34^2} \\[1.2ex]
&= \frac{7800 - 7854}{1400 - 1156} \\[1.2ex]
&= \frac{-54}{244} = -0.221
\end{aligned}\]
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{slope} = b_1 &= \frac{n\sum{xy}-\sum{x}\sum{y}}{n\sum{x^2}-(\sum{x})^2} \\[1.2ex]
&= \frac{7 \times 231-34 \times 39}{7 \times 200-34^2} \\[1.2ex]
&= \frac{1617 - 1326}{1400 - 1156} \\[1.2ex]
&= \frac{291}{244} = 1.19
\end{aligned}\]
With \(b_0\) and \(b_1\) in hand, we can compute a residual for any observed point. A residual, as in Section 2.4.1, is the difference between what we observed and what the line predicts. The symbol \(\hat y\) (read “y-hat”) is the value the line predicts:
\[\begin{aligned}
\hat y &= b_0 + b_1x \\
e &= y - \hat y
\end{aligned}\]
For the first row above (\(x=1\), \(y=2\)):
\[\begin{aligned}
\hat y &= -0.221 + 1.19(1) = 0.969 \\
e &= y - \hat y = 2 - 0.969 = 1.031
\end{aligned}\]
The residual is positive, so that point is above the line. Repeating this for every point, then squaring and summing the residuals, gives the sum of squared residuals, the quantity that \(b_0\) and \(b_1\) were chosen to make as small as possible.
The residual \(e\) is the sample’s version of the error \(\varepsilon\). The error \(\varepsilon\) belongs to the population line, which we never see, and the residual \(e\) belongs to the line we fit.


9.1.2 Parameters and sample statistics
The regression coefficients \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) are population parameters.








Symbol
What is it?
Do we know it?




\(\beta_0, \beta_1\)
True population intercept and slope
No. Estimated from the sample


\(b_0, b_1\)
Sample intercept and slope
Yes, calculated by fitting the line to our data

title: 9  Simple Linear Regression
section: 9.2 Worked regression example: stream temperature and dissolved oxygen
text:
9.2 Worked regression example: stream temperature and dissolved oxygen
Warmer water holds less dissolved gas, so ecologists expect dissolved oxygen (DO) to decline as stream temperature rises. This matters for stream health, because low DO can stress or kill fish and invertebrates. Figure 9.1 lays out the design.








Figure 9.1: A regression design. Instead of a few groups to sort sites into, every site is somewhere along a continuous range, and every temperature value is treated as its own group. A slope describes how the mean changes across that range.





Up to now every design put units into groups and asked whether the groups differed. Now, with a continuous predictor, every temperature value is treated as its own group. Each of the 30 sites falls somewhere along the range, usually alone at its temperature, and the line gives a predicted mean DO at every temperature, the way a group mean did in earlier chapters. The question becomes how much DO changes per degree rather than whether two groups differ.
The 30 sites in this example are invented. We built them from a population line with \(\beta_0 = 13.5\) mg/L and \(\beta_1 = -0.28\) mg/L per °C, plus random scatter, so here, unlike in a real study, we know the true slope that \(b_1\) estimates.








Figure 9.2: Stream temperature and dissolved oxygen at 30 sample sites, with the fitted regression line.





The scatterplot in Figure 9.2 shows a clear downward trend. Just from the graph, we can guess a couple of things:

Pearson’s \(r\) should be negative, since DO falls as temperature rises. Pearson’s \(r\) and the slope \(b_1\) describe the same line in different ways. \(r\) measures how closely the points follow a straight line, on a scale from \(-1\) to \(1\) with no units. \(b_1\) measures how much \(y\) changes for each one-unit change in \(x\), in the units of the data (here mg/L per °C).
Pearson’s \(r\) should be well short of \(-1\), since the points scatter noticeably around the line.

Regression tests whether a relationship like this one is more than chance by writing it as a model.

9.2.1 The regression model
We model dissolved oxygen as a linear function of stream temperature, plus error:
\[DO = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{Temperature}) + \varepsilon\]
\(\beta_0\) is the population intercept, \(\beta_1\) is the population slope, and \(\varepsilon\) is the error, the part of DO that temperature alone doesn’t explain.
We don’t know \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). We estimate them from the sample as \(b_0\) and \(b_1\), using the same least-squares logic from Chapter 2.
In R, this is a single line of code:

fit <- lm(DO ~ stream_temp, data = stream_df)

In Figure 9.3, each red vertical segment is one site’s residual, the distance from its observed DO to the line. The fitted line is the line that makes the sum of those squared residuals as small as possible.








Figure 9.3: Stream temperature and dissolved oxygen with the fitted line. Vertical red segments are residuals.





summary(fit) prints the estimate, standard error, \(t\), and \(p\) for each coefficient, and confint(fit) gives their 95% confidence intervals. The table below combines the two.

summary(fit)

\(\widehat{DO} = 15.34 - 0.36 \times \text{Temperature}\).
The hat over \(DO\) marks it as a predicted value, what the model outputs for a given temperature, as distinct from an actually observed \(DO\) measurement.

The intercept (\(b_0 = 15.34\)) is the model’s predicted DO at 0°C. That temperature is outside the range we sampled (10.0 to 23.3°C), so reading the line at 0°C would be extrapolation (Section 9.7), and we won’t interpret the intercept.
The slope (\(b_1 = -0.36\)) is the part we care about most. For every 1°C increase in stream temperature, predicted dissolved oxygen drops by about 0.36 mg/L.

title: 9  Simple Linear Regression
text:
9.3 Testing the slope
The slope \(b_1\) is a sample estimate. The hypothesis test for the slope asks whether the population slope \(\beta_1\) could plausibly be zero:

Null (\(H_0\)): no linear relationship between stream temperature and dissolved oxygen, \(\beta_1 = 0\).
Alternative (\(H_a\)): a linear relationship, \(\beta_1 \neq 0\).

Like any other statistic, \(b_1\) varies from sample to sample. If we drew a new sample of streams and fit a new line, we’d get a slightly different \(b_1\), just by chance. The test asks whether our \(b_1\) is large relative to that sampling variability, the same signal-over-noise pattern as every test so far:
\[\text{statistic}=\frac{\text{effect}}{\text{error}}.\]
Here “error” means the standard error of \(b_1\), the standard deviation of its sampling distribution. It is a different quantity from the error term \(\varepsilon\) in the model.
R reports the \(t\)-test for the slope in the coefficient table from summary(fit), so there is no separate test to run.
The test statistic divides the estimated slope by its standard error, the SE column in the coefficient table above. R computes the standard error of the slope from the residuals and the spread of temperatures, \(SE(b_1) = \sqrt{\dfrac{\sum e^2/(n-2)}{\sum (x - \bar x)^2}}\). More scatter around the line makes it larger, and a wider spread of temperatures makes it smaller. For the stream data,
\[t = \frac{b_1}{SE(b_1)} = \frac{-0.357}{0.067} = -5.30\]
with \(df = n - 2 = 28\) (one degree of freedom spent estimating the intercept, one for the slope).
The \(p\)-value comes from a \(t\)-distribution. If temperature and DO were truly unrelated in the population, repeating this study many times would still produce a nonzero \(b_1\) just by chance, and a \(t\)-statistic that follows a \(t\)-distribution with \(df = 28\). Figure 9.4 shows that distribution, with the critical values marking the boundary of the most extreme 5% under \(H_0\), and our observed \(t\) marked against it.








Figure 9.4: The null distribution of \(t\) for the slope test at \(df = 28\) (blue dot-dash). The shaded tails beyond the red critical values are the rejection region at \(\alpha = 0.05\). The lime-green dotted line marks our observed \(t\), far into the left tail.





Our observed \(t = -5.30\) is far past the critical values of about \(\pm2.05\), well outside where 95% of \(t\)-values would fall if temperature and DO were unrelated. The \(p\)-value is the probability of a \(t\) that far out (or farther) in either tail under \(H_0\). Here \(p < 0.001\), which is smaller than \(\alpha = 0.05\).
We reject \(H_0\) and conclude that stream temperature is linearly related to dissolved oxygen.
The last two columns of the coefficient table give the 95% confidence interval for the slope, 95% CI [-0.50, -0.22] mg/L per °C. Because this interval does not contain 0, it agrees with the hypothesis test.
This is the same agreement you saw for \(z\) in Section 4.4.3 and for \(t\) in Section 6.3. Here the critical value is \(t_{crit} = 2.05\) at \(df = 28\). The test rejects \(H_0\) when the observed \(b_1\) is more than \(t_{crit}\) standard errors from 0, and the 95% interval contains every slope within \(t_{crit}\) standard errors of \(b_1\). So 0 falls outside the interval exactly when the two-tailed test rejects \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\).
The interval also contains \(\beta_1 = -0.28\), the true slope we built into the data. A 95% interval catches the true value in about 95% of samples, and this sample is one of them.

title: 9  Simple Linear Regression
text:
9.4 Partitioning variation: regression as ANOVA
Besides testing the slope, we want to know how much of the variation in DO the line explains. We answer that the same way as one-way ANOVA in Chapter 8, by splitting the total variation into a piece the model explains and a piece it leaves over.
Figure 9.5 shows the three pieces for the stream data. Each site’s distance from mean DO (gray, left panel) splits into two pieces, the distance from the mean to the line (middle), which the line explains, and the distance from the line to the point (right), the residual.








Figure 9.5: Partitioning variation in dissolved oxygen. Left: each site’s distance from mean DO (dashed line). Middle: the part of that distance explained by the line. Right: what is left over, the residuals. Squaring and summing each set of segments gives the three sums of squares.





\(SS_\text{Total}\) is the sum of the squared distances from each point to mean DO. \(SS_\text{Regression}\) is the sum of the squared distances from the line to mean DO. \(SS_\text{Residual}\) is the sum of the squared residuals, the distances from each point to the line. For each site, the two shorter segments add up to the long one. After squaring each segment and summing over all 30 sites, the totals still add up, as they did in Chapter 8:
\[SS_\text{Total} = SS_\text{Regression} + SS_\text{Residual}, \qquad 122.44 = 61.35 + 61.10\]
The pieces line up with Chapter 8’s. \(SS_\text{Regression}\) is the variation the predictor explains, the role \(SS_\text{Between}\) played for group means. \(SS_\text{Residual}\) is what’s left over around the line, the role \(SS_\text{Within}\) played around each group’s mean. Treating every temperature value as its own group means that the line supplies a predicted mean at each value of \(x\), in place of one mean per group.
R-squared (\(R^2\)) is the proportion of the total variation explained by the line:
\[R^2 = \frac{SS_\text{Regression}}{SS_\text{Total}} = \frac{61.35}{122.44} = 0.50\]
It runs from 0 to 1, and it is the same quantity as \(\eta^2\) from Chapter 8. For simple regression with one predictor, \(R^2\) is also Pearson’s \(r\) from Chapter 2, squared: \((-0.708)^2 = 0.501\).
The regression ANOVA table. Dividing each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom gives mean squares, and their ratio is \(F\), exactly as in Chapter 8. The regression row uses 1 degree of freedom, one for the slope. The residual row uses \(n-2\), since the line estimated two things, an intercept and a slope.

anova(fit)

\[F = \frac{MS_\text{Regression}}{MS_\text{Residual}} = \frac{SS_\text{Regression}/1}{SS_\text{Residual}/28} = \frac{61.35/1}{61.10/28} = \frac{61.35}{2.182} = 28.12\]
With one predictor, \(F\) and the slope’s \(t\) test the same thing: \(F = t^2 = (-5.30)^2 = 28.12\), with the same \(p\). \(F\) is the form that generalizes to models with more than one predictor, which is why software reports both.
Here \(R^2 = 0.50\), so stream temperature explains about 50% of the variation we observed in dissolved oxygen across sites. The remaining 50% comes from everything else the model doesn’t capture (discharge, shading, groundwater input, and so on), and it shows up as the residuals.

title: 9  Simple Linear Regression
section: 9.5 Consider both significance and effect size
text:
9.5 Consider both significance and effect size
As with every test in this book, we report an effect size alongside the significance test. Testing the slope asks whether \(\beta_1\) differs from 0. \(R^2\), regression’s effect size, says how much of the variation the line explains. The two can disagree in either direction.
A sample of thousands of observations, common in remote sensing and other big-data environmental work, can make a trivial effect significant, because more observations shrink the standard error until almost any nonzero slope clears \(p<0.05\). A small sample can fail the other way and miss a real, sizeable effect because its standard error is too large.
Figure 9.6 shows three of these combinations, using invented data: a strong relationship with a non-significant slope (underpowered, Section 5.4), a weak relationship with a significant slope (a large sample), and a relationship that is both strong and significant. In the left panel, six points give \(R^2 = 0.63\) but \(p = 0.058\). In the middle panel, 5,000 points give \(p = 0.004\) for a line that explains 0.2% of the variation. We built a true slope of 0.05 into that panel. With \(x\) running from 0 to 10, the line rises \(0.05 \times 10 = 0.5\) units across the whole range.








Figure 9.6: R-squared and the slope’s p-value can disagree. Left: a strong relationship (high R-squared) that isn’t statistically significant. Middle: a weak relationship (low R-squared) that is significant anyway. Right: strong and significant together.











CautionWarning: How big is a “good” \(R^2\)?



It depends on the field. In studies of human behavior, where many unmeasured factors shape any outcome, 0.20 is a strong result. Environmental systems tend toward more direct physical relationships, so 0.5 to 0.8 for a well-chosen single predictor isn’t unusual. An \(R^2\) that looks too good, say 0.98 from a single predictor in a noisy field system, more often points to a mistake in the analysis, such as a predictor that is computed from the DV, than to a real result.

title: 9  Simple Linear Regression
text:
9.6 Checking assumptions
Simple linear regression has three test-specific assumptions, plus the universal independence assumption from Chapter 6. Table 9.3 lists all four with the check this chapter uses.



Table 9.3: Assumptions of simple linear regression and how to check them.











Assumption
What it means
How to check
What a violation looks like




Linearity
The true relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) is a straight line.
Residuals-versus-fitted plot
A curve, such as a U-shape


Independence
Each observation’s error is unrelated to the others’.
The study design
Sites along the same stream, or repeated measurements over time


Constant variance (homoscedasticity)
The spread of residuals is about the same across the whole range of \(x\), the regression version of Chapter 8’s homogeneity of variance.
Residuals-versus-fitted plot
A funnel that widens or narrows


Normal residuals
The residuals are approximately normally distributed.
Q-Q plot and Shapiro-Wilk
Points bending away from the Q-Q diagonal







9.6.1 When the true relationship is curved

You can do linear regression without thinking about whether the phenomenon you’re modeling is actually close to linear. But you shouldn’t.
Jordan Ellenberg, How Not to Be Wrong

A straight line may be the wrong shape for your data. A residuals-versus-fitted plot puts each point’s fitted value \(\hat y\), the value the line predicts for it, on the \(x\)-axis and its residual on the \(y\)-axis. It checks two of the assumptions above at once. A curve means linearity is violated, and a funnel shape means constant variance is violated.








Figure 9.7: Residuals versus fitted values for the stream temperature model. A random scatter around zero, with no funnel shape or curve, supports linearity and constant variance.





Figure 9.7, for our stream temperature data, shows residuals scattered evenly above and below zero, with no curve and no funnel shape.
To see what a violation looks like, we fit a straight line to a second data set, 14 days of invented avian influenza case counts. We built the counts from an exponential curve, \(6e^{0.28 \times \text{day}}\), which grows by about 32% each day, plus random scatter, so we know the true shape that a straight line will miss. The design has the same structure as the stream example, with time as the continuous predictor.








Figure 9.8: The outbreak data as a design.













Figure 9.9: New avian influenza cases per day, days 1-14 of an outbreak, with a fitted straight line.





A straight line fit to these 14 days gives \(R^2 = 0.81\) and \(p < 0.001\), which is higher than the 0.5 to 0.8 that is common for a single predictor in environmental work, and significant. Neither number alone suggests a problem, but the plot does. The fitted line starts at about -40 cases on day 1, and a count of cases can’t be negative.
Check the residuals. Figure 9.10 shows the residuals-versus-fitted plot for the outbreak model.








Figure 9.10: Residuals versus fitted values for the linear outbreak model. The residuals form a U-shape instead of a random scatter, which happens when a straight line is fit to a curved relationship.





The residuals form a U. The residuals are positive early and late in the outbreak, so the observed counts are above the line there and the line underpredicts. In the middle they are negative, so the line overpredicts.
If a residual plot curves instead of scattering randomly, a straight line is the wrong model for the data.
Fixes typically include:

a different model (often adding an \(x^2\) term, which lets the fitted line bend)
a transformation, re-expressing a variable on a different scale so a straight line fits it (log-transforming a variable that grows multiplicatively, like the outbreak data above, is the most common case)
or a nonlinear model entirely, beyond what this course covers



9.6.2 Checking normality
For normality, we check the residuals two ways: visually, with a Q-Q plot, and formally, with the Shapiro-Wilk test (Chapter 6).
A Q-Q plot sorts the residuals and compares them to where a perfectly normal distribution would place values at the same percentiles. If the residuals are normal, the points fall close to the diagonal line. A systematic curve or S-shape means they don’t.








Figure 9.11: Normal Q-Q plot of the stream temperature model’s residuals. Points close to the diagonal support normality.





Figure 9.11 looks close to straight, consistent with normal residuals. Shapiro-Wilk asks the same question formally. Its \(H_0\) is that the residuals come from a normal distribution, so a small \(p\)-value is evidence against normality.

shapiro.test(resid(fit))




Shapiro-Wilk test on the regression residuals


Statistic
p




0.97
0.663





Shapiro-Wilk does not reject normality here (\(p = 0.663\)). As with any formal normality test, treat this as one piece of evidence alongside the Q-Q plot and residual plot. Shapiro-Wilk has the least power to detect real departures when the sample is small, which is also when the visual checks matter most.
Now apply the same two normality checks to the avian influenza model, the one we already know is badly nonlinear.








Figure 9.12: Normal Q-Q plot of the outbreak model’s residuals. The lowest residuals bend away from the diagonal, but not by enough for Shapiro-Wilk to reject normality.





The Q-Q plot bends away from the diagonal at the low end, but Shapiro-Wilk does not reject normality (\(p = 0.060\)). On a model we already know is the wrong shape, the normality checks give at most borderline evidence of a problem. They check normality of the residuals, which is a different assumption from linearity, and a model can badly violate linearity while its residuals look only mildly non-normal.






ImportantResults reporting: regression



We report a regression result the same way as any other test: the slope, the test statistic with its degrees of freedom, \(p\), the slope’s confidence interval, and \(R^2\) as the effect size.

Dissolved oxygen declined significantly with stream temperature, \(b_1 = -0.36\) mg/L per °C, \(t(28) = -5.30\), \(p < 0.001\), 95% CI [-0.50, -0.22] mg/L per °C, \(R^2 = 0.50\).
