title: 9  Simple Linear Regression
text:
9.7 Using the model: prediction
Once the slope test shows a significant linear relationship, the fitted equation lets us predict DO at any temperature inside the range we sampled. Plugging temperature into the fitted line directly gives the prediction: at 20°C,
\[\widehat{DO} = b_0 + b_1(20) = 15.34 + (-0.36)(20) = 8.20\]
R gives the same number, along with a confidence interval. predict() takes the fitted model and a small data frame holding the new temperature. The column name, stream_temp, has to match the predictor’s name in the model.

predict(fit, newdata = data.frame(stream_temp = 20), interval = "confidence")




Predicted dissolved oxygen at 20°C, with 95% confidence interval


Stream temperature
Predicted
CI low
CI high




20
8.2
7.57
8.83





At 20°C, the model predicts DO of 8.20 mg/L, 95% CI [7.57, 8.83]. Because 20°C falls inside the observed range of 10.0 to 23.3°C, this prediction is interpolation. Interpolation is predicting \(y\) at an \(x\) value inside the range of \(x\) we observed, which is what regression is good for.
This confidence interval is for the population mean DO of all streams at 20°C, the value the model predicts at \(x = 20\), \(\beta_0 + 20\beta_1\). It is a different interval from the ones in the coefficient table, which give a range of plausible values for each parameter, \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). A single stream at 20°C will scatter around that mean by about as much as the points scatter around the line, so its DO can fall well outside this interval.
Extrapolation is predicting \(y\) at an \(x\) value outside the range of \(x\) we observed. Predicting DO at, say, 35°C would be extrapolation. The fitted line gives 2.8 mg/L at 35°C, a number with no data behind it. Nothing in the data tells us the relationship stays linear (or even stays a relationship at all) beyond the range we actually observed, and the further outside that range, the less trustworthy the prediction. Figure 9.13 shows both zones on the same line.








Figure 9.13: The fitted line within the observed temperature range (solid blue, interpolation) and extended beyond it in both directions (dashed red, extrapolation). Dotted gray lines mark the lowest and highest observed temperatures, 10.0 and 23.3°C.





Regression is used for extrapolation all the time, and often reasonably. A well-understood physical process can justify projecting a line beyond the data we collected. Extrapolating a straight line is only safe if the true relationship stays straight past the range we observed.
Figure 9.14 shows four very different relationships, exponential growth, a sigmoid, a hump-shaped curve, and a truly straight line, each with the same short observed window highlighted in blue. In each panel a straight line (dashed red) is fit to that window and extended. Once you see the full curve (gray), you can see how badly linear extrapolation beyond the range of observed data would perform in each case.








Figure 9.14: Four different true relationships that all look locally linear over a short observed window (blue). A line fit to each window (dashed red) matches it closely inside the window, but only the linear case stays correct once the full curve (gray) is revealed.





Suppose officials use the linear fitted line from the outbreak example above to project avian influenza cases at day 30, well past the 14 days observed.








Figure 9.15: The linear fit extended (dashed) past the observed range, against the true exponential trajectory (dotted gray). The straight line badly underestimates how large the outbreak actually becomes.





In Figure 9.15, the dashed line keeps rising slowly past day 14, while the true exponential curve rises far above it.
The linear model predicts about 530 cases on day 30. On the exponential curve the data were built from, the count is closer to 26,682, roughly 50 times higher.
Planning surveillance and containment staffing off the linear forecast would leave the response badly under-resourced for the outbreak that actually arrives.
This problem calls for a different model. More data or a better-fitting straight line would not fix it. Fitting a curve or a transformed model is beyond this course. You can still recognize when a straight line is the wrong model by plotting the data and the residuals.

title: 9  Simple Linear Regression
text:
9.8 Chapter Summary
Why it matters. Chapter 2 drew a best-fit line through a scatterplot. This chapter tests that line’s slope, measures how much variation it explains with \(R^2\), and uses it to predict new values. Chapter 11 adds a categorical factor to this same line.
Core ideas

The slope can be tested. Chapter 2 compared \(r\) to a simulated chance window but gave no formal test with a \(p\)-value. Fitting a line turns that relationship into a model whose slope we can test: \(H_0: \beta_1 = 0\) says there is no linear relationship. The test statistic is the slope divided by its standard error, \(t = b_1 / SE(b_1)\), with \(df = n-2\).
Regression partitions variation the way ANOVA does. \(SS_\text{Total}\) splits into \(SS_\text{Regression}\) (Chapter 8’s between) and \(SS_\text{Residual}\) (Chapter 8’s within), and \(F = MS_\text{Regression}/MS_\text{Residual}\), which equals \(t^2\) with one predictor. \(R^2\), the proportion of variation explained by the line, is the effect size. A relationship can be real (\(p\) small) and still explain very little, which is why you report both.
Look at your data, then look at your residuals. The test-specific assumptions are linearity, constant variance, and roughly normal residuals, on top of independence. A residuals-versus-fitted plot can show a violation that \(R^2\), the slope test, and Shapiro-Wilk all miss, as the outbreak example showed.
Predict inside the observed range, and extrapolate beyond it only with good reason. Interpolating within the observed range of \(x\) is what regression is for. Extrapolating beyond it is sometimes justified, but only when you have good reason to believe the relationship stays the same shape past the range you observed.
A good \(R^2\) can still be the wrong model. The outbreak example fit a straight line to exponential growth and got \(R^2=0.81\), a residuals-versus-fitted plot that clearly curved, and an extrapolated forecast about 26,000 cases short of the exponential curve the data came from. A normality check on the same residuals gives only a borderline signal, because it tests a different assumption.

title: 10  Factorial ANOVA
text:
10.1 Factorial basics
Download this chapter (PDF)
In science, outcomes rarely depend on just one thing. Climate, soil type, and water availability all act together to influence ecosystems in ways a single-factor design can’t capture. Factorial designs let us study several factors, and how they interact with each other, at once.
Chapter 8’s one-way ANOVA tested a single factor, the ANOVA name for an independent variable (IV). This chapter uses both words. This chapter covers how to compute a factorial ANOVA, including a full by-hand walkthrough of the sums-of-squares arithmetic, and how to interpret the result. With more than one factor, interpretation is harder, because an interaction changes what every other number in the results table means.
Imagine investigating the growth rate of a plant species, with IVs like soil pH or water availability. Each added IV multiplies the number of conditions you can observe, and with it, the questions you can ask about how those factors work together. Table 10.1 shows three designs built around the same plant-growth question.
Now we have two IVs, soil pH and water availability, each with two levels. A factorial design has two or more IVs, and each of its conditions is a combination of one level from each IV.
A fully factorial design includes every combination of the levels of its IVs. A design with this property is also called fully crossed. A factorial design that leaves some combinations of levels unmeasured is only partly crossed. Every design in this chapter is fully factorial, so the rest of the chapter uses factorial to mean fully factorial.

10.1.1 Factorial notation
Each combination of soil pH and water availability is one condition. With 2 IVs, each with 2 levels, there are 2x2 = 4 conditions in which to measure growth rate.
The name of a factorial design gives one number per IV, and each number is that IV’s count of levels. Multiplying the numbers gives the number of conditions. Here are a few examples:

2x2: Two IVs, each with two levels (yields four unique conditions).
2x3: Two IVs, with the first having two levels and the second three (yields six unique conditions).
3x2: Similar to the 2x3, but the first IV has three levels, and the second has two, also giving us six unique conditions.
4x4: Two IVs, each with four levels, resulting in sixteen conditions.

title: 10  Factorial ANOVA
text:
10.2 Pollution, flow, and stream life
The rest of this chapter uses one example throughout.
The question. Streams are affected by pollution, but also by how fast the water moves. Fast-moving water flushes contaminants downstream and re-oxygenates the channel. Slow water lets them sit. So pollution might do more damage in a sluggish stream than a fast one. To measure that damage, we need to operationalize stream health.
The dependent variable is macroinvertebrate species count, the number of distinct kinds of aquatic insects, snails, worms, and crustaceans that live in a stream. This is a standard measure of stream health. These animals are in the middle of the food web, many are pollution-sensitive, and they can’t flee a degraded stream the way fish can. More species present means a healthier stream.
The design. We run an experiment in artificial stream channels, each assigned one pollution condition and one flow rate. The species counts in this chapter are invented, chosen so the arithmetic stays easy to follow. Figure 10.1 summarizes it.








Figure 10.1: A fully crossed factorial design, read as arithmetic: two pollution levels times two flow levels gives four conditions. Every combination is measured, which is what ‘fully crossed’ means.





With two IVs of two levels each, this is a 2x2 design. Reading the schematic left to right also shows why the notation works the way it does. Crossing two levels with two levels is the multiplication that gives four conditions.
That four-cell grid resembles the chi-square table from Section 7.4.2, but the cells mean different things. There, the cells held counts of city blocks that already had a given land use and either did or did not top 40°C, and nobody put them there. Here, the cells are conditions we assign channels to, and within each one we then measure something else entirely, the species count.
Predictions. No pollution plus high flow should support the most species, and pollution plus low flow the fewest. The other two combinations are the informative ones. They show whether pollution matters only when flow is low, with fast water washing its effect away, or hurts a stream no matter how fast the water moves. A one-factor study could not tell these apart, and the interaction test in a factorial experiment can.

10.2.1 Cell means and marginal means
Each condition, such as no pollution with low flow, is a cell, the same word Section 7.4.2 used for one combination in a table of counts. A cell mean is the mean of the scores in one cell. Here, each cell mean averages the species counts of the five stream channels assigned to that condition. A marginal mean is the mean for one level of a factor, averaged across the levels of the other factor. For example, the no-pollution marginal mean averages the two no-pollution cells, one at each flow rate. Table 10.3 shows the means from the experiment this chapter analyzes.

title: 10  Factorial ANOVA
text:
10.3 Why factorial designs matter
Factorial designs let us ask more nuanced questions than a single-factor study can. Suppose we ignored flow entirely and just compared polluted to unpolluted channels. That compares the two pollution marginal means, 11.1 vs. 6.8 species, shown in Figure 10.2.








Figure 10.2: Mean macroinvertebrate species count under no pollution vs. pollution, averaged across flow rate (the pollution marginal means).





A factorial design lets us ask whether the effect of pollution itself depends on flow, which a one-factor design can’t. With flow rate added as a second IV, there are four cell means instead of two, so we can compare polluted and unpolluted channels within each flow rate, shown in Figure 10.3.








Figure 10.3: The effect of pollution within each flow rate (the gap between the two bars) is larger under low flow than under high flow.





Under low flow, species count drops sharply with pollution (9.6 to 3.6, a difference of 6.0). Under high flow, the drop is smaller (12.6 to 10.0, a difference of 2.6). The effect of pollution depends on flow rate.

10.3.1 Main effects and interactions
A factorial design gives you two kinds of results: main effects and interactions. How many of each depends on the number of IVs.
A main effect is the difference between the marginal means of one IV. Each IV has one main effect, so a 2x2 design has two, one for Pollution and one for Flow. A 2x2x2 design and a 3x3x3 design both have three main effects, because the count depends on the number of IVs, not their levels.
A simple effect is the effect of one IV at a single level of the other IV, such as the pollution effect under low flow. Figure 10.3 shows two of them, one per flow rate, and the main effect of pollution is their average: \((6.0 + 2.6)/2 = 4.3\), the same 4.3 you get by subtracting the pollution marginal means.
An interaction occurs when the effect of one IV depends on the level of another. Figure 10.3 shows one, since the simple effect of pollution changed with flow.
Equivalently, an interaction is a difference between differences. Each simple effect of pollution is a difference (unpolluted minus polluted). If that difference itself changes across flow rates, that’s an interaction. The interaction sum of squares later in this chapter measures this difference between differences.
Table 10.4 collects the four quantities a 2x2 design gives, with the stream experiment’s value for each.



Table 10.4: Cell mean, main effect, simple effect and interaction in the stream experiment.










Term
Definition
Stream experiment




Cell mean
The mean of the channels in one condition
No pollution with low flow: 9.6 species


Main effect
The difference between one factor’s marginal means, averaged across the levels of the other factor
Pollution: \(11.1 - 6.8 = 4.3\) species


Simple effect
The effect of one factor at a single level of the other
Pollution under low flow: 6.0 species. Under high flow: 2.6 species.


Interaction
The effect of one factor depends on the level of the other. The simple effects differ, a difference between differences.
\(6.0 - 2.6 = 3.4\) species






The number of possible interactions scales with the number of IVs. A 2x2 design has exactly one interaction, Pollution × Flow. A design with three IVs (A, B, C) has three two-way interactions, each between two of the IVs (A×B, A×C, B×C), and one three-way interaction among all three (A×B×C).

title: 10  Factorial ANOVA
text:
10.4 What a 2x2 actually tests
A factorial ANOVA with two factors is also called a two-way ANOVA. It tests three effects and therefore has three null hypotheses:

a main effect of pollution,
a main effect of flow, and
a pollution × flow interaction.

The hypotheses are about the population mean species count for each condition, written \(\mu\). The cell means computed from the 20 channels, written \(\bar{Y}\) later in this chapter, estimate them. We can represent the four conditions and their mean species counts as:

10.4.1 Hypotheses
Main effect of pollution

Null (\(H_0\)): Averaged across flow rates, mean species count is the same with and without pollution (\(\mu_{\text{NoPoll}} = \mu_{\text{Poll}}\)).
Alternative (\(H_a\)): Averaged across flow rates, mean species count differs with and without pollution (\(\mu_{\text{NoPoll}} \neq \mu_{\text{Poll}}\)).

Main effect of flow

Null (\(H_0\)): Averaged across pollution conditions, mean species count is the same at low and high flow (\(\mu_{\text{Low}} = \mu_{\text{High}}\)).
Alternative (\(H_a\)): Averaged across pollution conditions, mean species count differs between low and high flow (\(\mu_{\text{Low}} \neq \mu_{\text{High}}\)).

Pollution × flow interaction

Null (\(H_0\)): The effect of pollution is the same at both flow rates. (In symbols: \((\mu_{\text{NoPoll,Low}}-\mu_{\text{Poll,Low}})=(\mu_{\text{NoPoll,High}}-\mu_{\text{Poll,High}})\).)
Alternative (\(H_a\)): The effect of pollution differs across flow rates.

Under the interaction null, the gap between polluted and unpolluted channels is the same whether the water is moving fast or slow. If that gap changes, for example if pollution does far more damage under low flow, you’ve found an interaction.






NoteNote: The interaction null for any two factors



You’ll sometimes see this written in abstract terms, with “Factor A” and “Factor B.” For example,
\[H_0: (\mu_{A1,B1}-\mu_{A2,B1})=(\mu_{A1,B2}-\mu_{A2,B2})\]
The logic is the same, with A and B standing for your own variables.

title: 10  Factorial ANOVA
text:
10.5 What the ANOVA compares
An interaction is a difference between differences. Table 10.3 gives the four cell means to compute it with, before any sums of squares. Writing a simple effect as \(\Delta\), with the level it is computed at after the bar:
\[\Delta_\text{Pollution|Low} = \bar{Y}_\text{NoPoll,Low} - \bar{Y}_\text{Poll,Low} = 9.6 - 3.6 = 6.0\]
\[\Delta_\text{Pollution|High} = \bar{Y}_\text{NoPoll,High} - \bar{Y}_\text{Poll,High} = 12.6 - 10.0 = 2.6\]
Those two numbers aren’t the same, so the effect of pollution isn’t constant across flow rates, which is exactly what an interaction means. The gap between them, \(6.0 - 2.6 = 3.4\), is a first, informal look at the interaction itself. The formal test below tells us whether a gap that size is larger than chance would produce.

text:
10.6 Computing a factorial ANOVA by hand
In our between-subjects 2x2 design, 5 stream channels are assigned to each condition, 20 channels total, and no channel appears in more than one condition. The logic is the same as the one-way ANOVA in Chapter 8, which partitions the total variance into parts. For a 2x2 design, there’s now one more part, the interaction:
\[SS_\text{Total} = SS_\text{Pollution} + SS_\text{Flow} + SS_\text{Interaction} + SS_\text{Error}\]
The tables below build up each piece with one row per channel, showing what that channel’s score gets replaced with, its distance from the grand mean, and that distance squared.

Every low-flow channel is replaced by the low-flow marginal mean, 6.6, and every high-flow channel by the high-flow marginal mean, 11.3. Every distance from the grand mean is either -2.35 or 2.35, so \(SS_\text{Flow} = 20 \times 2.35^2 = 110.45\).


10.6.4 SS Interaction
The interaction is the one new piece a factorial ANOVA adds. It asks whether the four cell means behave differently than the two main effects alone would predict.
If the main effects told the whole story, each cell mean would be the grand mean, shifted by that cell’s pollution effect and its flow effect. Take the no-pollution, low-flow cell.
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{No-pollution shift} &= 11.1 - 8.95 = +2.15 \\
\text{Low-flow shift} &= 6.6 - 8.95 = -2.35 \\
\text{Predicted cell mean} &= 8.95 + 2.15 - 2.35 = 8.75 \\
\text{Observed cell mean} &= 9.6 \\
\text{Leftover} &= 9.6 - 8.75 = 0.85
\end{aligned}\]
The leftover is the part of that cell the two main effects can’t explain. Those leftovers, one per cell, are what the interaction captures.
Each cell’s predicted mean is the grand mean plus the pollution shift plus the flow shift, which simplifies:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Predicted} &= \bar{Y}_\text{grand} + (\bar{Y}_\text{Pollution marginal} - \bar{Y}_\text{grand}) + (\bar{Y}_\text{Flow marginal} - \bar{Y}_\text{grand}) \\
&= \bar{Y}_\text{Pollution marginal} + \bar{Y}_\text{Flow marginal} - \bar{Y}_\text{grand}
\end{aligned}\]
Subtracting that from the cell mean gives each channel’s leftover:
\[\bar{Y}_\text{cell} - \bar{Y}_\text{Pollution marginal} - \bar{Y}_\text{Flow marginal} + \bar{Y}_\text{grand}\]

In a balanced 2x2, the four leftovers are the same size, two positive and two negative, so every channel’s squared leftover is \(0.85^2\). Summing over the 20 channels gives \(SS_\text{Interaction} = 20 \times 0.85^2 = 14.45\).


10.6.5 SS Error
The last piece follows by subtraction, since every other term in the identity is already known:
\[SS_\text{Error} = SS_\text{Total} - SS_\text{Pollution} - SS_\text{Flow} - SS_\text{Interaction}\]
\[SS_\text{Error} = 242.95 - 92.45 - 110.45 - 14.45 = 25.6\]
\(SS_\text{Error}\) is the same quantity as \(SS_\text{Within}\) in the one-way ANOVA (Section 8.4.4), the spread of channels around their own cell mean. We can check it directly. The squared distances of the channels from their own cell mean sum to 5.2 in each of the first three cells and 10.0 in the pollution, high-flow cell, and \(5.2 + 5.2 + 5.2 + 10.0 = 25.6\). It is the variation none of the three effects can explain.


10.6.6 Degrees of freedom, mean squares, and \(F\)
Each sum of squares becomes a mean square the same way it did in the one-way ANOVA (Section 8.4.6), by dividing by its degrees of freedom. With \(a\) levels of pollution, \(b\) levels of flow, and \(N\) channels in all:

\(df_\text{Pollution} = a-1 = 1\)
\(df_\text{Flow} = b-1 = 1\)
\(df_\text{Interaction} = (a-1)(b-1) = 1\), the product of the two main effects’ degrees of freedom
\(df_\text{Error} = N-ab = 20-4 = 16\), one lost for each of the four cell means
\(df_\text{Total} = N-1 = 19\), and \(1+1+1+16 = 19\)

Each effect gets its own \(F\), and all three share the same denominator:
\[\begin{aligned}
F_\text{Pollution} &= \frac{MS_\text{Pollution}}{MS_\text{Error}} \\[1.2ex]
F_\text{Flow} &= \frac{MS_\text{Flow}}{MS_\text{Error}} \\[1.2ex]
F_\text{Interaction} &= \frac{MS_\text{Interaction}}{MS_\text{Error}}
\end{aligned}\]
Here \(MS_\text{Error} = 25.60/16 = 1.60\). Every effect has 1 degree of freedom, so each effect’s \(MS\) equals its \(SS\), and Table 10.5 gives each \(F\).

10.6.7 Check your work
R’s aov() builds the same table directly. The * in the formula tells R to include both main effects and their interaction. R writes the interaction row as Pollution:Flow and the error row as Residuals.

all_df <- data.frame(
  Number_species = c(10, 8, 11, 9, 10,  5, 4, 3, 4, 2,
                     12, 13, 14, 11, 13,  9, 8, 10, 11, 12),
  Pollution = rep(c("No Pollution", "Pollution", "No Pollution", "Pollution"), each = 5),
  Flow      = rep(c("Low Flow", "Low Flow", "High Flow", "High Flow"), each = 5)
)
aov_fit <- aov(Number_species ~ Pollution * Flow, data = all_df)
summary(aov_fit)

The SS column matches the hand-calculated values above: 92.45 for Pollution, 110.45 for Flow, 14.45 for the interaction, 25.6 for Error. All three effects are significant here, including the interaction we previewed informally. The difference in the pollution effect between the two flow rates is larger than chance would produce.
This example is balanced (Section 8.5.2), with five stream channels in every condition. With unequal numbers, two things change. First, R computes the sums of squares one term at a time in the order the terms appear in aov(), so changing the order can change the results. Second, the marginal means become estimates from the fitted model, called estimated marginal means, instead of simple averages of the scores. Balanced designs avoid both complications, so plan equal sample sizes when you can.


10.6.8 Checking the assumptions
A factorial ANOVA has the same test-specific assumptions as the one-way ANOVA (Section 8.5.2): similar spread in every cell and approximately normal residuals. Check them the same way, with Levene’s test across the four cells and a Q-Q plot or Shapiro-Wilk test on the residuals of aov_fit.


10.6.9 Effect size in a factorial design
The one-way ANOVA had one effect and so needed one effect size, \(\eta^2 = SS_\text{Between}/SS_\text{Total}\) (Section 8.5.3). A 2x2 runs three tests, so it needs three effect sizes, and the sums of squares we just computed by hand are all the ingredients required.
The direct extension keeps \(SS_\text{Total}\) in the denominator for every effect:
\[
\eta^2 = \frac{SS_\text{Effect}}{SS_\text{Total}}
\]
Each effect then reports its share of all the variation in the study, so the three values plus error’s share add to 1. Adding a second factor that changes the outcome adds that factor’s differences between conditions to the spread of all the scores, so \(SS_\text{Total}\) grows. The larger denominator shrinks the \(\eta^2\) of a factor whose behavior did not change at all, only because you studied something else alongside it.
Partial eta-squared (\(\eta_p^2\)) is the share of the variation left after setting the other effects aside that one effect explains. Its denominator is that effect’s \(SS\) plus \(SS_\text{Error}\):
\[
\eta_p^2 = \frac{SS_\text{Effect}}{SS_\text{Effect} + SS_\text{Error}}
\]
Because each effect gets its own denominator, partial values do not sum to 1. They are always at least as large as the corresponding \(\eta^2\), because \(SS_\text{Effect} + SS_\text{Error}\) is never larger than \(SS_\text{Total}\).
The distinction never came up in Chapter 8, because a one-way ANOVA has only one effect, so there are no other factors to set aside, and \(SS_\text{Effect} + SS_\text{Error}\) is \(SS_\text{Total}\). The two formulas give the same number there.

Flow explains 45% of the total variation, pollution 38%, and the interaction 6%. The interaction is significant, and it is also the smallest of the three effects. Significance and size answer different questions (Chapter 5). A significant \(F\) says the effect is probably not zero, and \(\eta^2\) says how large it is. The interaction still changes what the pollution main effect means.
Say which one you report. Most statistical software, including SPSS and R’s effectsize package, gives you \(\eta_p^2\) by default, and it is the more common choice in published work. Either is defensible, but say which you used, because the two can differ substantially: pollution is \(\eta^2 = 0.38\) but \(\eta_p^2 = 0.78\) here. Reporting the larger number without labeling it overstates the effect. Do not compare \(\eta_p^2\) from one study with \(\eta^2\) from another, because the two use different denominators.

title: 10  Factorial ANOVA
text:
10.7 Interpreting main effects and interactions
A main effect is the difference between the marginal means of one IV, which average across the levels of the other factor. An interaction means the effect of one IV depends on the level of another. So when there is an interaction, the main effect of at least one factor is an average of effects that differ across conditions.

10.7.1 Reading patterns in a 2x2
In any 2x2 ANOVA, each of the three effects is either present or absent, so there are \(2 \times 2 \times 2 = 8\) possible outcome patterns. You don’t need to memorize all eight, but you should learn to read them in a line plot:

These are abstract illustrations of every combination that can occur, so a few of them describe patterns you would not expect ecologically. Use them to learn to recognize the shapes.
Every figure in this chapter puts flow rate on the x-axis and draws one line (or bar) per pollution condition, blue for no pollution and red for pollution.
The eight panels below are numbered to match the table above, so panel “Pattern 3” in the figure is row 3 in the table, and so on.








Figure 10.4: Eight example patterns of main effects and interactions in a pollution × flow design, numbered to match the pattern table above.





Figure 10.5 shows the same patterns in line graph form:








Figure 10.5: Line graphs showing eight possible outcomes for a pollution × flow design. In Patterns 1 and 6 the two lines lie on top of each other.





In the line graphs, interactions are easiest to see:

Parallel lines mean no interaction (the pollution effect is the same at both flow rates).
Non-parallel lines mean an interaction (the pollution effect differs by flow). The lines may cross inside the plot, or they may converge or diverge, which means they would cross if you extended them.
The average gap between the two lines is the main effect of pollution, and the lines’ average rise or fall from low to high flow is the main effect of flow.







TipTip: Which factor goes on the x-axis?



The statistics are identical either way, since the same cell means get plotted regardless. Two rules of thumb make the picture easier to read. Put the factor with more levels on the x-axis, since one long line is easier to follow than several short, crowded ones. And draw the factor whose effect you’re asking about as the lines, so its simple effect at each level of the other factor is the gap between the lines. This chapter puts flow on the x-axis because the question is how the effect of pollution changes with flow.




10.7.2 Simple effects
When an interaction is present, the natural follow-up is to describe each simple effect, the effect of one factor at a single level of the other. Start with the \(\Delta\) values from the cell means, as we did earlier:
\[\begin{aligned}
\Delta_\text{Pollution|Low} &= 9.6 - 3.6 = 6.0 \\
\Delta_\text{Pollution|High} &= 12.6 - 10.0 = 2.6
\end{aligned}\]
Those two numbers describe the interaction. Pollution costs 6.0 species under low flow and 2.6 under high flow. But saying “pollution reduced species count under low flow” is still a claim, and like any claim in this book, it needs its own test, not just a look at the plot.
Testing a simple effect asks whether pollution’s effect holds at one specific level of flow, so it looks like a two-sample comparison: no pollution vs. pollution, at low flow only. One option is to pull out the 10 low-flow channels and run a two-sample \(t\)-test on them alone. That test estimates the error variance from those 10 channels, with 8 degrees of freedom, and ignores the 10 high-flow channels. The omnibus ANOVA above (Chapter 8) already gives a better estimate of that error variance, \(MS_\text{Error}\), from all 20 channels.
The simple-effects test reuses that pooled estimate, \(MS_\text{Error}\) with its 16 degrees of freedom, in a two-sample \(t\):
\[t = \frac{\bar{Y}_\text{NoPoll} - \bar{Y}_\text{Poll}}{\sqrt{MS_\text{Error}\left(\dfrac{1}{n_\text{NoPoll}}+\dfrac{1}{n_\text{Poll}}\right)}}, \qquad df = df_\text{Error}\]
Here the two means are the no-pollution and pollution cell means at one flow rate. Using \(MS_\text{Error}=1.60\) and \(df=16\) from the omnibus table computed earlier, the denominator is the same at both flow rates. Under low flow,
\[\begin{aligned}
\sqrt{MS_\text{Error}\left(\tfrac{1}{5} + \tfrac{1}{5}\right)} &= \sqrt{1.60(0.4)} = 0.80 \\[1.2ex]
t &= \frac{6.0}{0.80} = 7.50
\end{aligned}\]
Table 10.7 gives both tests.




Table 10.7: Simple effects of pollution, tested separately within each flow rate, using the pooled error term from the full model.






Simple effect

Both comparisons clear the critical value, \(t_{crit}(16) = 2.12\) at \(\alpha=0.05\), two-tailed, with \(t = 7.50\) under low flow and \(t = 3.25\) under high flow. So the interaction here does not mean “pollution matters at low flow but not at all at high flow.” That pattern would show up as one significant row and one not. The interaction means “pollution matters at both flow rates, but far more at low flow.”
When a factor has only two levels, as Pollution does here, each simple-effects test compares those two levels, so it is the full answer. When a factor has three or more levels, a significant simple effect says only that some levels differ at that level of the other factor, and pairwise comparisons are needed to say which.


10.7.3 Order of interpretation
When we conduct a two-way ANOVA, we always begin by reading the interaction term, because it decides what the main effects mean.

If the interaction is not significant, examine the two main effects separately, interpreting each as an overall difference averaged across the other factor. If a significant main effect has three or more levels, follow it with Tukey HSD on that factor, exactly as in Section 8.5.4.
If the interaction is significant, lead with the simple effects: how one factor behaves at each level of the other. “Pollution reduced species count sharply under low flow, and less under high flow” is a simple-effects sentence. “There was a main effect of pollution” on its own is not enough. Whether the main effect is still worth reporting depends on the direction of the simple effects:

If the simple effects all point the same way and differ only in size, the main effect still describes something real. Report it, qualified by the interaction: “There was a main effect of pollution, qualified by a Pollution × Flow interaction.”
If one simple effect is near zero, or they point in opposite directions, the main effect is an average that describes no actual condition. Don’t report it as a general effect of that factor.

If neither the interaction nor either main effect is significant, there is nothing to follow up on. Do not run, or interpret, post-hoc tests on a result that never cleared the omnibus test in the first place.

The three examples below show each case of that rule.


10.7.4 A consistent main effect and an interaction








Figure 10.6: Pollution shows a general (main) effect, but the size of that effect differs by flow rate (interaction).





Figure 10.6 shows both a main effect and an interaction. Unpolluted channels are above polluted ones at both flow rates. That is the main effect. But the size of that gap is larger under low flow (12 vs. 5) than under high flow (14 vs. 11), so there’s an interaction too.
There was a main effect of pollution, qualified by a Pollution × Flow interaction. The size of the pollution effect changed with flow rate, larger under low flow and smaller under high flow. The main effect is still real. Pollution is associated with lower species counts at both flow rates. Flow changes how much lower, not the direction.


10.7.5 An “averaged” main effect driven by an interaction








Figure 10.7: An apparent main effect of pollution arises from averaging over an interaction.





Figure 10.7 shows a starker pattern, with a large difference between polluted and unpolluted channels under low flow and no difference at all under high flow.
Yet an ANOVA on data with these cell means can still report a significant main effect of pollution when the error variance is small. Averaged across flow rates, unpolluted channels give \((10+5)/2=7.5\) species and polluted channels give \(5\), a main-effect difference of 2.5. That number is real, but it doesn’t describe what pollution actually does. Pollution removes 5 species under low flow and none under high flow, not 2.5 everywhere. The “main effect” here is an artifact of averaging over a strong interaction.
The ANOVA shows a significant main effect of pollution, but it should not be reported as a general effect, because the pollution effect was large under low flow and zero under high flow. In a case like this, it’s fair to doubt whether pollution has a general effect on species count at all. It may only do damage under specific conditions, in combination with other factors, rather than on its own.


10.7.6 A main effect masked by an interaction








Figure 10.8: Pollution’s effect reverses direction between flow rates, so the main effect averages to zero even though pollution matters at both.





Figure 10.8 shows the most misleading pattern of the three. Under low flow, pollution reduces species count (8 vs. 4). Under high flow, pollution increases it (8 vs. 12). Both are real, sizable effects, just pointed in opposite directions.
Average across flow rates to get a main effect, and the two effects cancel:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{Unpolluted} &= (8+8)/2 = 8 \\
\text{Polluted} &= (4+12)/2 = 8
\end{aligned}\]
The main-effect difference is exactly 0. An ANOVA on data with these cell means would report no main effect of pollution at all, because its two opposite effects average each other out.
This is the case the “read the interaction first” rule exists for. A non-significant main effect here would be true and misleading. Pollution has no effect on average and a large effect in each condition. Reporting only the main effect would suggest pollution is irrelevant, when it has a large effect at both flow rates, in opposite directions.

10.7.7 Reporting the stream result
Back to the stream experiment. Figure 10.9 plots its four cell means. Pollution lowers species count at both flow rates, so the lines never cross. They converge, because the gap under high flow is smaller. This matches the first case in Table 10.8, a consistent main effect and an interaction, so we report the simple effects and the main effect of pollution with its qualification attached.








Figure 10.9: Cell means from the stream experiment. Pollution lowers species count at both flow rates, by more under low flow.











ImportantResults reporting: factorial ANOVA



Lead with the interaction, then give the simple effects. Report a main effect only when the simple effects point the same way, and then with its qualification attached. Every effect gets its own effect size, labeled so the reader knows whether it is \(\eta^2\) or \(\eta_p^2\).

The effect of pollution on macroinvertebrate species count depended on flow rate, \(F(1, 16) = 9.03\), \(p = 0.008\), \(\eta_p^2 = 0.36\). Under low flow, polluted channels supported 6.0 fewer species than unpolluted ones (3.6 vs. 9.6), \(t(16) = 7.50\), \(p < 0.001\). Under high flow that gap narrowed to 2.6 species (10.0 vs. 12.6), \(t(16) = 3.25\), \(p = 0.005\). Both main effects were also significant, pollution \(F(1, 16) = 57.78\), \(p < 0.001\), \(\eta_p^2 = 0.78\), and flow \(F(1, 16) = 69.03\), \(p < 0.001\), \(\eta_p^2 = 0.81\), but each should be read in light of the interaction: pollution costs a stream far more species when the water is moving slowly.

title: 10  Factorial ANOVA
text:
10.8 More complicated designs
Up until now we have focused on the simplest case for factorial designs, the 2x2 design, with two IVs, each with 2 levels. The same logic extends to larger designs.

10.8.1 3x2 design
This design works like the 2x2, with one more level added to one factor. The test structure is the same (two main effects and one interaction).
The same stream example extends to a 3x2. Suppose we examine macroinvertebrate species count (the dependent variable, DV) under three flow rates (low, medium, high) crossed with two pollution conditions (no pollution vs. pollution).

The main effect of pollution tests whether, on average, polluted and unpolluted channels differ in species count across all flow rates.
The main effect of flow tests whether mean species count differs among flow rates.
The interaction tests whether the pollution effect (unpolluted − polluted) changes with flow rate.

In a 2x2 design, you look for an interaction by checking whether the lines are parallel. In a 3x2, the idea is the same, but with three points per line the patterns are harder to read.
You have three hypotheses in a 3x2 factorial design:
Hypothesis 1: Main effect of flow

Null (\(H_{0,\text{Flow}}\)): \(\mu_{\text{Low}} = \mu_{\text{Medium}} = \mu_{\text{High}}\)
Alternative (\(H_{a,\text{Flow}}\)): At least one flow rate mean differs from the others.

Hypothesis 2: Main effect of pollution

Null (\(H_{0,\text{Pollution}}\)): \(\mu_{\text{NoPoll}} = \mu_{\text{Poll}}\)
Alternative (\(H_{a,\text{Pollution}}\)): Mean species count differs between polluted and unpolluted channels.

Hypothesis 3: Pollution × flow interaction

Null (\(H_{0,\text{int}}\)): The pollution effect is the same across all flow rates. \([ (\mu_{\text{NoPoll,Low}}-\mu_{\text{Poll,Low}}) = (\mu_{\text{NoPoll,Medium}}-\mu_{\text{Poll,Medium}}) = (\mu_{\text{NoPoll,High}}-\mu_{\text{Poll,High}}) ]\)
Alternative (\(H_{a,\text{int}}\)): The pollution effect differs across flow rates, meaning at least one of the three pollution differences is not equal to the others.

One factorial ANOVA is better than a separate \(t\)-test of polluted vs. unpolluted channels at each of the three flow rates, for two reasons. First, the ANOVA estimates the error variance from all six cells, which gives more degrees of freedom and so more power for each test. Second, it gives a formal test of the interaction, which is often the scientific question.
Figure 10.10 shows example means for this design.








Figure 10.10: Example means for a 3 × 2 pollution × flow design.





The figure shows invented means for all six conditions.

Main effect of pollution. Averaged across flow rates, unpolluted channels support higher species counts (10 vs. 7.3). The “No Pollution” line sits above the “Pollution” line at low and medium flow, and the two coincide at high flow.
Main effect of flow. Averaged over pollution condition, species counts are lowest at low flow (8) and higher at medium and high flow (9 each).
Interaction between pollution and flow. An interaction occurs when the effect of one IV depends on the levels of another. The pollution gap is 6 species at low flow, 2 at medium, and 0 at high. So the size of the pollution effect changes with flow rate, which is also why the pollution main effect above describes no single flow condition well. The interaction test in the ANOVA would say whether these differences are larger than chance would produce.

If there were no interaction and no main effect of flow, we would see something like the pattern in Figure 10.11.








Figure 10.11: Example means for a 3 × 2 design with a main effect of pollution and no other effects.





Figure 10.12 shows a different interaction pattern.








Figure 10.12: Example means for a 3 × 2 design showing a different interaction pattern.





The means show an interaction here too. The pollution effect is measured three times, once at each flow rate. It is the same at low and medium flow but much smaller at high flow, so its size depends on the level of flow.

title: 10  Factorial ANOVA
text:
10.9 Designs beyond this course
Larger factorial designs use the same logic as the 2x2. But complexity grows quickly, both in the number of effects and in how hard they are to interpret.

10.9.1 2x2x2 (three-factor) designs
A 2x2x2 design adds a third IV with two levels. Start from the two-way interaction in the stream experiment. Pollution lowered species count by 6.0 under low flow and by 2.6 under high flow, so the pollution × flow interaction is the difference between those two simple effects, \(6.0 - 2.6 = 3.4\) species.
Now suppose the same experiment ran in summer and again in winter, so season is a third IV. Each season has its own 2x2 and its own pollution × flow interaction. A three-way interaction means that the two-way interaction changes across the third factor. If the interaction were 3.4 species in summer and close to 0 in winter, the pollution × flow interaction would depend on season, which is a three-way interaction. If both seasons showed about 3.4, there would be no three-way interaction, even though each season has a two-way interaction. With three IVs, each interaction between two of them is a two-way interaction. Table 10.10 lists all seven effects.



Table 10.10: The seven effects in a 2x2x2 design, using the stream experiment with season added.










Effect
How many
What it asks, with season added




Main effects
3
Does pollution change the mean? Flow? Season? Each is averaged across the other two IVs


Two-way interactions
3
Does the pollution effect depend on flow, or on season? Does the flow effect depend on season?


Three-way interaction
1
Does the pollution × flow interaction change between summer and winter?






Graph it as two 2x2 plots side by side, one for each season. A three-way interaction shows up as a different pattern of lines in the two plots. In applied research, most studies stop at two factors unless there’s a strong reason to add more.


10.9.2 Mixed designs
A mixed design has at least one between-subjects factor and at least one within-subjects factor. For example, sites or treatments could be a between-subjects factor, and repeated measures over time a within-subjects factor.
The interpretation of main effects and interactions is the same, but the error terms used in the \(F\)-tests differ, and the data structure must account for repeated measures. These models are important in longitudinal and environmental time-series studies, but they’re beyond our current scope.

title: 10  Factorial ANOVA
text:
10.10 Chapter Summary
Why it matters. Single-factor designs can tell you whether something has an effect. Factorial designs tell you what changes that effect, which is usually the more interesting scientific question, and often the more realistic one for environmental systems where drivers act together. An interaction changes what every other term in the table means, so interpreting the table is part of the analysis. Chapter 11 replaces one factor with a continuous covariate.
Core ideas

Fully crossed means every combination. A factorial design pairs every level of each IV with every level of the others. The notation says the structure: 2x2 is four conditions, 3x2 is six.
A 2x2 tests three things. One main effect per factor, plus their interaction. That means three null hypotheses, and you should be able to state all three in plain language before running anything.
An interaction is a difference between differences. It asks whether the effect of one factor changes across levels of another. The interaction sum of squares measures it.
The partition extends the one-way logic. \(SS_\text{Total}\) now splits into each main effect, the interaction, and error (\(SS_\text{Error}\), Chapter 8’s \(SS_\text{Within}\) in the one-way ANOVA). Each effect gets its own \(F\), all sharing \(MS_\text{Error}\) as the denominator. Working one table through by hand shows that the interaction term is the only new piece.
Three tests, three effect sizes. \(\eta^2\) divides each effect’s \(SS\) by \(SS_\text{Total}\), and \(\eta_p^2\) divides it by that effect plus error. Partial values are at least as large and do not sum to 1, so label which one you are reporting. A significant effect can still be a small one, which is exactly the case for this chapter’s interaction.
Read the interaction first. If it’s significant, lead with simple effects: what factor A does at each level of B, as \(\Delta\) values from the cell means, tested with the pooled \(MS_\text{Error}\). A main effect can still be reported, qualified, when the simple effects all point the same way. When one is near zero or they reverse, the main effect describes no actual condition. When the interaction is not significant, interpret each main effect as an overall difference, with Tukey HSD for a factor with three or more levels.
Learn to read the picture. In a line plot, parallel lines mean no interaction, and lines that cross, inside the plot or if extended, mean an interaction. The average gap between the lines is one main effect, and the lines’ average rise or fall is the other. There are eight possible patterns in a 2x2. The plot shows which pattern the cell means follow, and the interaction \(F\) test says whether the lines differ from parallel by more than chance would produce.
An averaged main effect can be an artifact. A factor that matters a lot in one condition and not at all in another can still produce a “significant main effect” once you average across conditions. That number is correct arithmetic, but it matches the pollution effect at neither flow rate.
Bigger designs, same tests, harder reading. A 3x2 has the same three tests as a 2x2, but three points per line are harder to read than two. Beyond that, a three-factor design brings three main effects, three two-way interactions, and a three-way interaction, and interpretability falls off fast. Use only as many factors as your question actually needs.

title: 11  Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA)
text:
11.1 Why adjust for anything?
Download this chapter (PDF)
We’ve now covered regression (Chapter 9) and ANOVA (Chapters 8 and 10). This chapter merges them:
\[\text{Regression} + \text{ANOVA} = \text{ANCOVA}\]
The last chapter compared macroinvertebrate species count across two discrete Pollution categories, present or absent, and two Flow categories, low or high. But suppose you measured each channel’s pollution concentration instead of labeling it present or absent.
In each question, a continuous variable is related to the outcome, and a categorical variable splits the observations into groups.
The first question points to a limitation of the last chapter. “Pollution: present or absent” simplifies a continuous measurement, a concentration in parts per billion. Sorting continuous measurements into “high” and “low” buckets throws away the information a covariate needs, which is how much more polluted a channel is, not just whether it is polluted. Whenever you have the measured values, analyze them as a continuous covariate instead of forcing them into groups first. With a categorical factor still in the design, that analysis is ANCOVA. With no categorical factor left, it is plain regression.
Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) is a linear model with a continuous outcome, at least one continuous predictor (the covariate), and at least one categorical predictor (the factor). ANCOVA is built directly on the regression equation from Chapter 9. A simple linear model is
\[y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \varepsilon\]
Here \(\beta_0\) is the intercept, \(\beta_1\) is the slope, and \(\varepsilon\) is the error. The model describes a single line.
ANCOVA adds a categorical factor to that equation. The chapter asks whether every group follows the same line, whether the groups share a slope but need different intercepts, or whether each group needs its own slope.
We answer it in order: first check that the model explains anything at all, then test whether the groups have different slopes, and only if the slopes are parallel, test whether the groups differ in adjusted means. Step 2 below defines adjusted means, the group means you would expect if both groups had the same average covariate value.
Table 11.1 places ANCOVA beside regression and the two kinds of ANOVA from Chapters 8 to 10, each written as a model.
Adjusting for a variable means comparing groups at the same value of that variable. Simpson’s paradox, where a pattern in combined data reverses once you split the data into meaningful groups, shows what can go wrong without adjusting.
The case fatality rate (CFR) is the percentage of confirmed cases that ended in death. During the COVID-19 pandemic, early data showed that Italy’s overall case fatality rate was higher than China’s. But once researchers split the cases by age group, the trend flipped. In every age group except the youngest, where neither country recorded a death, the fatality rate was higher in China. The apparent contradiction was explained by differences in the age distribution of cases (von Kügelgen et al. 2021).
The numbers below are the ones that study compared. China’s cases and deaths by age are as reported on February 17, 2020, and Italy’s are as reported on March 9, 2020.
Figure 11.1: Crude case fatality rates. Italy appears to have a higher fatality rate than China when all cases are combined.
At face value, Italy looks worse. But the two countries’ cases might differ in age, and age matters because older people are much more likely to die from COVID than younger people. In these numbers, 13.2% of Italy’s cases aged 80 and over died, against none of the 43 cases under 10. So we split cases into 10-year age bands. Within every band where anyone died, China’s fatality rate is higher.
Figure 11.2: Fatality rates by age group. In every age band where anyone died, China’s CFR exceeds Italy’s.

Table 11.2 lists the rates themselves. The reversal happens because Italy’s cases were older on average and China’s were younger (Figure 11.3). A country’s overall fatality rate is an average of its age-band rates, weighted by the share of that country’s cases in each band. Italy had a larger share of its cases in the oldest bands, where fatality rates are highest, so its overall rate is pulled up. China had a larger share of its cases in the younger bands, where fatality rates are low, so its overall rate is pulled down. Aggregating without adjusting for age hid the within-group pattern entirely. Age is a confounding variable (Section 2.5.6), related both to which country a case came from and to whether the case was fatal.
Figure 11.3: Case age distribution by country. Italy’s cases are older on average, and China’s are younger.
This kind of reversal happens when the groups differ in their mix of a third variable, here age. Once you compare within each level of the third variable, here within each age band, the within-group pattern shows up again.
ANCOVA handles this situation when the third variable is continuous, instead of grouped into categories like the age bands above. It compares groups at the same covariate value, so a difference between the groups on that covariate does not distort the comparison.

title: 11  Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA)
text:
11.2 Covariates and fixed factors
A covariate is a continuous predictor that is related to the outcome and helps explain part of its variation. In environmental studies, common covariates include temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, and pollution concentration. Including one lets us remove the variation it explains, so the test of the group difference is clearer.
A fixed factor is a categorical predictor whose levels the researcher chose on purpose, such as urban vs. rural or shaded vs. open canopy. A random factor is a categorical predictor whose levels are a sample from a larger population of possible levels. For example, the counties your streams are in could be a random factor. You aren’t interested in those ten counties for their own sake. They represent a larger population of counties, and you want your conclusions to apply beyond the ones you sampled.
Every categorical predictor in this chapter is a fixed factor. The distinction between fixed and random factors matters once you build mixed-effects models, which contain both kinds of factor. This course does not cover them. Mixed-effects models are a different idea from the mixed design (Section 10.9.2), which mixes between-subjects and within-subjects factors.

title: 11  Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA)
text:
11.3 What ANCOVA is
ANCOVA asks whether a relationship holds up across groups. That framing fits environmental work particularly well, because you usually can’t experimentally strip out a covariate like temperature, rainfall, or season anyway. Often you wouldn’t want to. It may be the reason you designed the study in the first place. In this chapter’s main example, the covariate’s relationship with the outcome is the question, and the interaction is the result you are testing for.






NoteNote: ANCOVA with a nuisance covariate



Elsewhere the covariate is a nuisance instead, a variable you adjust for so a group comparison is fair (the second example at the end of this chapter). In that version, you test the interaction to check whether the slopes can be treated as parallel before comparing the groups.
A classic version from psychology compares anxiety scores across two therapy groups after treatment, adjusting for pre-treatment scores.
Both versions use the same test and the same math. They differ only in which term you came to interpret, so decide that before you fit anything.


For ANCOVA, you need:

A continuous dependent variable (the outcome)
At least one continuous independent variable (covariate)
At least one categorical independent variable (a fixed factor, in this course)


11.3.1 Indicator variables and how they work
Before reading coefficients off an ANCOVA table, it helps to see how one equation can represent two groups at once.
An indicator variable is a variable that equals 1 for observations in one group and 0 for all other observations. Categorical predictors get into a linear model as indicator variables (you’ll also see them called dummy variables). For a factor with \(k\) groups you include \(k-1\) indicators. The group left out needs no indicator of its own, because an observation with 0 on every indicator must belong to it. That group is the reference group, and every coefficient involving the factor is interpreted relative to it. With two groups, one indicator does the whole job:
\[G = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{group 1 (the reference group)} \\ 1 & \text{group 2} \end{cases}\]
In R, lm(y ~ x + Group) creates these indicators for you automatically.
An indicator can change the intercept, the slope, or both. When an indicator variable is turned on (set to 1), it activates the terms multiplied by that variable. Where the indicator appears in the model decides which of these changes.
Consider two predictors: a continuous variable \(x\) and an indicator \(G\) (0 or 1). The numbers below are arbitrary, chosen to make the arithmetic clean. The worked example later in this chapter plugs in fitted coefficients for air pollution and area type. Use this model:
\[y = 3 + 2x - 7G + 1(xG)\]
When \(G = 0\) (indicator off), only the baseline terms are active:
\[y = 2x + 3 \qquad \text{slope} = 2, \ \text{intercept} = 3\]
When \(G = 1\) (indicator on), the term \(1(xG)\) becomes \(1x\) and the term \(-7G\) becomes \(-7\). Adding them to the baseline terms and collecting the \(x\) terms and the constants gives
\[\begin{aligned}
y &= (2x + 3) + (1x - 7) \\
&= (2 + 1)x + (3 - 7) \\
&= 3x - 4
\end{aligned}\]
so the slope is 3 and the intercept is \(-4\).
Turning on the indicator adds +1 to the slope and −7 to the intercept. The one equation gives two different lines, and the value of the indicator decides which one applies.
Linear models represent different groups this way. The indicator (\(G\)) and its interaction with \(x\) let a single equation shift the intercept and the slope for each group. ANCOVA uses exactly this logic to test, in order, whether the slopes differ between groups (the \(x G\) term) and, if they don’t, whether the adjusted means differ (the \(G\) term).
Naming the pieces. Written in the general form, the same equation gives each coefficient a name and a meaning:
\[y = \underbrace{\beta_0}_{\text{reference intercept}} + \underbrace{\beta_1 x}_{\text{reference slope}} + \underbrace{\beta_2 G}_{\text{intercept shift}} + \underbrace{\beta_3 x G}_{\text{slope shift}} + \varepsilon\]

\(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) describe the line for the reference group (\(G=0\)).
\(\beta_2\) is how much the intercept moves for the other group.
\(\beta_3\) is how much the slope changes for the other group. This is the interaction term. In Chapter 10, an interaction meant that the effect of one factor depended on the level of the other factor. Here it means that the effect of \(x\), its slope, depends on the group. Both are the same idea, because an interaction means the effect of one predictor depends on the value of another, whether that predictor is a factor or a covariate.

The parallel-lines model includes \(\beta_2\) but leaves out \(\beta_3\), so the intercept can shift between groups but the slope cannot, and the two lines are parallel. When the slope difference is not significant, we use this simpler model instead of keeping the interaction term.






NoteNote: How R names the four coefficients



These are the four coefficients R reports for this model, and each one can be checked against a graph of the two group lines. For lm(y ~ x * Group), where Group has levels A (the reference) and B, R names the rows (Intercept) for \(\beta_0\), x for \(\beta_1\), GroupB for \(\beta_2\), and x:GroupB for \(\beta_3\). The worked example below follows the same pattern: (Intercept), AirPollution, AreaTypeUrban, and AirPollution:AreaTypeUrban.




11.3.2 The steps of an ANCOVA
Model. For one covariate (\(x\)) and a two-level group indicator \(G\in\{0,1\}\),
\[y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\beta_2 G+\beta_3(x\times G)+\varepsilon\]
Figure 11.4 shows the three possibilities this model can produce.








Figure 11.4: The question ANCOVA answers. Left: one line describes both groups. Middle: the groups need different intercepts but share a slope, so the lines are parallel. Right: the groups need different slopes, so the lines are not parallel and the gap between them depends on where you look.





ANCOVA works right to left across that figure. It first asks whether the rightmost panel is what we have (do the slopes differ?), and only if the answer is no does it ask whether we have the middle panel or the leftmost (are the parallel lines at different heights?).
Step 0: Does the model explain anything? Before looking at any single term, check the whole-model \(F\)-test, the regression \(F\) from Section 9.4 applied to all the terms at once, which asks whether the covariate, the group, and their interaction together explain more of \(y\) than chance would.

Null (\(H_0\)): none of the three terms explains \(y\), \(\beta_1=\beta_2=\beta_3=0\).
Alternative (\(H_a\)): at least one of \(\beta_1\), \(\beta_2\), \(\beta_3\) is not 0.

R reports it on the last line of summary(lm(...)). If it is not significant, stop. The data give no evidence that the covariate, the group, or their interaction explains \(y\), so no single term is worth interpreting.
Step 1: Are slopes equal across groups?

Null (\(H_{0,\text{int}}\)): parallel lines, the same slope in both groups, \(\beta_3=0\).
Alternative (\(H_{a,\text{int}}\)): different slopes, \(\beta_3\neq 0\).

If Step 1 rejects. The slopes differ, so stop testing the group term. There is no single group difference to test, because the gap between the lines changes along the covariate. Describe each group’s line instead. The model gives both slopes (the reference group’s is \(\beta_1\), the other group’s is \(\beta_1+\beta_3\)), but it does not test whether each one differs from zero. To test each slope, fit a separate simple regression within each group.
Step 2: Are adjusted means equal? (only if Step 1 did not reject \(H_{0,\text{int}}\), so the slopes are treated as parallel) Drop the interaction and refit the parallel-lines model,
\[y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\beta_2 G+\varepsilon\]

Null (\(H_{0,\text{group}}\)): no difference between the groups at the same covariate value, \(\beta_2=0\).
Alternative (\(H_{a,\text{group}}\)): the groups differ at the same covariate value, \(\beta_2\neq 0\).

With parallel lines, \(\beta_2\) is the vertical gap between the two lines, and it is the same at every value of \(x\). The adjusted difference is how much the groups differ when they are compared at the same covariate value, so with parallel lines it equals \(\beta_2\).
The adjusted means are the group means you would expect if both groups had the same average covariate value. To get them, evaluate each group’s line at the overall mean of \(x\). Raw group means compare the groups at whatever covariate values each group happens to have. Adjusted means compare them at one shared covariate value, the overall mean of \(x\). So if one group happens to have higher covariate values, that difference does not enter the comparison. The second example at the end of this chapter works through one.
In the parallel-lines model, \(\beta_1\) is the common slope.
Intercepts and centering. Intercepts are evaluated at \(x=0\). In the model with an interaction, the lines can have different slopes, so \(\beta_2\) compares the groups at \(x=0\) only, which may be far outside the data. Centering the covariate means subtracting its mean from every value, \(\tilde x = x - \bar x\). After centering, \(\tilde x = 0\) where \(x = \bar x\), so the intercept and \(\beta_2\) now describe the lines at the average covariate value. In the parallel-lines model the gap is the same everywhere, so centering changes the intercept but not \(\beta_2\).
What to report.

If \(x\times G\) is significant: “The effect of \(x\) differs by group,” then each group’s line with its own slope test, and a figure with separate fitted lines.
If \(x\times G\) is not significant: the common slope \(\beta_1\) and the adjusted group difference \(\beta_2\) (or the adjusted means), with a figure showing parallel lines.

As always, statistical significance doesn’t guarantee ecological or practical importance. Interpret a rejected null in light of the study’s design, measurement precision, and the actual size of the effect, not just its \(p\)-value.






CautionWarning: Two ways to misread an ANCOVA




Interpreting the group term when the interaction is significant. With different slopes, the gap between the groups changes along the covariate, so no single group difference or adjusted mean describes it.
Comparing intercepts when \(x\) is not centered. The intercepts then compare the groups at \(x = 0\), which may be outside the data.





11.3.3 Checking ANCOVA’s assumptions
Most of these are ones ANOVA already needed. Three are new because a covariate has entered the model (Table 11.3).



Table 11.3: Assumptions of ANCOVA and how to check them.










Assumption
New with ANCOVA?
How to check




Normal residuals and similar variances across groups
No (Sections 8.5.2 and 9.6)
Q-Q plot, residuals-versus-fitted plot, Levene’s test


Linearity within each group
Yes
A scatter plot with a fitted line for each group


Homogeneity of slopes (the groups’ lines are parallel)
Yes
The interaction test (Step 1), not a check run beforehand


The covariate is measured with little error and is not affected by the group factor (the treatment)
Yes
The study design






If the covariate is measured with error, ANCOVA only partly adjusts for group differences in the covariate, and the leftover difference can look like a treatment effect. If the treatment changes the covariate, adjusting for the covariate removes part of the treatment’s own effect, and the adjusted difference understates it.
Table 11.4 collects the three steps of an ANCOVA on one card.



Table 11.4: Test card: ANCOVA.









Purpose
Does the covariate’s relationship with the outcome differ between groups?
If not, do the groups differ at the same covariate value?


Hypotheses
Step 0: \(H_0: \beta_1=\beta_2=\beta_3=0\)
Step 1: \(H_{0,\text{int}}: \beta_3 = 0\) (parallel lines)
Step 2, only if Step 1 fails to reject: \(H_{0,\text{group}}: \beta_2 = 0\) in the parallel-lines model


Assumptions
Normal residuals and similar variances across groups
Linearity within each group
Homogeneity of slopes (tested in Step 1)
A covariate measured with little error and not affected by the treatment


Test statistic
Model: \(y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\beta_2 G+\beta_3(x\times G)+\varepsilon\)
Step 0: whole-model \(F(3, N-4)\)
Step 1: \(F(1, N-4)\) for the \(x \times G\) row
Step 2: \(t = b_2/SE(b_2)\), \(df = N - 3\)


Report
If \(x \times G\) is significant: its \(F(df)\), \(p\), model \(R^2\), and each group’s slope from a separate regression with \(t(df)\) and \(p\)
If not: the adjusted difference \(b_2\) with \(t(df)\), \(p\) and 95% CI, the adjusted means, the common slope, and the interaction \(F\)

title: 11  Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA)
text:
11.4 Full ANCOVA example

11.4.1 Birds, air pollution and area type
Suppose we are studying the effect of air pollution, measured as PM2.5 (fine particulate matter, in µg/m³), on bird density, in birds per hectare, and we want to know whether that relationship differs between urban and rural areas. Figure 11.5 lays out the design.








Figure 11.5: An ANCOVA design: one continuous predictor and one categorical factor.





This design has the same structure as the factorial design in Chapter 10. Both cross two predictors and ask whether one changes the effect of the other. The only difference is that factorial’s second predictor has levels, while ANCOVA’s is a continuous range.
Both groups span the full pollution range, so rural sites are not simply the clean ones. An adjusted comparison compares the groups at the same pollution level, and that only works where both groups have sites at that level. Without the overlap, each group’s line would have to be extended past its own data, the extrapolation problem from Section 9.7.
We might expect pollution to have a stronger negative effect in urban areas. Urban habitat is already fragmented and offers birds fewer clean patches to retreat to, while rural areas have more intact habitat nearby.
In the ANCOVA model, area type enters as an indicator variable, and air pollution enters as the covariate.


11.4.2 Null and alternative hypotheses in our example ANCOVA
First, we state the hypotheses for each step:

Whole model. Do air pollution, area type, and their interaction together explain bird density?
\(H_0: \beta_1=\beta_2=\beta_3=0\)
Slopes (interaction). Does air pollution affect bird density the same way at urban and rural sites?
\(H_{0,\text{int}}: \beta_3 = 0\) (parallel lines)
\(H_{a,\text{int}}: \beta_3 \neq 0\)
A significant interaction means the slopes differ, and air pollution’s relationship with bird density depends on area type.
Adjusted means (only if the slopes are parallel). At the same level of air pollution, do urban and rural sites differ in bird density?
\(H_{0,\text{group}}: \beta_2 = 0\)
\(H_{a,\text{group}}: \beta_2 \neq 0\)



11.4.3 The data
The data in this example are invented. There are 200 sites, about half urban and half rural, with PM2.5 between 5 and 30 µg/m³. The true slope is \(-0.25\) birds per hectare for each 1 µg/m³ of PM2.5 at rural sites and \(-0.75\) at urban sites, plus random scatter, so the fitted slopes below come out near these values but not on them. In this draw the fitted urban slope is about twice the rural slope, though the true urban slope is three times as steep.
Before fitting the model, look at the data. Figure 11.6 shows the outcome, bird density, by area type, which gives a quick sense of whether urban and rural areas differ on average.








Figure 11.6: Bird density by area type. Rural sites have higher bird density than urban ones.





Bird density is higher at rural sites, with a median of 35 birds against 25 at urban sites, consistent with what we might expect ecologically.
Next, check the covariate, air pollution. If the covariate differs sharply between groups, ANCOVA adjusts for that difference. If it doesn’t, the adjusted group difference will be close to the raw difference in group means.








Figure 11.7: Air pollution by area type. The two groups look broadly similar, so there is no large covariate imbalance for the model to adjust away.





Air pollution is similar at urban and rural sites. The medians are 17.1 at rural sites and 15.2 at urban sites, a small gap compared with the range of about 5 to 30 µg/m³. This plot doesn’t test anything, but it tells us what to expect. Because pollution is similar in the two groups, a group difference in bird density is unlikely to come from a difference in pollution.


11.4.4 Results of the ANCOVA model
Fit the model. This is the same aov() call we used for one-way and factorial ANOVA. Because AirPollution is numeric instead of a factor, aov() treats it as a continuous covariate, so R needs no separate ANCOVA function.

ancova <- aov(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution * AreaType, data = data)

Step 0: the whole model. summary(lm()) reports \(F(3, 196) = 120.44\), \(p < 0.001\), with \(R^2 = 0.65\). The model explains more of the variation in bird density than chance would, so we continue.
Step 1: the interaction. The AirPollution:AreaType row tests \(H_{0,\text{int}}\): \(F(1, 196) = 10.99\), \(p = 0.001\). We reject \(H_{0,\text{int}}\), so the slopes are not parallel. Air pollution’s relationship with bird density depends on area type, so we stop here and do not test adjusted means.
What the other two rows are. The table still has rows for AirPollution and AreaType, both with \(p < 0.001\), so it is tempting to read them, but they don’t answer this chapter’s question. R builds these rows in sequence, which means each row tests its term after the terms listed above it have been fitted. AirPollution tests one average slope for all 200 sites, ignoring area type, and AreaType tests a group difference after that single slope is fitted. Once the interaction says the slopes differ, neither row describes the data. There is no single slope, and the group difference depends on where along the pollution gradient you look. Because the rows are built in sequence and the groups are unequal in size (97 rural, 103 urban), listing the terms in a different order would also change their sums of squares.
Reading the coefficients.
Fitting the same model with lm() shows the regression coefficients directly, so we can see how each term contributes to predicting bird density.

ancova_lm <- lm(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution * AreaType, data = data)

R automatically converts the categorical AreaType variable into a 0/1 indicator, the same \(G\) from the indicator-variable section earlier in this chapter. It picks one level (here, “Rural,” alphabetically first) as the reference, and every coefficient involving AreaType is interpreted relative to that reference. That’s why you see a coefficient called AreaTypeUrban but no separate AreaTypeRural term.
These coefficients give the direction and magnitude of each effect:

(Intercept). Estimated mean bird density for rural sites (the reference group) when air pollution is zero.
AirPollution. Slope of the relationship between pollution and bird density in rural sites. This is not the same quantity as the AirPollution row of the ANOVA table above, which was one average slope for both groups.
AreaTypeUrban. Difference in intercept between urban and rural areas, which compares the groups at air pollution = 0.
AirPollution:AreaTypeUrban. Difference in slope between urban and rural areas (the interaction).

Visualize the interaction.
A scatter plot with fitted regression lines (Figure 11.8) lets us see how air pollution relates to bird density for each area type.








Figure 11.8: Bird density against air pollution, with a separate fitted line for each area type. Both lines slope down, but the urban line falls about twice as steeply.





The two fitted lines have different slopes, which is the interaction the test detected. Both lines slope downward, so pollution is associated with fewer birds in both settings, but the urban line drops roughly twice as fast. The lines are about 7.6 birds apart at the lowest pollution levels and about 15.5 apart at the highest.
Testing each group’s slope. The interaction told us the two slopes differ from each other. It did not tell us whether each one differs from zero, so we fit a separate simple regression within each group.

lm(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution, data = subset(data, AreaType == "Rural"))
lm(BirdDensity ~ AirPollution, data = subset(data, AreaType == "Urban"))

Both slopes are significant. Bird density falls with pollution at rural sites and falls about twice as steeply at urban sites. The slope estimates match the ANCOVA’s, \(-0.346\) for rural and \(-0.346 + (-0.319) \approx -0.665\) for urban, because a model with an interaction fits each group its own line. Only the tests are new, and their standard errors differ slightly because each regression estimates its own error variance.
The points scatter around each line. The model’s \(R^2\) is 0.65, so air pollution, area type, and their interaction explain about 65% of the variation in bird density. The remaining 35% is the random scatter built into these invented data. In field data, that remainder would include other factors, measurement noise, and natural variability. An \(R^2\) this large is strong by the standards of field data, and it is large here partly because the data were invented to illustrate the method.
Centering the covariate.
Interpreting intercepts at \(x = 0\) can be misleading when “zero pollution” isn’t meaningful.
By centering the covariate (subtracting its mean), we make the intercept the predicted bird density for rural sites at mean air pollution instead.

Centering doesn’t change the slopes, the interaction, or their \(p\)-values. It moves the intercept and the group term, and the group term’s test now compares the groups at average pollution instead of at zero, so its \(p\)-value changes too.
Interpreting the centered model. The mean pollution level is about 17 µg/m³.

Intercept (35.8). Predicted bird density for rural sites at average air pollution.
AreaTypeUrban (\(-11.4\)). At the mean pollution level, urban sites have about 11 fewer birds than rural sites.
AirPollution_c (\(-0.346\)). Slope for rural sites: bird density falls by about 0.35 birds per hectare for each additional 1 µg/m³ of PM2.5.
Interaction (\(-0.319\)). Difference in slopes between groups. The urban slope = \(-0.346 + (-0.319) \approx -0.66\), roughly twice as steep a decline as in rural sites.

The group difference changed when we centered, from \(-5.9\) to \(-11.4\). Uncentered, the term compares groups at pollution = 0, a value outside the observed data. Centered, it compares them at average pollution, a value inside the observed range. When slopes differ, “the group difference” is not one number. It depends on where along the covariate you look.
Summarize and interpret.
The significant interaction shows that air pollution’s effect on bird density depends on area type. Bird density declines with pollution in both settings, but the decline is about twice as steep in urban sites. Because the interaction is significant, we focus on these different slopes, not on adjusted mean differences.
If the interaction had not been significant, we would instead drop the interaction term and interpret the parallel-lines model, comparing adjusted means between groups. The next example shows that case.






ImportantResults reporting: ANCOVA




Results from the ANCOVA indicated that air pollution’s effect on bird density depended on area type, \(F(1, 196) = 10.99\), \(p = 0.001\), model \(R^2 = 0.65\). Separate regressions showed that bird density declined with increasing pollution at both rural sites, \(b_1 = -0.35\) birds per hectare for each 1 µg/m³ of PM2.5, \(t(95) = -5.29\), \(p < 0.001\), and urban sites, \(b_1 = -0.66\), \(t(101) = -9.43\), \(p < 0.001\), with the urban decline roughly twice as steep. These findings suggest that urbanization intensifies the pollution-bird density relationship and may point toward the need for area-specific conservation strategies.
