section: 11.5 Second example: when the covariate is a nuisance
text:
11.5 Second example: when the covariate is a nuisance
In the bird example, the covariate relationship was the question, and the interaction was the finding. The other way you’ll see ANCOVA reverses those roles. A nuisance covariate is a covariate you adjust for so that a group comparison is fair, when the group comparison is the question. This is also the continuous version of the Simpson’s paradox problem the chapter opened with.
Table 11.6 compares the two ways this chapter uses ANCOVA.



Table 11.6: Two roles for the covariate in ANCOVA.











Role of the covariate
The covariate is
What you interpret
Example in this chapter




Covariate as the question
The relationship you came to study
The interaction term \(\beta_3\), which tests whether the slopes differ
Air pollution and bird density, urban vs. rural sites


Nuisance covariate
Something to adjust for so the group comparison is fair
The group term \(\beta_2\), the adjusted difference, from the parallel-lines model
Occupancy and electricity use, retrofitted vs. standard buildings







11.5.1 Retrofits and electricity use
A city facilities office wants to know whether energy retrofits (new insulation, lighting, and controls) reduced electricity use. It compares 30 retrofitted buildings with 30 standard ones. Electricity use depends heavily on how many people are in a building, and the retrofitted buildings happen to be the busier ones. These buildings are invented. In the invented data, a retrofit cuts electricity use by 40 kWh per day at any occupancy, both kinds of building use 2 more kWh per day for each extra occupant, and retrofitted buildings hold 60 to 120 people against 30 to 90 for standard ones.
Occupancy also passes the last check on the assumptions list. A retrofit changes a building’s equipment, not how many people use it, so adjusting for occupancy doesn’t remove any of the retrofit’s own effect.


11.5.2 The raw comparison
Average daily occupancy is 93.5 people in the retrofitted buildings and 59.4 in the standard ones. Figure 11.9 compares electricity use without adjusting for occupancy. Retrofitted buildings use more, 342.1 vs. 318.0 kWh per day, and a two-sample \(t\)-test calls that difference significant, \(t(58) = 2.16\), \(p = 0.035\). Taken at face value, the retrofits made things worse.








Figure 11.9: Daily electricity use by building type, ignoring occupancy. Diamonds mark the group means.







11.5.3 The ANCOVA
Step 0: the whole model. \(F(3, 56) = 56.61\), \(p < 0.001\). The model explains more of the variation in electricity use than chance would, so we continue.
Step 1: the interaction. The Occupancy:Type row gives \(F(1, 56) = 0.01\), \(p = 0.927\). We fail to reject \(H_{0,\text{int}}\), so we treat the slopes as parallel. Each additional occupant adds about the same amount of electricity in either kind of building. We drop the interaction and refit.
Step 2: the adjusted difference. Table 11.7 shows the parallel-lines model.

lm(Energy ~ Occupancy + Type, data = energy)





Table 11.7: Parallel-lines model: electricity use on occupancy and building type.

The Occupancy coefficient is the common slope, about 1.95 kWh per day for each additional occupant. The TypeRetrofitted coefficient is \(b_2\), the estimate of \(\beta_2\), the adjusted difference. At the same occupancy, retrofitted buildings use 42.5 kWh per day less than standard ones, \(t(57) = -5.38\), \(p < 0.001\). The \(t\) has 57 degrees of freedom, 60 buildings minus the 3 coefficients the model estimates. We reject \(H_{0,\text{group}}\).
Figure 11.10 shows what that coefficient measures. The adjusted means express the same comparison as one value for each building type. Evaluating each line at the overall mean occupancy, 76.4 people, gives 351.3 kWh per day for standard buildings and 308.8 for retrofitted ones. Their difference is \(b_2\).








Figure 11.10: Electricity use against occupancy, with the parallel lines from the model. Open circles mark the adjusted means, each line’s value at the overall mean occupancy (dashed line). The arrow is the adjusted difference, which is the same at every occupancy.





The raw comparison and the adjusted one point in opposite directions, for the same reason as in the COVID example. The groups differed in a third variable. The retrofitted buildings were busier, and busier buildings use more electricity. Compared at the same occupancy, retrofitted buildings use less electricity.
Adjusting for occupancy also shrank the error term. In the raw comparison the error mean square is 1864, and in the parallel-lines model it is 508. Much of the building-to-building variation in electricity use comes from occupancy, and once the model accounts for it, that variation no longer counts as error. Repeated-measures ANOVA gains power the same way in Section 8.6. There the known source of variation was the units themselves (the monitoring stations), and here it is a measured covariate. Either way, removing it from \(MS_\text{Error}\) makes the denominator of the test smaller, so a real group difference is easier to detect.






ImportantResults reporting: ANCOVA with parallel slopes




After adjusting for occupancy, retrofitted buildings used less electricity than standard buildings, \(b_2 = -42.5\) kWh per day, \(t(57) = -5.38\), \(p < 0.001\), 95% CI [-58.3, -26.7] kWh per day. Adjusted means at the average occupancy of 76.4 people were 308.8 kWh per day for retrofitted buildings and 351.3 for standard ones. The occupancy × building type interaction was not significant, \(F(1, 56) = 0.01\), \(p = 0.927\), so a common slope was used (1.95 kWh per day per occupant).

title: 11  Analysis of Covariance (ANCOVA)
text:
11.6 Chapter Summary
Why it matters. Environmental relationships rarely play out identically everywhere. ANCOVA tests whether a continuous relationship, such as pollution’s effect on bird density, is the same in every group. When it is, ANCOVA also compares the groups at the same covariate value.
Core ideas

ANCOVA is regression plus a categorical factor. It takes the familiar \(y=\beta_0+\beta_1 x+\varepsilon\) line and lets a categorical grouping shift the intercept, the slope, or both, using the same indicator-variable machinery that underlies every linear model in this book.
Check the whole model, then the interaction. If the whole-model \(F\) is not significant, stop. Otherwise test whether the groups’ slopes differ (\(H_{0,\text{int}}:\beta_3=0\)). That answer decides how everything else gets interpreted.
If the interaction is significant, report the two lines. If slopes differ, describe how the relationship changes by group instead of reducing it to a single adjusted-mean comparison, which assumes parallel lines. Test each group’s slope with its own regression, since the interaction only says the slopes differ from each other.
If slopes are parallel, compare adjusted means. Drop the interaction term and test \(\beta_2\), the gap between the parallel lines. When the groups differ on the covariate, the adjusted comparison can point the opposite way from the raw one, as it did for the retrofitted buildings.
A covariate also shrinks the error term. Variation the covariate explains leaves the error mean square, which is the same way repeated-measures ANOVA gains power by removing unit-to-unit variation.
Center the covariate when the intercept should mean something. Left uncentered, the intercept describes the groups at covariate = 0, a value the data may never actually contain.





von Kügelgen, Julius, Luigi Gresele, and Bernhard Schölkopf. 2021. “Simpson’s Paradox in COVID-19 Case Fatality Rates: A Mediation Analysis of Age-Related Causal Effects.” IEEE Transactions on Artificial Intelligence 2 (1): 18–27. https://doi.org/10.1109/TAI.2021.3073088.

title: Choosing a Test

title: Glossary
text:
A
Each entry gives the definition the book uses and the chapter that defines it. The definitions match the chapter text word for word or nearly so, so a definition you learn here is the one the chapter uses.

title: Glossary
text:
adjusted difference

How much the groups differ when they are compared at the same covariate value. (Chapter 11)

adjusted means

The group means you would expect if both groups had the same average covariate value. (Chapter 11)

alpha (α)

See significance level (α).

alternative hypothesis (Hₐ)

The claim that the population mean does not equal \(\mu_0\). It can also point in one direction only, larger or smaller. (Chapter 4)

Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA)

A linear model with a continuous outcome, at least one continuous predictor (the covariate), and at least one categorical predictor (the factor). (Chapter 11)

ANOVA table

An ANOVA table lists the sums of squares, degrees of freedom, mean squares, and \(F\) for each source of variation. (Chapter 8)

title: Glossary
text:
B

balanced

A design is balanced when every group, or every combination of conditions, has the same number of observations. (Chapter 8)

best-fit line

The straight line that summarizes the pattern of dots with the least error. (Chapter 2)

beta (β)

See Type II error.

between-subjects

A between-subjects design has different units in each condition, and each unit is measured once. (Chapter 6)

biased estimator

See unbiased and biased estimators.

biased sample

A sample where some part of the design (who, where, when, or how you measure) pushes results in one direction, on purpose or not. More data does not fix it. (Chapter 3)

title: Glossary
text:
C

categorical variable

See nominal variable.

causal directionality problem

The causal directionality problem arises when \(X\) and \(Y\) are causally linked but no outside knowledge, such as the physics of the system or which variable came first, settles the direction. (Chapter 2)

cell

One combination of categories or conditions in a table, such as one land use with one temperature outcome, or one pollution condition with one flow rate. (Chapter 7)

cell mean

The mean of the scores in one cell. (Chapter 10)

centering

Subtracting a covariate’s mean from every value, \(\tilde x = x - \bar x\). (Chapter 11)

central limit theorem (CLT)

As \(n\) grows, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal shape, whatever the shape of the population, as long as the population has a finite standard deviation. It is the only one of the three facts about the sampling distribution that concerns shape. (Chapter 3)

central tendency

A single representative value near the center of a distribution, summarizing what most of the data are like. (Chapter 1)

chance window

The distribution of results that chance alone produces when a study with no real effect is repeated many times. (Chapter 2)

chi-square distribution

The family of curves that the \(\chi^2\) statistic approximately follows when \(H_0\) is true and expected counts are large enough. (Chapter 7)

chi-square goodness-of-fit test

The chi-square goodness-of-fit test checks how well (the “goodness”) the observed counts for one categorical variable match (the “fit”) the counts expected under a stated pattern. (Chapter 7)

chi-square test of independence

A test of whether two categorical variables measured on the same units are related. (Chapter 7)

chi-square (χ²) tests

Tests that compare the counts observed in each category with the counts expected under \(H_0\). (Chapter 7)

Cohen’s d

The raw difference, \(\Delta\), divided by the population standard deviation, so it gives the effect in standard deviations. (Chapter 5)

conditional probability

The probability of one thing given that something else has already happened. (Chapter 3)

confidence interval (CI)

A range of plausible values for the population mean, built by a method that captures the true mean a known percentage of the time across repeated samples. That percentage, such as 95%, is the confidence level, \(1 - \alpha\). (Chapter 3)

confidence level

See confidence interval (CI).

confounding variable

A third variable that drives both of the variables you are looking at, creating an apparent relationship between them or inflating a real one. (Chapter 2)

continuous variable

A variable that can, in principle, take on any value within a range. (Chapter 1)

correlation

A relationship in which values of one variable tend to go with values of another. It is positive when higher values go with higher values, negative when higher values go with lower values, and absent when there is no consistent pattern. (Chapter 2)

covariance

The mean of the products of paired deviations, \((x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})\). Its sign shows whether being above the mean on \(X\) tends to come with being above or below the mean on \(Y\). (Chapter 2)

covariate

A continuous predictor that is related to the outcome and helps explain part of its variation. (Chapter 11)

critical value

The value of the test statistic that cuts off the most extreme \(\alpha\) of the sampling distribution under \(H_0\). (Chapter 4)

title: Glossary
text:
D

degrees of freedom

The number of values still free to vary once something has been estimated from the data. It sets which \(t\), \(F\) or \(\chi^2\) curve applies. (Chapter 6)

dependent variable (DV)

The variable being explained, written \(Y\). (Chapter 1)

descriptive statistics

The numbers and plots that summarize a dataset. (Chapter 1)

deviation score

A score minus the mean, \(x_i - \bar{x}\). Not the same as a difference score. (Chapter 2)

difference score

One unit’s second measurement minus its first. (Chapter 6)

discrete variable

A variable with separate, distinct values and nothing in between. (Chapter 1)

distribution

The pattern of which values occur in a dataset and how often each occurs. (Chapter 1)

title: Glossary
text:
E

effect

The difference a study is about, such as how far apart two group means are, or how far a mean is from the value \(H_0\) states. (Chapter 5)

effect size

The number that says how large the effect is, in the study’s units or in standard deviations. (Chapter 5)

error term

The part of the DV that the population line does not explain, \(\varepsilon\). (Chapter 9)

estimated population distribution

A normal curve centered at the sample mean, \(\bar{x}\), with the sample’s standard deviation, \(s\), as its spread. (Chapter 4)

estimation

Estimation uses sample data to give a best guess of a population value, along with how uncertain that guess is. (Chapter 3)

eta-squared

The usual effect size for ANOVA, the proportion of the total variation in the response that the grouping variable explains. (Chapter 8)

expected count

The expected count for a category is the total count times the probability \(H_0\) gives that category. (Chapter 7)

expected value

The mean of a probability distribution, the long-run average of the outcomes if the random process were repeated forever. (Chapter 3)

experimental research

Research in which the researcher deliberately manipulates something (the IV) and measures its effect (the DV). An experiment needs the manipulation, a control or comparison group, and random assignment of units to the groups. (Chapter 1)

extrapolation

Extrapolation is predicting \(y\) at an \(x\) value outside the range of \(x\) we observed. (Chapter 9)

title: Glossary
text:
F

factor

In ANOVA, an independent variable. The groups it defines are its levels. (Chapter 8)

factorial design

A factorial design has two or more IVs, and each of its conditions is a combination of one level from each IV. (Chapter 10)

familywise error rate

The chance of at least one false positive across a set of tests. (Chapter 8)

F distribution

The theoretical distribution of \(F\) when the null hypothesis is true. Its shape is set by two degrees of freedom. (Chapter 8)

formal power analysis

Finding the sample size \(n\) that gives a target power, usually 80%, for a chosen \(\Delta\), \(\sigma\), \(\alpha\) and number of tails, before any data are collected. (Chapter 5)

F statistic

The ratio \(MS_\text{Between}/MS_\text{Within}\). A large \(F\) means the differences between group means are large relative to the variation within groups. (Chapter 8)

title: Glossary
text:
G

grand mean

The mean of all of the scores, across every group. (Chapter 8)

title: Glossary
text:
H

histogram

A plot that summarizes data by grouping values into bins rather than showing each point separately. (Chapter 1)

homogeneity of variance

The groups have roughly equal spread around their own means. One of ANOVA’s assumptions. (Chapter 8)

title: Glossary
text:
I

independent events

Two events are independent when knowing that one occurred tells you nothing about whether the other did. Every test in this book assumes independent observations. (Chapter 3)

independent-samples t-test

A test that compares the means of two separate groups, with a standard error built from the pooled standard deviation. (Chapter 6)

independent variable (IV)

The variable used to explain another, written \(X\). (Chapter 1)

indicator variable

A variable that equals 1 for observations in one group and 0 for all other observations. (Chapter 11)

inference

Using data from a sample to draw conclusions about the broader population the sample came from. (Chapter 3)

inferential statistics

Inferential statistics is the branch of statistics concerned with drawing conclusions about populations or causal relationships from sample data. (Chapter 3)

interaction

An interaction occurs when the effect of one IV depends on the level of another. (Chapter 10)

interpolation

Interpolation is predicting \(y\) at an \(x\) value inside the range of \(x\) we observed. (Chapter 9)

interval variable

A variable with equal spacing between values, so differences are meaningful. Its zero does not mean none of the quantity, so ratios between values are not meaningful. (Chapter 1)

title: Glossary
text:
K

Kruskal-Wallis test

The rank-based, nonparametric alternative to one-way ANOVA. (Chapter 8)

title: Glossary
text:
L

law of large numbers

As the sample size grows, the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) of a random sample converges toward the population mean \(\mu\). (Chapter 3)

left-skewed distribution

A distribution with a long tail of low values stretching out to the left. (Chapter 1)

levels

The groups a factor defines. (Chapter 8)

linear regression

Linear regression fits the straight line that best predicts one variable from another. (Chapter 2)

title: Glossary
text:
M

main effect

The difference between the marginal means of one IV. (Chapter 10)

Mann-Whitney-Wilcoxon test

The rank-based alternative to the independent-samples \(t\)-test, which does not assume normality. (Chapter 7)

marginal mean

The mean for one level of a factor, averaged across the levels of the other factor. (Chapter 10)

mean

The sum of a set of numbers divided by how many numbers there are. Also called the average. (Chapter 1)

mean difference

One group’s mean minus another group’s mean. (Chapter 4)

mean square

A sum of squares divided by its degrees of freedom. (Chapter 8)

median

The exact middle of the data once they are ordered from smallest to largest. (Chapter 1)

mixed design

A mixed design has at least one between-subjects factor and at least one within-subjects factor. (Chapter 10)

mode

The most frequently occurring value. (Chapter 1)

model

An equation that describes how the DV changes with a predictor, plus a term for the variation the equation leaves out. (Chapter 9)

multiplication rule

The probability that two events both happen is the probability of the first times the conditional probability of the second given the first. For independent events, it is the product of their separate probabilities. (Chapter 3)

title: Glossary
text:
N

nominal variable

A variable whose values are names with no order. Also called a categorical variable. (Chapter 1)

non-experimental research

Research in which the researcher observes conditions instead of assigning them. (Chapter 1)

nonparametric test

A test whose null distribution does not depend on the population having a particular shape, such as normal. (Chapter 7)

nuisance covariate

A covariate you adjust for so that a group comparison is fair, when the group comparison is the question. (Chapter 11)

null distribution

The distribution of a test statistic across many samples when \(H_0\) is true. (Chapter 6)

null hypothesis (H₀)

The claim of no effect or no difference. In a one-sample test, it says the population mean equals a reference value, \(\mu_0\). It is a statement about the population, and it never mentions the sample mean. (Chapter 4)

null population distribution

The population we would have if \(H_0\) were true. (Chapter 4)

title: Glossary
text:
O

omnibus test

A single test that covers several comparisons at once. (Chapter 8)

one-sample t-test

A test that compares one sample mean with a reference value, \(\mu_0\), using the standard deviation estimated from the sample. (Chapter 6)

operational definition

The result of operationalization, the specific quantity chosen to stand for a concept. (Chapter 1)

operationalization

Turning an abstract concept into a specific, measurable procedure. (Chapter 1)

ordinal variable

A variable whose values have a meaningful order, but the spacing between values is not defined. (Chapter 1)

outcome

When \(X\) is used to predict \(Y\) rather than manipulated, \(Y\) is the outcome. (Chapter 1)

outlier

A value much farther from the bulk of the data than the rest of the values. (Chapter 1)

title: Glossary
text:
P

paired t-test

A test that compares two measurements on the same units by running a one-sample \(t\)-test on the difference scores. (Chapter 6)

parallel-lines model

The parallel-lines model includes \(\beta_2\) but leaves out \(\beta_3\), so the intercept can shift between groups but the slope cannot, and the two lines are parallel. (Chapter 11)

parametric test

One whose null distribution we can know only by assuming something specific about the shape of the population the data came from. (Chapter 7)

partial eta-squared

Partial eta-squared (\(\eta_p^2\)) is the share of the variation left after setting the other effects aside that one effect explains. (Chapter 10)

Pearson’s r

Pearson’s \(r\) is the covariance of \(X\) and \(Y\) divided by the product of their standard deviations. (Chapter 2)

pooled standard deviation

The square root of the pooled variance, \(s_p\). The standard error of the difference is built from it. (Chapter 6)

pooled variance

One combined estimate of the variance the two groups share, a weighted average of the two sample variances, each weighted by its degrees of freedom. (Chapter 6)

population

The (usually much larger) set of all individuals or observations you want to draw conclusions about. (Chapter 3)

population parameters

Population parameters are the numbers that describe a population distribution, such as its mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\). (Chapter 3)

post-hoc comparisons

Post-hoc comparisons are tests run after a significant omnibus test to find which pairs of groups differ. (Chapter 8)

post-hoc power

Power computed after a study, using the effect size the study observed. It is a restatement of the \(p\)-value, so it should not be reported. (Chapter 5)

power

The probability that a design correctly rejects \(H_0\) when a real effect of a specified size exists, at the chosen \(\alpha\). It equals \(1 - \beta\). (Chapter 5)

practical significance

The effect is large enough to change what someone does about it. This is a judgment about the world, not a calculation. (Chapter 5)

predictor

When \(X\) is used to predict \(Y\) rather than manipulated, \(X\) is the predictor. (Chapter 1)

probability

The long-run proportion of times an event would occur if the process were repeated many times (the frequentist view this book uses). (Chapter 3)

probability density

Probability density is the height of a continuous distribution’s curve at a point, written \(p(x)\). (Chapter 3)

probability distribution

A rule that assigns probabilities to all possible outcomes of a random variable. (Chapter 3)

p-value

The probability, assuming \(H_0\) is true, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed. (Chapter 4)

title: Glossary
text:
Q

Q-Q plot

A Q-Q plot sorts the residuals and compares them to where a perfectly normal distribution would place values at the same percentiles. (Chapter 9)

quasi-experiment

A non-experimental study that compares conditions the researcher did not create. (Chapter 1)

title: Glossary
text:
R

randomization

Assigning each unit to a condition by chance. (Chapter 1)

random variable

Any quantity whose value is not settled in advance, such as the flavor the next customer picks or the number of rainy days next month. (Chapter 3)

range

The largest value minus the smallest value. (Chapter 1)

rank

The rank of a value is its position when the data are put in order from smallest to largest (first, second, third, and so on). (Chapter 7)

ratio variable

A variable with equal spacing between values and a true zero, where zero means none of the quantity, so ratios between values are meaningful. (Chapter 1)

regression coefficients

The intercept and slope of a regression line, \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\). (Chapter 9)

rejection region

The set of test-statistic values beyond the critical value(s). (Chapter 4)

repeated-measures design

A design that measures the same units under every condition. Also called a within-subjects design. (Chapter 8)

residual

The vertical distance from a data point to the fitted line, the observed \(y\) minus the \(y\) the line predicts. (Chapter 2)

right-skewed distribution

A distribution with a long tail of high values stretching out to the right. (Chapter 1)

R-squared (R²)

The proportion of the total variation in \(y\) explained by the line. (Chapter 9)

title: Glossary
text:
S

sample

The finite set of data points a study actually collects. (Chapter 3)

sample mean

The average of one sample, \(\bar{x}\). (Chapter 3)

sample statistics

Sample statistics are numbers calculated from the data in a sample, such as \(\bar{x}\) and \(s\). (Chapter 3)

sampling distribution

The distribution of a statistic, such as the mean, across many samples of the same size \(n\). (Chapter 3)

sampling distribution of the sample mean

The distribution of the means of many samples of size \(n\), as if the study were repeated many times. (Chapter 3)

sampling distribution of the sample mean under H₀

How \(\bar{x}\) would vary across many samples if \(H_0\) were true, \(N(\mu_0, SE_{\bar{x}}^2)\). The critical values and the \(p\)-value come from it. (Chapter 4)

sampling error

A larger sample shrinks sampling error, the gap between a sample statistic and the population value that comes from seeing only a subset. (Chapter 3)

scale of measurement

A variable’s scale of measurement says which comparisons its values support, such as putting them in order, subtracting them, or forming ratios. (Chapter 1)

scatter plot

A plot that shows each subject as one dot, placed by one measurement on the horizontal x-axis and the other on the vertical y-axis. (Chapter 2)

Shapiro-Wilk test

A formal test of normality. Its \(H_0\) is that the data (or the residuals) came from a normal distribution. (Chapter 6)

significance level (α)

The probability of rejecting \(H_0\) given that \(H_0\) is true, chosen before the test. It is the Type I error rate. (Chapter 4)

sign test

A test that looks only at whether each difference is positive or negative. (Chapter 7)

simple effect

The effect of one IV at a single level of the other IV, such as the pollution effect under low flow. (Chapter 10)

simple random sample

A sample chosen so that every member of the population has the same chance of being selected. (Chapter 3)

Simpson’s paradox

A pattern in combined data that reverses once the data are split into meaningful groups. (Chapter 11)

spurious correlation

A correlation that does not come from a link between the two variables. (Chapter 2)

standard deviation (SD)

The square root of the variance. It is in the units of the data and gives the typical size of a deviation from the mean. (Chapter 2)

standard error (SE)

The standard deviation of a sampling distribution. (Chapter 3)

standardizing

Standardizing converts a raw score, the value as measured, into a \(z\)-score by subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation. (Chapter 3)

standard normal

The normal distribution with \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\). A variable with this distribution is written \(Z\). (Chapter 3)

statistical significance

A result is statistically significant when \(p < \alpha\), which means the data would be unlikely if \(H_0\) were true. (Chapter 5)

Student’s t distribution

The sampling distribution of \(t\) when the population standard deviation is estimated from the sample. Its shape depends on the degrees of freedom. (Chapter 6)

sum of squares (SS)

The total of the squared deviations from the mean. (Chapter 2)

symmetric distribution

A distribution whose left and right halves are mirror images around the center. (Chapter 1)

title: Glossary
text:
T

test statistic

The effect you observed divided by how much it varies by chance. (Chapter 4)

three-way interaction

A three-way interaction means that the two-way interaction changes across the third factor. (Chapter 10)

true population distribution

The population the data actually came from. It is never known, and \(H_a\) is a claim about it. (Chapter 4)

Tukey HSD (honestly significant difference)

A post-hoc method that compares every pair of groups while keeping the familywise error rate at \(\alpha\). (Chapter 8)

two-way interaction

With three IVs, an interaction between two of them. (Chapter 10)

Type I error

Rejecting \(H_0\) when it is actually true, a false positive. Its rate is \(\alpha\). (Chapter 5)

Type II error

Failing to reject \(H_0\) when it is actually false, a missed signal. Its rate is \(\beta\). (Chapter 5)

title: Glossary
text:
U

unbiased and biased estimators

An estimator is unbiased when its expected value, its average across many samples, equals the population parameter it estimates. It is biased if its expected value systematically differs from that parameter. (Chapter 3)

title: Glossary
text:
V

variable

What you record for each observation once the measure is applied. (Chapter 1)

variance

The mean of the squared deviations, which is the sum of squares divided by the number of scores. (Chapter 2)

variation

How spread out the values in a dataset are. (Chapter 1)

title: Glossary
text:
W

weighted mean

A mean that multiplies each value by a weight \(w_i\), which sets how much that value counts, adds the products, and divides by the sum of the weights. (Chapter 1)

Welch’s t-test

The independent-samples \(t\)-test without the assumption of equal variances. It uses each group’s own variance, and it is R’s t.test() default. (Chapter 6)

Wilcoxon signed-rank test

The rank-based alternative to the one-sample or paired \(t\)-test, which does not assume normality. (Chapter 7)

within-subjects design

See repeated-measures design.

title: Glossary
text:
Z

z-score

A \(z\)-score is the number of standard deviations a value is above or below its mean. (Chapter 3)

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.10 The standard error
The law of large numbers gives a direction. As \(n\) grows, \(\bar{x}\) settles near \(\mu\). The standard error, named below, gives a size. For one fixed \(n\), it gives the spread of the sample means. Figure 3.13 shows both at once.
The distribution of sample means is the sampling distribution of the sample mean, defined earlier in the chapter. It also goes by the shorter name sampling distribution of the mean.
Figure 3.13 animates this idea with a normal population (orange curve) that has \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\), at four sample sizes. Each frame draws one new sample in every panel. The top row shows that sample’s values as gray points, with its mean as a lime-green dotted line. The bottom row collects the means of all the samples drawn so far, one green dot per sample. This chapter calls that collection the pile of sample means. Watch three things:

The spread of the values in one sample stays near \(\sigma = 1\) as \(n\) grows. The \(s\) shown in each panel bounces around 1. At \(n = 2\) it swings from below 0.1 to about 3 from frame to frame, and at \(n = 128\) it stays within about 0.15 of 1. A sample’s standard deviation estimates \(\sigma\), which is a fixed feature of the population, so collecting more values does not shrink it.
The spread of the sample means shrinks. The pile of means is wide at \(n = 2\) and narrow at \(n = 128\). The SE shown in each panel is \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\), the standard deviation this pile of means approaches as more samples are drawn. It halves each time \(n\) is multiplied by 4, from 0.71 at \(n = 2\) to 0.35, 0.18 and 0.09. The formula is explained below.
One sample’s mean gets closer to \(\mu\). The lime-green line jumps around at \(n = 2\) and stays near 0 at \(n = 128\). This is the law of large numbers from the previous section.

The pile is bell-shaped at every \(n\) here because the population itself is normal. The central limit theorem, below, describes the shape when the population is not normal.








Figure 3.13: One new sample per frame from a normal population (orange curve, \(\mu = 0\), \(\sigma = 1\)), at four sample sizes. Top row: the sample’s values (gray points) and its mean (lime-green dotted line). Bottom row: the means of all samples so far. The sample SD, \(s\), does not shrink as \(n\) grows, while the pile of means narrows.





So the sampling distribution of the mean is itself a distribution, with its own spread. The standard error (SE) is the standard deviation of a sampling distribution. In this context, it is the standard error of the mean, written \(SE_{\bar{x}}\). The standard deviation describes how spread out the individual values are. The standard error describes how spread out the sample means are. Collecting more data does not shrink the standard deviation, but it does shrink the standard error.
Two facts about the sampling distribution of the mean hold at every sample size, for any population with a finite standard deviation:

Its mean equals the population mean, \(\mu\). This is what it means to call \(\bar{x}\) unbiased.
Its standard deviation, the standard error, equals the population \(\sigma\) divided by \(\sqrt{n}\):

\[SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
This is the standard error when \(\sigma\) is known. Usually it is not, and then the same standard error is estimated by \(s/\sqrt{n}\), as the end of this chapter shows. Both are written \(SE_{\bar{x}}\), so each time you compute one, note which SD went into it.
Neither fact needs the central limit theorem. Both come from how averages of independent values behave, and both hold even at \(n = 2\). The second fact is why the pile of means in Figure 3.13 narrows. Its spread is \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\), and \(\sqrt{n}\) grows with \(n\). The law of large numbers is about where one sample’s mean heads as \(n\) grows, and the central limit theorem is about the shape of the pile.
The law of large numbers follows from the standard error. Because \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) shrinks toward zero as \(n\) grows, a single sample’s \(\bar{x}\) becomes very likely to be close to \(\mu\). The formal argument uses Chebyshev’s inequality, but this is the idea we need.
The second fact also gives the width of Figure 3.11. The numbers 1 to 10 have mean 5.5. Their population variance is the average squared distance from 5.5, and with \(n = 20\) the formula gives the standard error:
\[\begin{aligned}
\sigma^2 &= \frac{1}{10}\sum_{x=1}^{10}(x - 5.5)^2 = 82.5/10 = 8.25 \\[1.2ex]
\sigma &= \sqrt{8.25} = 2.87 \\[1.2ex]
SE_{\bar{x}} &= \sigma/\sqrt{n} = 2.87/\sqrt{20} = 2.87/4.47 = 0.64
\end{aligned}\]
The standard deviation of the 10,000 sample means in Figure 3.11 is 0.64, matching the formula.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.11 The central limit theorem
The central limit theorem (CLT) states a third fact about the sampling distribution, and the only one about shape:

As \(n\) grows, the sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal shape, no matter what shape the population has, as long as the population has a finite standard deviation.

The CLT is why the normal curve appears so often in statistics. It describes sample means even when the underlying data are skewed or flat. The full theorem is more general and has a complicated proof, but this is the part we need.
The next three figures show histograms of sample means drawn from populations with different shapes. These are distributions of sample means, not of individual observations.
In Figure 3.14, we are sampling from a normal distribution (orange line). The sampling distribution of the mean (green bars) is also normal.








Figure 3.14: Means of 10,000 samples of size 10 and of size 50 from a normal population (orange curve). The sample means are normal at both sample sizes, and narrower at n = 50.





Return to the uniform population of the numbers 1 to 10 from Figure 3.9. Figure 3.15 shows the means of 10,000 samples at each of two sample sizes, \(n = 10\) and \(n = 50\). The population is flat (orange line), but the sampling distribution of the mean (green bars) is bell-shaped at both sample sizes.








Figure 3.15: Means of 10,000 samples of size 10 and of size 50, drawn from the uniform distribution of the numbers 1 to 10 (orange line). Even though the population is flat, the distribution of sample means is approximately normal.





The exponential population in Figure 3.16 is right-skewed, with most values near 0 and a long right tail (orange curve).








Figure 3.16: Sampling distributions of the mean from a strongly right-skewed exponential population. At n = 10 the sample means are still somewhat right-skewed; at n = 50 they are close to normal and narrower.





At \(n = 10\) the sample means are still a little right-skewed. At \(n = 50\) their histogram is close to a bell shape.
Together, these figures show the central limit theorem at work. The sampling distribution of the mean approaches a normal shape whether the population is normal, flat, or skewed. Its center and spread follow the two facts from before, at every sample size: mean \(\mu\) and standard error
\[SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.\]
This formula shows how sample size controls the precision of \(\bar{x}\), meaning how little \(\bar{x}\) varies from sample to sample. As \(n\) increases, the denominator grows and the SE falls. The SE falls with the square root of \(n\). Doubling \(n\) divides the SE by \(\sqrt{2} = 1.41\). Writing \(SE_n\) for the standard error with \(n\) observations and \(SE_{2n}\) for the standard error with twice as many,
\[SE_{2n} = \frac{SE_n}{\sqrt{2}} = \frac{SE_n}{1.41} = 0.71 \times SE_n,\]
a cut of about 30%. Each further increase in sample size gives a smaller gain in precision. In Figure 3.13, going from \(n = 2\) to \(n = 8\), six more observations, cuts the SE from 0.71 to 0.35. Going from \(n = 32\) to \(n = 128\), 96 more observations, cuts it from 0.18 to 0.09.
The facts about sample means in this chapter fall into two groups: three facts about the pile of sample means, and the law of large numbers, which is about a single sample.
The pile of sample means is the means of every possible sample of size \(n\). It is theoretical. A simulation draws many samples (10,000 in this chapter) to approximate it. More draws make the histogram smoother, not narrower. Its width depends on \(\sigma\) and on \(n\), the size of each sample behind one \(\bar{x}\) in the pile, not on how many samples are drawn. For a random sample of \(n\) independent observations from a population with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), Table 3.5 describes the pile.



Table 3.5: The pile of sample means. Only the central limit theorem is about shape.










Question
Answer
Where you saw it




Where is the pile centered?
At \(\mu\), at every \(n\)
Figure 3.11, centered on 5.5


How spread out is the pile?
Its standard deviation is the standard error, \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\), at every \(n\)
Bottom row of Figure 3.13, and the SD of 0.64 in Figure 3.11


What shape is the pile?
Approximately normal when \(n\) is large enough (the central limit theorem). Normal at every \(n\) if the population is normal
Figure 3.15 and Figure 3.16






The law of large numbers says that as \(n\) grows, a sample’s statistics settle near the population’s values.

One sample’s \(\bar{x}\) settles near \(\mu\) (Figure 3.8, and the lime-green line in Figure 3.13). This follows from the standard error: \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) shrinks toward 0.
\(s\) settles near \(\sigma\). The spread of the values stays about the same size as \(n\) grows.
The sample’s shape settles on the population’s shape. The share of values in each range settles on the population’s share, so a sample’s histogram looks more like the population as \(n\) grows (Figure 3.8). Skewed data stay skewed. Only the pile of sample means becomes approximately normal.
This needs random sampling. With a biased method, each of these settles on the values of whatever population the method reaches, however large \(n\) is.


3.11.1 How large is large enough?
The CLT says the sampling distribution of the mean approaches normal as \(n\) grows. It does not say how fast. That depends on the shape of the population. The three populations simulated in this chapter show the range:







Population shape
What this chapter’s simulations show




Normal
Sample means are normal at every sample size (Figure 3.14)


Flat (uniform, the numbers 1 to 10)
Sample means are already bell-shaped at \(n = 10\) (Figure 3.15)


Strongly right-skewed (exponential)
Sample means are still right-skewed at \(n = 10\) and close to a bell shape by \(n = 50\) (Figure 3.16)



You will often see \(n \ge 30\) given as the sample size at which sample means become roughly normal. No single cutoff works for every population. The exponential example needs more than 30, and a population with a longer tail or extreme outliers needs more still.
The skew fades as \(n\) grows because each unusually large value gets averaged with more ordinary ones. The longer the tail, the more ordinary values it takes.
Later chapters use “once the sample is large enough” to mean a sample size from this table. With a small sample from a skewed population, the sample means may not be close to normal, and Section 6.3.5 comes back to this case.

title: 3  Probability and Distributions
text:
3.14 Estimating a confidence interval
So far, we’ve focused on using sample data to estimate population parameters, but every estimate comes with some uncertainty. A single number, like “the mean IQ in this sample is 104,” does not show how confident we are. A confidence interval (CI) is a range of plausible values for the population mean, built by a method that captures the true mean a known percentage of the time, such as 95%, across repeated samples.
You’ll use this directly in Section 4.4.3, where a confidence interval becomes one of three equivalent ways to decide whether to reject the null hypothesis, \(H_0\). The same cutoff, 1.96, appears there as a critical value. In a confidence interval, 1.96 standard errors sets how far the interval reaches on each side of \(\bar{x}\). In a test, it marks how far the test statistic must be from 0 before we reject \(H_0\).
Sample means fall within about 1.96 standard errors of \(\mu\) 95% of the time. Thanks to the central limit theorem, we know the sampling distribution of the mean is approximately normal. In a normal distribution, 95% of values fall within about 1.96 standard deviations of the mean.
The standard deviation of that sampling distribution is the standard error, so 1.96 standard deviations of \(\bar x\) are 1.96 standard errors. If we knew the population mean and SD (\(\mu\), \(\sigma\)), the standard error would be
\[SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]






NoteNote: Which direction?



The switch from probability to statistics. Until now, every simulation in this chapter started from a population we chose and asked what samples it produces. That is probability, model → data. Here we start from one observed \(\bar{x}\) and reason back to \(\mu\), which we don’t know. That is statistics, data → model, and it is the direction the rest of the book runs.


The statement “\(\bar x\) is within 1.96 standard errors of \(\mu\)” is the inequality \(|\bar{x} - \mu| \le 1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt{n}\). Without the absolute value, it says \(-1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt{n} \le \bar{x} - \mu \le 1.96\,\sigma/\sqrt{n}\). Subtracting \(\bar{x}\) from each part and multiplying by \(-1\), which reverses the inequality signs, gives
\[\bar{x} - 1.96\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \le \mu \le \bar{x} + 1.96\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
so the 95% confidence interval is
\[CI_{95} = \bar{x} \pm 1.96\,\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}\]
For a level other than 95%, replace 1.96 with the corresponding normal quantile. For 70%, 15% is left in each tail, so the cutoff is the 85th percentile of the standard normal, qnorm(0.85) = 1.04.
The \(\pm\) form is how you compute the interval, not how you report it. Report the interval by its two bounds, in square brackets. For example, a sample mean of 50 with a standard error of 2 gives \(50 \pm 1.96(2) = 50 \pm 3.92\), reported as 95% CI [46.1, 53.9].
What the 95% means
The 95% describes the method, not any one interval. Imagine repeating the whole process many times: draw a new sample, compute its \(\bar{x}\), build a new interval. About 95% of those intervals would contain \(\mu\), and about 5% would miss it. The interval you have either contains \(\mu\) or it does not, and you do not know which.
Figure 3.24 shows 50 such intervals, each from a sample of \(n = 25\) from the IQ population, \(\text{Normal}(100, 15)\). Each line is one sample’s interval. Most cross the dashed line at \(\mu\), and the red ones miss it. A 95% method misses about 5% of the time, or about 2.5 of every 50 intervals on average.








Figure 3.24: 95% confidence intervals from 50 samples of size 25 from a normal population with \(\mu = 100\) and \(\sigma = 15\). Each horizontal line is one interval, with a dot at its sample mean, and the dashed orange line marks \(\mu = 100\). Dark blue intervals contain \(\mu\). 4 of the 50 intervals miss \(\mu\) (red).











CautionWarning: Don’t misread a confidence interval



Table 3.6 sets each misreading beside the correct reading.



Table 3.6: Misreadings of a confidence interval and the correct readings.









Not this
This




There is a 95% chance that \(\mu\) is in [46.1, 53.9]
About 95% of intervals built this way contain \(\mu\)


95% of individual values are between 46.1 and 53.9
The CI is a range for the population mean \(\mu\). Individual values spread much more widely.


\(50 \pm 3.92\)
95% CI [46.1, 53.9]








When \(\sigma\) is unknown
This formula assumes we know the population standard deviation \(\sigma\). But in practice, \(\sigma\) is almost never known. When it is unknown, we estimate the same standard error by putting the sample standard deviation \(s\) in place of \(\sigma\). The result is an estimated standard error, written with the same symbol:
\[SE_{\bar{x}} = \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\]
The \(n-1\) correction is already built into \(s\), so the denominator here is still \(\sqrt{n}\).
Estimating \(\sigma\) with \(s\) adds uncertainty, because \(s\) itself varies from sample to sample, as Figure 3.23 showed. To account for this, we swap the normal cutoffs for those from the \(t\)-distribution (Chapter 6), which depends on sample size. With small \(n\), the \(t\) values are larger, so the CI widens. At \(n = 5\) the 95% cutoff is 2.78 instead of 1.96. As \(n\) grows, \(t\) values shrink toward 1.96 (2.05 at \(n = 30\)), and the \(t\)-based CI becomes indistinguishable from the normal version.
A confidence interval shows how precise an estimate is. A larger \(n\) gives a smaller standard error and so a narrower interval. With \(\sigma = 15\):
\[\begin{aligned}
n = 25: \quad SE &= 15/\sqrt{25} = 3, \quad \bar{x} \pm 1.96 \times 3 = \bar{x} \pm 5.88 \\[1.2ex]
n = 100: \quad SE &= 15/\sqrt{100} = 1.5, \quad \bar{x} \pm 1.96 \times 1.5 = \bar{x} \pm 2.94
\end{aligned}\]
A wide interval means the estimate is imprecise, and a narrow one means it is precise.

title: 5  Errors, Power, and Effect Size
text:
Type I error: rejecting \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is true. It is a false positive, or false alarm, like a smoke alarm going off when there is no fire. If \(H_0\) is true, the probability of a Type I error is \(\alpha\), the significance level from Chapter 4. By convention, \(\alpha\) is often set at 0.05 (5%).
Type II error: failing to reject \(H_0\) when \(H_0\) is false. It is a missed signal, like a smoke alarm staying silent when there is a fire. The probability of a Type II error is \(\beta\). Its value depends on how far the true mean is from \(\mu_0\), which the figures below show.











Decision
If the null hypothesis is True
If the null hypothesis is False




Reject \(H_0\)
Type I error (prob = \(\alpha\))
Correct (prob = \(1 - \beta\), the power)


Fail to reject \(H_0\)
Correct (prob = \(1 - \alpha\))
Type II error (prob = \(\beta\))









Table 5.1: The cost of each error in three tests.











Test
Type I error here
Type II error here
Which is worse here (a judgment call)




No-idling rule near schools, \(H_0\): the rule did not change PM2.5
Keep a rule that does nothing
Drop a rule that works
Here, Type II would be worse. Kids would breathe idling exhaust that the rule would have cut.


Discharge permit limit, \(H_0\): \(\mu = 10\) mg/L
Act on an exceedance that is not there
Keep operating while the discharge exceeds the limit
Here, Type II is worse for the river, which keeps getting the excess discharge. Type I is probably worse for the plant, which pays to fix a problem it does not have.


Removing a species’ protected status, \(H_0\): the population has not recovered
Remove protection from a population that has not recovered
Keep protecting a population that has recovered
Here, Type I would be worse. Losing protection too early could send the population back into decline, while extra years of protection mostly cost money and paperwork.









In Figure 5.2, the true population mean (orange) is the same as \(\mu_0\). By chance, however, the sample mean is 2.4 standard errors from \(\mu_0\), past the critical value at 1.96 standard errors, and the 95% confidence interval (CI, Chapter 4) excludes \(\mu_0\). The test rejects \(H_0\) even though it is true, which is a Type I error.



In Figure 5.3, the true population mean (orange) is 4 standard errors from \(\mu_0\). By chance, however, the sample mean is only 1.5 standard errors from \(\mu_0\), inside the critical value, and the CI includes \(\mu_0\). The test fails to reject \(H_0\) even though it is false, which is a Type II error.







\(\alpha\) is the red area in the tails of the blue curve, past the critical values. If \(H_0\) is true, \(\alpha\) is how often the sample mean falls in the rejection region by chance. Computing \(\alpha\) needs only the blue curve, so the top panel has no orange curve. The orange curve appears in the bottom panel, for \(\beta\).
\(\beta\) is the gray area under the orange curve between the critical values. If \(\mu = \mu_a\), that is how often the sample mean fails to reach the rejection region and a real difference goes undetected.
Power, \(1-\beta\), is the rest of the orange curve, the part past the critical values.




5.1.1 Effect of sample size on errors
Sample size mainly affects Type II error. As \(n\) grows, the sampling distribution narrows, true effects are easier to detect, \(\beta\) falls, and power rises. With a fixed \(\alpha\) and correct assumptions, the long-run Type I error rate stays at \(\alpha\) for any \(n\), because the critical values are placed so that the area past them under the \(H_0\) curve is \(\alpha\) at every sample size.
The actual Type I rate can differ from \(\alpha\) in two cases. At small \(n\), it can drift from \(\alpha\) when the sampling distribution of the mean is not close to normal (Chapter 3), for example when the population is strongly skewed. Testing the data again each time new observations arrive also raises the Type I rate, at any \(n\), because each new test is another chance for the sample mean to fall in the rejection region by chance.
Figure 5.5 shows the effect of \(n\) on Type II error with the same \(\mu_0\) and the same true \(\mu\). In both panels the sample mean is equally unlucky, 2.5 standard errors below \(\mu\). With the smaller sample, \(\mu\) is 4 standard errors from \(\mu_0\), so \(\bar{x}\) is 1.5 standard errors from \(\mu_0\), inside the critical value. The confidence interval still catches \(\mu_0\), and we fail to reject. With four times the sample, the standard error halves, because \(\sqrt{4} = 2\). The same distance from \(\mu_0\) to \(\mu\) is now 8 standard errors, so \(\bar{x}\) is 5.5 standard errors from \(\mu_0\). The interval clears \(\mu_0\), and we reject \(H_0\).








Figure 5.5: The Type II situation at two sample sizes, with the same \(\mu_0\), true \(\mu\) and population. In both, \(\bar{x}\) is 2.5 standard errors below \(\mu\). Top: the confidence interval catches \(\mu_0\), so we fail to reject. Bottom: with four times the sample, the standard error halves, the same bad luck leaves the interval clear of \(\mu_0\), and we reject.







5.1.2 How to interpret \(p\)-values
A \(p\)-value is the probability, assuming \(H_0\) is true, of obtaining a test statistic at least as extreme as the one we observed. We reject at level \(\alpha\) when \(p<\alpha\). \(\alpha\) is chosen before the data are collected, and it sets how far out the critical values are. The \(p\)-value is computed from the data, and it measures how far out the observed test statistic is.
Tails. The \(p\)-value includes the area in the tail or tails that \(H_a\) points to. For a two-tailed test, add the areas in both tails. For a one-tailed test, use only the tail in the direction \(H_a\) states.






CautionWarning: Three misreadings of a \(p\)-value




\(p\) is the probability of a test statistic at least this extreme if \(H_0\) is true. It is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true.
A tiny \(p\) is not “super significant.” It means only that the data would be very unlikely if \(H_0\) were true. The effect itself can still be tiny and not worth acting on, especially with a large \(n\). Report an effect size and a CI so a reader can judge whether it matters.
A large \(p\) does not show that there is no effect. With small \(n\), true effects can yield large \(p\) (low power).
crumbs: 5  Errors, Power, and Effect Size

title: 5  Errors, Power, and Effect Size
text:
5.3 Effect size
Effect size comes in two kinds of units. You can express it in original units, which carry practical meaning, or in standardized units, which let you compare across scales.
Practical (original units). Use the scale stakeholders recognize.

Exams: “Treatment improved scores by 5 percentage points” (half a letter grade).
Time-on-task: “New training reduces practice time by 1,000 hours out of 10,000” (a 10% reduction).

These statements are easy to interpret, but they are hard to compare across contexts or measures. To say whether a 5-point exam gain is a larger effect than a 1,000-hour cut in practice time, you need each one measured against the variability of its own scale.
Standardized (unitless). When units are unfamiliar or scales differ, standardize by typical variability. The most common standardized effect size is Cohen’s \(d\) (Cohen 1988). Cohen’s \(d\) is the raw difference, \(\Delta\), divided by the population standard deviation, so it gives the effect in standard deviations:
\[\text{Cohen's } d = \frac{\Delta}{\sigma}\]
\(\Delta\) is the effect in the study’s units. It is \(\mu_1 - \mu_2\) when comparing two groups, or \(\mu - \mu_0\) when testing one mean against a reference value.
Cohen’s \(d\) and \(z\) both put the effect in the numerator but divide by different things. Section 4.4.1 gave the general shape, effect over error, and filled it in with the \(z\):
\[z = \frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \qquad \text{versus} \qquad \text{Cohen's } d = \frac{\mu-\mu_0}{\sigma}\]
In \(z\) the numerator is the observed effect, \(\bar{x}-\mu_0\). In Cohen’s \(d\) it is the true effect, \(\mu-\mu_0\), which \(\bar{x}-\mu_0\) estimates. The test statistic divides by the standard error, which shrinks as \(n\) grows, so \(z\) gets larger with more data even when the effect stays exactly the same. Quadrupling \(n\) halves the standard error, so the same \(\bar{x}-\mu_0\) gives twice the \(z\). Cohen’s \(d\) divides by the standard deviation, which does not shrink with \(n\), so Cohen’s \(d\) reports the size of the effect itself. Table 5.2 lines the two up.



Table 5.2: The test statistic \(z\) and the effect size Cohen’s \(d\) compared.











\(z\)
Cohen’s \(d\)




Numerator
\(\bar{x}-\mu_0\) (observed effect)
\(\mu-\mu_0\) (true effect, estimated by \(\bar{x}-\mu_0\))


Denominator
\(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\)
\(\sigma\)


As \(n\) grows
Grows for the same effect
Stays the same


Answers
Is the effect distinguishable from 0?
How large is the effect?






A large test statistic therefore does not mean a large effect. In a one-sample test, dividing by \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) is the same as dividing by \(\sigma\) and multiplying by \(\sqrt{n}\), so \(z = \frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma}\sqrt{n}\). The fraction is Cohen’s \(d\) computed from the sample, with \(\bar{x}\) in place of \(\mu\), so \(z = (\text{Cohen's } d)\sqrt{n}\). For an observed Cohen’s \(d = 0.05\):
\[\begin{aligned}
n = 100: \quad z &= 0.05 \times \sqrt{100} = 0.5 \\[1.2ex]
n = 10{,}000: \quad z &= 0.05 \times \sqrt{10{,}000} = 5
\end{aligned}\]
The \(t\) in Chapter 6 is the same ratio with an estimated \(s\) in place of a known \(\sigma\), so the same holds for \(t\).
Environmental example (biodiversity index). Suppose an index increases from 3 to 4 after reforestation.

In raw units: +1 index point.
In standardized terms:

If the SD across sites is 1.0, then Cohen’s \(d = 1.0\), a large shift by the usual guideline (0.8 or more is large, see the Tip below).
If the SD is 10, then Cohen’s \(d = 0.10\), a small shift (below the guideline’s 0.2).


The same 1-point increase is a large effect where the index varies little across sites and a small one where it varies a lot.
Planning starts from \(\Delta\). To plan a study, choose the value of \(\Delta\) to plan for, in the units of the study. It might be the effect you expect to see, or the smallest difference that would change what you do. A power analysis also needs an estimate of \(\sigma\), and with \(\Delta\) and \(\sigma\) you have Cohen’s \(d = \Delta/\sigma\).






TipTip: Estimating and reporting Cohen’s \(d\) in practice




With measured data, \(\sigma\) is unknown, so estimate it from the sample. For two groups, use the pooled SD from Section 6.5.
Heuristics (context matters): Cohen’s \(d \approx 0.2\) (small), 0.5 (medium), 0.8 (large).
A “small” Cohen’s \(d\) can still be important (e.g., small reductions in lead or PM2.5 can matter for health).
Report the effect in the study’s units with a 95% CI, to show how precisely it was estimated. Report Cohen’s \(d\) as a single number.



Suppose we’re measuring final exam performance (percent correct). The class mean is 65% with a standard deviation of 5 percentage points. Group A is a control, while Group B receives some instructional treatment.
Figure 5.7 shows four possible scenarios, with Group B’s mean shifted by Cohen’s \(d = 0\), 0.5, 1 and 2.








Figure 5.7: Exam scores for a control group A (mean 65, \(\sigma = 5\)) and a treatment group B whose mean is shifted by Cohen’s \(d = 0\), 0.5, 1 and 2, that is, by 0, 2.5, 5 and 10 points.





In Figure 5.7, a half-SD shift (Cohen’s \(d = 0.5\), 2.5 points) leaves the two curves mostly overlapping, and a two-SD shift (Cohen’s \(d = 2\), 10 points) separates them.
In practice, we rarely know beforehand how big a shift to expect, so the power curves later in this chapter show power across a range of effect sizes.

title: 5  Errors, Power, and Effect Size
text:
5.4 Power
A design’s power is the probability that it correctly rejects \(H_0\) when a real effect of a specified size exists, at your chosen \(\alpha\). Effects vary in size, and designs vary in power. A design with low power will usually fail to reject \(H_0\) even when a real effect exists.
Power rises when:

Effect size is larger.
Sample size (\(n\)) is larger (smaller standard error).
The cutoff for rejecting \(H_0\) is less strict (larger \(\alpha\)).
Variability in the population is lower (smaller \(\sigma\)), for example from less measurement noise.

When you plan a study, you need to know how large \(n\) must be to reach 80% power, with \(\alpha\) fixed at 0.05, for the smallest effect that matters. Figure 5.10 answers that question for one effect size.

5.4.1 Estimating power by simulation
A simulation with the exam-score example shows how design choices change power. We simulate two groups of \(n=10\) each. We draw Group A (control) from a normal distribution with mean 65 and \(\sigma = 5\), and Group B (treatment) from one with mean 67.5, a shift of 2.5 points, or Cohen’s \(d=0.5\), a medium effect. These are the two distributions in Panel 2 of Figure 5.7.
Each simulated experiment compares the two groups with an independent-samples \(t\)-test. Section 6.5 covers this test. For now, treat it as a test that returns a \(p\)-value for the difference between two group means, the same job the \(z\) statistic in Chapter 4 does for one mean.
Before you look. One simulated experiment draws 10 scores for Group A and 10 for Group B, runs the \(t\)-test, and saves the \(p\)-value. The simulation repeats this 1,000 times and counts how often \(p < 0.05\), which is how often the test rejects \(H_0\) at \(\alpha = 0.05\). In every one of the 1,000 experiments, Group B’s true mean is 2.5 points higher. Decide roughly how often you expect the test to detect that difference with 10 per group.
The test detected the 2.5-point difference in about 22% of the 1,000 experiments. The proportion of simulated experiments that reject \(H_0\) estimates the design’s power, the probability that the test detects a real difference of this size. With \(n = 10\) per group, the test misses this medium-sized effect in about 78% of experiments.


5.4.2 How power changes
Each of the next three simulations changes one part of the previous design and reruns the 1,000 experiments.

Larger \(n\). Doubling to \(n=20\) per group divides the standard error of each group mean by \(\sqrt{2}\), about 1.41, because the standard error is \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) and \(\sqrt{20}/\sqrt{10} = \sqrt{2}\).

That increases power to about 35%, up from about 22% at \(n = 10\) (rows 1 and 2 of Table 5.3).

Smaller \(\alpha\). Making the cutoff stricter (e.g., \(\alpha=0.01\)) lowers power, because only experiments with \(p < 0.01\) now count as significant. We reuse the same \(n=20\) simulations and change only the cutoff.

Power falls to about 14% (row 3).

Larger effect. If the treatment produces a 2-SD shift, Group B’s mean is \(65 + 2 \times 5 = 75\). We rerun the simulation with the same design at the same \(\alpha=0.01\).

The test rejected \(H_0\) in 100% of the 1,000 experiments (row 4). With a 2-SD difference, rejecting \(H_0\) is close to certain, even with 20 per group and \(\alpha = 0.01\).

5.4.3 Power curves
A design’s power depends on how large the true effect is. A power curve plots the power of a design against one quantity that varies, such as the true effect size or the sample size, with everything else held fixed. Figure 5.9 fixes the design at an independent-samples \(t\)-test with \(n=10\) per group and \(\alpha=0.05\), and plots power against the true effect size, Cohen’s \(d\).








Figure 5.9: Power vs. effect size (Cohen’s \(d\)) for an independent-samples \(t\)-test with \(n=10\) per group and \(\alpha=0.05\).





With 10 per group, this design detects a medium effect (Cohen’s \(d=0.5\)) only about 19% of the time, a larger effect (Cohen’s \(d=0.8\)) about 40% of the time, and a very large effect (Cohen’s \(d=2\)) almost every time (about 99%). Only effects of about Cohen’s \(d = 1.3\) or larger reach 80% power with this design.
The simulation above estimated power at Cohen’s \(d = 0.5\) as about 22%. The two numbers differ because 1,000 simulated experiments give an estimate, while the curve is computed exactly.
The second curve holds the effect size fixed and varies the sample size. Suppose prior research suggests the effect is small (Cohen’s \(d=0.2\)). Figure 5.10 plots power against sample size for Cohen’s \(d=0.2\), with a dashed line at 80% power, a common planning target.








Figure 5.10: Power vs. sample size for detecting Cohen’s \(d = 0.2\) with an independent-samples \(t\)-test at \(\alpha = 0.05\). The dashed line marks 0.80 power.





At 10 per group, power to detect Cohen’s \(d=0.2\) is about 7%. Reaching 80% power takes about 394 per group. At that sample size, 20% of studies would still fail to reject \(H_0\) for a real effect of Cohen’s \(d = 0.2\).
In a power analysis (defined in the next section), the \(n\) that reaches a power target such as 0.80 depends on the effect size and standard deviation you assumed. The 394 per group above assumes Cohen’s \(d = 0.2\), and assuming Cohen’s \(d = 0.3\) instead gives 176 per group. Report the assumed effect size and standard deviation alongside the \(n\).


5.4.4 Planning your design
Planning a study means working through the following, in order:

Choose the \(\Delta\) to plan for, the smallest difference that would change what you do, stated in the units of the measurement.
Choose \(\alpha\) (often 0.05; justify if different).
Estimate variability, \(\sigma\) (pilot data, literature, or historical monitoring). With \(\Delta\) and \(\sigma\) you have Cohen’s \(d\), which is what a power analysis needs.
Choose one- or two-tailed before data collection. The choice changes the critical value, so it changes the \(n\) you need.
Compute \(n\) for \(\ge 80\%\) power (or explain tradeoffs if you can’t reach it).

This sequence is a formal power analysis. A formal power analysis finds the sample size \(n\) that gives a target power, usually 80%, for a chosen \(\Delta\), \(\sigma\), \(\alpha\) and number of tails, before any data are collected. It applies while you can still choose \(n\), for example when deciding how many plots to establish or how many samples a permit application commits you to. When the data already exist, as in your course project, \(n\) is fixed. Report the effect and its confidence interval instead.






CautionWarning: Post-hoc power



Post-hoc power is power computed after a study, using the effect size the study observed. It is a restatement of the \(p\)-value, so a non-significant result always has low post-hoc power. For a two-tailed \(z\)-test, a result with \(p = 0.05\) exactly has post-hoc power of about 50%, and any larger \(p\) gives less. Do not compute it. Power for a difference chosen in advance, such as the smallest effect that matters, is fine to report.




5.4.5 Low power and very large samples

A significant result from a low-power study often fails to replicate. A design with 30% power to detect an effect that is really there rejects \(H_0\) in only about 3 of 10 repeats, so a significant first result is usually followed by non-significant replications.
A significant result from a small study overstates the effect. When a small study does reach significance, its estimated effect size tends to be too large. When the null is true, that large estimate makes a false positive look convincing.
Huge \(n\) finds tiny effects. With very large samples, trivial differences can register as statistically significant. For example, a utility comparing two billing designs across 2 million households can find a 0.1% difference in electricity use statistically significant, even though a difference that small would not change which design it adopts. Report an effect size and a confidence interval alongside each \(p\)-value so a reader can judge whether a difference matters.

Figure 5.11 shows that a significant result from a small study overstates the effect. Each dot in the figure is one simulated study in which the true mean is exactly \(\mu_0\). We ran 1,000 studies at each of four sample sizes (10, 50, 100, and 1,000) and kept only the ones that gave \(p < 0.05\), about 50 at each size.
When the null hypothesis is true, 5% of tests still give \(p < 0.05\). In small samples, those false positives come with large estimated effect sizes, even though the true effect is zero. A one-sample \(t\)-test (Section 6.3) reaches \(p < 0.05\) only when \(|t|\) is beyond the \(t\) critical value. Because \(t = (\text{Cohen's } d)\sqrt{n}\) as well (the effect size section), \(|\text{Cohen's } d| = |t|/\sqrt{n}\) must be at least the critical value divided by \(\sqrt{n}\) (Table 5.5).

title: 6  \(t\)-Tests
text:
6.4 The paired \(t\)-test
When the same units are measured twice (before/after, matched pairs), the question is whether they changed. The data for the test are difference scores. A difference score is one unit’s second measurement minus its first.
Design in this worked example. Ecologists measured soil moisture at 20 field plots before wetland restoration and again one year later, to see whether restoration increased moisture enough to support plant reestablishment and carbon sequestration. The soil moisture values are invented. Figure 6.8 shows the design.








Figure 6.8: A paired design. The same 20 plots are measured before and after restoration.





The dashed boxes mark what makes this design paired. In the design figures in earlier chapters, the boxes held different units, and the test compared one set against another. Here both boxes hold the same 20 plots, so each plot’s Before value can be subtracted from its own After value.
Define differences and their meaning. Choose an order and stick to it:

\(d_i = \text{After}_i - \text{Before}_i\)
\(d_i>0\): plot had more soil moisture after restoration (increase)
\(d_i<0\): plot had less soil moisture after restoration (decrease)

This subtraction cancels between-plot variability (some plots are naturally wetter than others) and focuses on within-plot change, so the difference scores vary less than the raw soil moisture values do. A smaller \(s_d\) gives a smaller standard error, so the paired test has more power than an independent-samples test (the third test in this chapter) on the same data.

Null (\(H_0\)): restoration did not change soil moisture, \(\mu_d = 0\), where \(\mu_d\) is the mean difference score in the population of plots.
Alternative (\(H_a\)): restoration changed soil moisture, \(\mu_d \neq 0\).

Test on differences (paired \(t\)). Compute one difference per plot, then run a one-sample \(t\) against 0:
\[\bar d=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n d_i, \quad
s_d=\text{SD}(d_1,\ldots,d_n), \quad
t = \frac{\bar d - 0}{s_d/\sqrt{n}}, \quad df=n-1.\]
Here \(n\) is the number of pairs, 20 plots in this study.
\(t\) has the same sign as \(\bar d\). If you subtracted Before from After, a positive \(t\) means moisture went up. Reversing the order flips the sign of every \(d_i\), \(\bar d\), and \(t\), and leaves \(p\) unchanged.
What to report. \(\bar d\) (the mean difference score), a 95% CI, \(t(df)\), and \(p\). Optionally add a standardized effect size, \(\bar d / s_d\), the paired version of Cohen’s \(d\). Cohen’s \(d\) is the effect size from Section 5.3.
Table 6.2 separates the two uses of the letter \(d\).

Cohen’s \(d\)
The effect size, always written out as “Cohen’s \(d\)”. For a paired design it is \(\bar d / s_d\).

To calculate \(t\) for a paired \(t\)-test, we use the one-sample \(t\)-test formula from the previous section, applied to the difference scores instead of raw scores.

At \(n=20\), \(t(19) = 2.50\), \(p = 0.022\), a significant result. The mean difference score (1.90 percentage points) is smaller than the 5-plot subset’s 2.8. The larger \(t\) comes from the standard error, which fell from 1.53 to 0.76 with four times as many plots. Four times as many plots doubles \(\sqrt{n}\), from \(\sqrt{5} = 2.24\) to \(\sqrt{20} = 4.47\), which halves the standard error. The SD of the differences barely changed, from 3.42 to 3.4. A mean increase of 1.9 points would be unlikely if restoration had no effect. With 20 plots, the test had more power to detect an effect of this size.
Analyzed wrongly as two independent groups, the same 20 plots give \(t(38) = 1.34\), \(p = 0.187\), and the test fails to reject \(H_0\). The pooled SD still contains the plot-to-plot differences that pairing removes.
Confidence interval. The CI for a paired test follows the same recipe as the one-sample CI, the estimate plus or minus \(t_{crit}\) times the estimate’s standard error. Here the estimate is \(\bar d\), its standard error is \(s_d/\sqrt{n}\), and \(t_{crit}\) comes from the \(t\) distribution with \(df = 19\):
\[\bar{d} \pm t_{crit} \cdot \frac{s_d}{\sqrt{n}} = 1.90 \pm 2.09 \times 0.76 = [0.31, 3.49]\]
This is the interval R reports in the table above. It is the 95% CI for the effect, the mean difference score for soil moisture, in percentage points.

title: 6  \(t\)-Tests
text:
6.5 The independent-samples \(t\)-test
The independent-samples \(t\)-test is the third and last design in this chapter.
A between-subjects design has different units in each condition, and each unit is measured once. The independent-samples \(t\)-test is the \(t\)-test for this design. In the example below, two groups of 5 sites make 10 units in total, none of them paired. Without repeated measures on the same unit, there’s no meaningful way to subtract scores between conditions the way the paired \(t\)-test does.
The numerator is the mean difference between groups, as in the other two tests. The denominator differs from the paired case, because now we need a single estimate of variability built from two separate samples instead of one.
A natural first guess is to average the two groups’ standard errors. Here \(SE_A = s_A/\sqrt{n_A}\) is the standard error of Group A’s mean, and \(SE_B\) is the same for Group B.
\[t = \frac{\bar{x}_A-\bar{x}_B}{\left(\dfrac{SE_A+SE_B}{2}\right)}\]
That average understates how much a difference between two means varies. The standard error of a difference between two independent means is \(\sqrt{SE_A^2 + SE_B^2}\), because variances add when two independent quantities are subtracted. This is always larger than the average of the two SEs. The pooled independent-samples \(t\)-test also assumes the two populations share one variance. Both samples estimate that shared variance, so the test combines them, which gives a better estimate, with more degrees of freedom, than either group alone. The pooled variance, \(s_p^2\), is that combined estimate, a weighted average of the two sample variances, \(s_A^2\) and \(s_B^2\), with each weighted by its degrees of freedom (the weighted mean, Section 1.9.5). The pooled standard deviation, \(s_p\), is its square root. Putting \(s_p^2\) in place of each group’s variance in \(\sqrt{SE_A^2 + SE_B^2}\) gives \(\sqrt{s_p^2/n_A + s_p^2/n_B} = s_p\sqrt{1/n_A + 1/n_B}\), the denominator below:
\[t = \frac{\bar{x}_A-\bar{x}_B}{s_p\sqrt{\dfrac{1}{n_A}+\dfrac{1}{n_B}}}\]
where (note \(s_A^2\) and \(s_B^2\) here are variances, not standard deviations)
\[s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_A-1)s_A^2 + (n_B-1)s_B^2}{n_A+n_B-2}}\]
The pooled test has \(df = n_A + n_B - 2\), one degree of freedom used for each group’s mean. With two groups of 5, that is \(df = 8\), the 8 in \(t(8)\) below.
The pooled test adds two test-specific assumptions: the outcome is approximately normal within each group, and the two groups have similar variances. When the spreads clearly differ, use Welch’s version instead, which does not pool the variances.
Table 6.4 compares the pooled test with Welch’s version.

The worked example compares bird species at ten field-edge sites. Five sites had their hedgerow removed (Group A), and five kept an intact hedgerow (Group B). At each site, one 10-minute point count recorded the number of bird species seen or heard. The counts are invented.

Null (\(H_0\)): hedgerows make no difference to the mean number of bird species, \(\mu_A = \mu_B\).
Alternative (\(H_a\)): the mean number of species differs, \(\mu_A \neq \mu_B\).

The code below follows the formula step by step in R, then checks it against t.test().


## By "hand" using R
# Bird species per point count
a <- c(1,2,3,4,5) # Group A, hedgerow removed
b <- c(3,5,4,7,9) # Group B, hedgerow intact
n_a <- length(a) # sample size for A
n_b <- length(b) # sample size for B

mean_difference <- mean(a)-mean(b) # compute mean difference

variance_a <- var(a) # compute variance for A
variance_b <- var(b) # compute variance for B

# Compute top part and bottom part of sp formula

sp_numerator <- (n_a - 1) * variance_a + (n_b - 1) * variance_b
sp_denominator <- n_a + n_b - 2
sp <- sqrt(sp_numerator/sp_denominator) # compute sp


# compute t following the formula

t <- mean_difference / (sp * sqrt(1/n_a + 1/n_b))

Group A’s counts (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) have mean 3.0 and variance 2.5. Group B’s counts (3, 5, 4, 7, 9) have mean 5.6 and variance 5.8. The pooled variance, the standard error of the difference, and \(t\) follow:
\[\begin{aligned}
s_p^2 &= (4 \times 2.5 + 4 \times 5.8)/8 = 4.15 \\[1.2ex]
s_p &= \sqrt{4.15} = 2.04 \\[1.2ex]
SE &= 2.04\sqrt{1/5 + 1/5} = 1.29 \\[1.2ex]
t &= (3.0 - 5.6)/1.29 = -2.02
\end{aligned}\]

t.test(a, b, var.equal = TRUE)

Confidence interval. The recipe is the same as before, the estimate plus or minus \(t_{crit}\) times its standard error. The estimate is \(\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B\), and its standard error, \(SE_\text{diff} = s_p\sqrt{1/n_A + 1/n_B}\), is the denominator of the \(t\) just computed. With \(t_{crit}\) from the \(t\) distribution with \(df = 8\):
\[(\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B) \pm t_{crit} \cdot SE_\text{diff} = -2.60 \pm 2.31 \times 1.29 = [-5.57, 0.37]\]
This is the interval R reports in the table above. It is the 95% CI for the effect, the mean difference in bird species between the two groups.
Cohen’s \(d\) for two independent groups divides the mean difference by the pooled standard deviation, \(\text{Cohen's } d = (\bar{x}_A - \bar{x}_B)/s_p\). Here \(s_p = 2.04\), so Cohen’s \(d = -2.6/2.04 = -1.28\). Sites without a hedgerow averaged 1.28 pooled standard deviations fewer bird species than sites with one.
