title: 8  Analysis of Variance (ANOVA)
text:
8.6 Repeated-measures ANOVA
Every unit in the salamander study was measured once: 24 plots, 8 per forest type. Many environmental studies instead measure the same monitoring stations in every season or the same streams before, during, and after a drought. A repeated-measures (within-subjects) design measures the same units under every condition, and it calls for a repeated-measures ANOVA.
This is ANOVA’s version of the paired \(t\)-test (Section 6.4). The paired \(t\)-test subtracted each plot’s before score from its own after score, so differences between plots dropped out and only the change was left. With three or more conditions there is no single difference to take, so repeated-measures ANOVA does the equivalent with sums of squares, measuring how much the units differ from one another and removing that variation from the error term.

8.6.1 Fine particulate matter at four monitoring stations
An air quality agency has four PM2.5 monitoring stations, ordered from the most rural (A) to the most urban (D). The concentrations in this example are invented. Table 8.15 gives each station’s mean PM2.5 concentration in winter, spring, and summer. The question is whether concentrations differ by season.

Null (\(H_0\)): mean PM2.5 is the same in every season, \(\mu_\text{Winter}=\mu_\text{Spring}=\mu_\text{Summer}\).
Alternative (\(H_a\)): at least one seasonal mean differs.

8.6.2 Splitting off the stations
A one-way ANOVA on these 12 numbers would split the variation into two pieces, as before. The grand mean is 10 and the season means are 13, 8, and 9. Each season mean counts once per station, so
\[SS_\text{Between} = 4\left[(13-10)^2 + (8-10)^2 + (9-10)^2\right] = 4(14) = 56.\]

Squaring and summing the 12 distances, one season at a time, gives
\[SS_\text{Total} = (1 + 1 + 36 + 64) + (64 + 4 + 1 + 1) + (36 + 9 + 4 + 9) = 230,\]
which leaves \(SS_\text{Within} = 230 - 56 = 174\).
A one-way ANOVA would also break the independence assumption, because each station contributes three of the 12 numbers, and readings from the same station tend to be alike.
Repeated-measures ANOVA splits \(SS_\text{Within}\) one more time. Part of it is station-to-station variation. The units measured repeatedly are called subjects, even when they are stations, so this piece is \(SS_\text{Subjects}\), computed exactly like \(SS_\text{Between}\) but from the station means instead of the season means. Each station mean counts once per season, so
\[SS_\text{Subjects} = 3\left[(5-10)^2 + (8-10)^2 + (13-10)^2 + (14-10)^2\right] = 3(54) = 162.\]
Whatever is left is the error term:
\[SS_\text{Error} = SS_\text{Within} - SS_\text{Subjects} = 174 - 162 = 12,\]
so the full split is
\[SS_\text{Total} = SS_\text{Between} + SS_\text{Subjects} + SS_\text{Error}, \qquad 230 = 56 + 162 + 12.\]
\(SS_\text{Error}\) is the part of the within-season variation that the stations’ own levels can’t explain. It measures how much each station’s seasonal pattern departs from the average seasonal pattern. Its degrees of freedom are the one-way \(df_\text{Within}\) minus the degrees of freedom the four station means use up, where \(n\) is the number of stations:
\[\begin{aligned}
df_\text{Within} &= N - k = 12 - 3 = 9 \\
df_\text{Subjects} &= n - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3 \\
df_\text{Error} &= 9 - 3 = 6 = (k-1)(n-1)
\end{aligned}\]
\(F\) uses the same numerator as before, \(MS_\text{Between} = 56/2 = 28\). Only the denominator changes:
\[\begin{aligned}
\text{One-way: } F &= \frac{28}{174/9} = \frac{28}{19.33} = 1.45 \\[1.2ex]
\text{Repeated measures: } F &= \frac{28}{12/6} = \frac{28}{2} = 14.00
\end{aligned}\]

The repeated-measures analysis removes them (dashed gray piece), so the error term shrinks from 174 to 12 and \(F\) grows from 1.45 to 14.00.

A repeated-measures design has more power than a between-subjects design with the same number of measurements when the units differ from one another, as monitoring stations usually do.

title: 9  Simple Linear Regression
text:
9.4 Partitioning variation: regression as ANOVA
Besides testing the slope, we want to know how much of the variation in DO the line explains. We answer that the same way as one-way ANOVA in Chapter 8, by splitting the total variation into a piece the model explains and a piece it leaves over.
Figure 9.5 shows the three pieces for the stream data. Each site’s distance from mean DO (gray, left panel) splits into two pieces, the distance from the mean to the line (middle), which the line explains, and the distance from the line to the point (right), the residual.








Figure 9.5: Partitioning variation in dissolved oxygen. Left: each site’s distance from mean DO (dashed line). Middle: the part of that distance explained by the line. Right: what is left over, the residuals. Squaring and summing each set of segments gives the three sums of squares.





\(SS_\text{Total}\) is the sum of the squared distances from each point to mean DO. \(SS_\text{Regression}\) is the sum of the squared distances from the line to mean DO. \(SS_\text{Residual}\) is the sum of the squared residuals, the distances from each point to the line. For each site, the two shorter segments add up to the long one. After squaring each segment and summing over all 30 sites, the totals still add up, as they did in Section 8.4:
\[SS_\text{Total} = SS_\text{Regression} + SS_\text{Residual}, \qquad 122.44 = 61.35 + 61.10\]
The pieces line up with Chapter 8’s. \(SS_\text{Regression}\) is the variation the predictor explains, the role \(SS_\text{Between}\) played for group means. \(SS_\text{Residual}\) is what’s left over around the line, the role \(SS_\text{Within}\) played around each group’s mean. Treating every temperature value as its own group means that the line supplies a predicted mean at each value of \(x\), in place of one mean per group.
R-squared (\(R^2\)) is the proportion of the total variation explained by the line:
\[R^2 = \frac{SS_\text{Regression}}{SS_\text{Total}} = \frac{61.35}{122.44} = 0.50\]
It runs from 0 to 1, and it is the same quantity as \(\eta^2\) from Section 8.5.3. For simple regression with one predictor, \(R^2\) is also Pearson’s \(r\) from Section 2.3.3, squared: \((-0.708)^2 = 0.501\).
The regression ANOVA table. Dividing each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom gives mean squares, and their ratio is \(F\), exactly as in Table 8.7. The regression row uses 1 degree of freedom, one for the slope. The residual row uses \(n-2\), since the line estimated two things, an intercept and a slope.

With one predictor, \(F\) and the slope’s \(t\) test the same thing: \(F = t^2 = (-5.30)^2 = 28.12\), with the same \(p\). \(F\) is the form that generalizes to models with more than one predictor, which is why software reports both.
Here \(R^2 = 0.50\), so stream temperature explains about 50% of the variation we observed in dissolved oxygen across sites. The remaining 50% comes from everything else the model doesn’t capture (discharge, shading, groundwater input, and so on), and it shows up as the residuals.

title: 9  Simple Linear Regression
text:
9.6 Checking assumptions
Simple linear regression has three test-specific assumptions, plus the universal independence assumption from Section 6.3.5. Table 9.3 lists the three test-specific ones with the check this chapter uses.



Table 9.3: Assumptions of simple linear regression and how to check them.











Assumption
What it means
How to check
What a violation looks like




Linearity
The true relationship between \(x\) and \(y\) is a straight line.
Residuals-versus-fitted plot
A curve, such as a U-shape


Constant variance (homoscedasticity)
The spread of residuals is about the same across the whole range of \(x\), the regression version of homogeneity of variance (Section 8.5.2).
Residuals-versus-fitted plot
A funnel that widens or narrows


Normal residuals
The residuals are approximately normally distributed.
Q-Q plot and Shapiro-Wilk
Points bending away from the Q-Q diagonal







9.6.1 When the true relationship is curved

You can do linear regression without thinking about whether the phenomenon you’re modeling is actually close to linear. But you shouldn’t.
Jordan Ellenberg, How Not to Be Wrong

A straight line may be the wrong shape for your data. A residuals-versus-fitted plot puts each point’s fitted value \(\hat y\), the value the line predicts for it, on the \(x\)-axis and its residual on the \(y\)-axis. It checks two of the assumptions above at once. A curve means linearity is violated, and a funnel shape means constant variance is violated.








Figure 9.7: Residuals versus fitted values for the stream temperature model. A random scatter around zero, with no funnel shape or curve, supports linearity and constant variance.





Figure 9.7, for our stream temperature data, shows residuals scattered evenly above and below zero, with no curve and no funnel shape.
To see what a violation looks like, we fit a straight line to a second data set, 14 days of invented avian influenza case counts. We built the counts from an exponential curve, \(6e^{0.28 \times \text{day}}\), which grows by about 32% each day, plus random scatter, so we know the true shape that a straight line will miss. The design has the same structure as the stream example, with time as the continuous predictor.








Figure 9.8: The outbreak data as a design.













Figure 9.9: New avian influenza cases per day, days 1-14 of an outbreak, with a fitted straight line.





A straight line fit to these 14 days gives \(R^2 = 0.81\) and \(p < 0.001\), which is higher than the 0.5 to 0.8 that is common for a single predictor in environmental work, and significant. Neither number alone suggests a problem, but the plot does. The fitted line starts at about -40 cases on day 1, and a count of cases can’t be negative.
Check the residuals. Figure 9.10 shows the residuals-versus-fitted plot for the outbreak model.








Figure 9.10: Residuals versus fitted values for the linear outbreak model. The residuals form a U-shape instead of a random scatter, which happens when a straight line is fit to a curved relationship.





The residuals form a U. The residuals are positive early and late in the outbreak, so the observed counts are above the line there and the line underpredicts. In the middle they are negative, so the line overpredicts.
If a residual plot curves instead of scattering randomly, a straight line is the wrong model for the data.
Fixes typically include:

a different model (often adding an \(x^2\) term, which lets the fitted line bend)
a transformation, re-expressing a variable on a different scale so a straight line fits it (log-transforming a variable that grows multiplicatively, like the outbreak data above, is the most common case)
or a nonlinear model entirely, beyond what this course covers



9.6.2 Checking normality
For normality, we check the residuals two ways: visually, with a Q-Q plot, and formally, with the Shapiro-Wilk test (Section 6.3.5).
A Q-Q plot sorts the residuals and compares them to where a perfectly normal distribution would place values at the same percentiles. If the residuals are normal, the points fall close to the diagonal line. A systematic curve or S-shape means they don’t.








Figure 9.11: Normal Q-Q plot of the stream temperature model’s residuals. Points close to the diagonal support normality.





Figure 9.11 looks close to straight, consistent with normal residuals. Shapiro-Wilk asks the same question formally. Its \(H_0\) is that the residuals come from a normal distribution, so a small \(p\)-value is evidence against normality.

shapiro.test(resid(fit))




Shapiro-Wilk test on the regression residuals


Statistic
p




0.97
0.663





Shapiro-Wilk does not reject normality here (\(p = 0.663\)). As with any formal normality test, treat this as one piece of evidence alongside the Q-Q plot and residual plot. Shapiro-Wilk has the least power to detect real departures when the sample is small, which is also when the visual checks matter most.
Now apply the same two normality checks to the avian influenza model, the one we already know is badly nonlinear.








Figure 9.12: Normal Q-Q plot of the outbreak model’s residuals. The lowest residuals bend away from the diagonal, but not by enough for Shapiro-Wilk to reject normality.





The Q-Q plot bends away from the diagonal at the low end, but Shapiro-Wilk does not reject normality (\(p = 0.060\)). On a model we already know is the wrong shape, the normality checks give at most borderline evidence of a problem. They check normality of the residuals, which is a different assumption from linearity, and a model can badly violate linearity while its residuals look only mildly non-normal.






ImportantResults reporting: regression



We report a regression result the same way as any other test: the slope, the test statistic with its degrees of freedom, \(p\), the slope’s confidence interval, and \(R^2\) as the effect size.

Dissolved oxygen declined significantly with stream temperature, \(b_1 = -0.36\) mg/L per °C, \(t(28) = -5.30\), \(p < 0.001\), 95% CI [-0.50, -0.22] mg/L per °C, \(R^2 = 0.50\).

title: 1  Measuring and Describing Data
text:
1.3 Scales of measurement
The previous section called the outcome of a measurement a variable. Variables come in different types, and the type determines which statistical tools make sense. You can average daily temperatures, for example, but you cannot average species. A variable’s scale of measurement says which comparisons its values support, such as putting them in order, subtracting them, or forming ratios. The four classic scales are nominal, ordinal, interval, and ratio (Stevens 1946).

1.3.1 Nominal scale
A nominal variable, also called a categorical variable, has values that are names with no order. It makes no sense to average them.
Example. Species. A wildlife survey might record each animal it detects as a green frog, a brook trout, an American crow, or a river otter. None of those is “greater” than another, so they cannot be put in a meaningful order, and there is no such thing as an average species.
A computer will still do the arithmetic, though. Field datasheets often record species as numeric codes, such as 1 for green frog and 4 for river otter, so the computer will average the codes and return a result. Figure 1.2 shows what comes back.








Figure 1.2: Averaging the numeric codes of four species returns a number, but not a species. No species has the code 2.5. Icons from Font Awesome Free (CC BY 4.0).





You get a number back, but no species has that code. Species have no order and no amount, so averaging their codes gives a meaningless number.
The codes exist only because someone chose numbers for a datasheet. Letters would have worked just as well and left nothing to average. Most nominal variables, like watershed name or trap type, have no numbers attached in the first place.


1.3.2 Ordinal scale
An ordinal variable has values with a meaningful order, but the spacing between values is not defined. You can rank the values, but you cannot calculate a meaningful average.
Example. Finishing position in a competition. First place comes before second, and second before third, but the ranks themselves tell you nothing about how far apart the competitors actually were.
An Olympic weightlifting event makes this concrete, because athletes are ranked by a weight, so we can see both scales at once. The weights in Figure 1.3 are invented.








Figure 1.3: The same three athletes shown two ways. On the podium, each step is one place above the last. On the scale below, the weights they lifted are 29 kg and 2 kg apart.





On the podium, second place looks exactly as far from first as it does from third. On the scale below, second place is 2 kg behind first and 29 kg ahead of third. Ranking keeps the order and throws away the distances.
A single event also gives us both kinds of variable. The finishing place is ordinal, the weight lifted is on a ratio scale (defined below), and only one of them can be averaged.


1.3.3 Interval scale
An interval variable has equal spacing between values, so differences are meaningful. Its zero does not mean none of the quantity, so ratios between values are not meaningful.
Example. Temperature in degrees Celsius.
A difference of 3\(^\circ\) means the same regardless of whether it is 7 → 10 or 15 → 18. But 0\(^\circ\)C does not mean “no temperature.” That zero is defined by the freezing point of water, which is a useful convention rather than a fact about heat. So you can say today is 3\(^\circ\) warmer than yesterday, but you cannot say 20\(^\circ\)C is “twice as hot” as 10\(^\circ\)C.
Another example. Calendar years. The ten years from 1990 to 2000 are the same length as the ten years from 2010 to 2020, so differences work fine. But the starting point of the count is a convention we agreed on, and other calendars start their count somewhere else and are equally correct. Because the zero is a convention, the year 2000 is not “twice as late” as the year 1000.


1.3.4 Ratio scale
A ratio variable has equal spacing between values and a true zero, where zero means none of the quantity. The true zero makes ratios between values meaningful. For example, 10 kg is twice 5 kg.
Example. Age in years. Zero means no age at all, and someone who is 20 really is twice as old as someone who is 10. Differences (20 - 10 = 10 years) and ratios (20 ÷ 10 = 2) are both meaningful.
Temperature makes an unusually clean comparison here, because the same physical quantity can be recorded on either kind of scale depending on where you put the zero. Figure 1.4 shows both.








Figure 1.4: The same physical range of temperatures on two scales. The scales differ only in where they put zero. Celsius anchors its zero to the freezing point of water, and Kelvin anchors it to the absence of thermal energy.





Going from 10\(^\circ\)C to 20\(^\circ\)C doubles the Celsius number, so it is tempting to call it twice as hot. On the Kelvin scale those same two temperatures are 283 K and 293 K. The increase is 10 K, and 10 / 283 is about 0.035, a physical increase of about 3.5%. The doubling was an artifact of where Celsius happens to put its zero.
Kelvin has a true zero, so its ratios hold. A gas molecule at 200 K has, on average, twice the kinetic energy of one at 100 K.

1.3.5 Continuous versus discrete variables
Another useful distinction is whether a variable can take on values in between others.

A continuous variable can, in principle, take on any value within a range. For example, consider height. If you are 72 inches tall and your friend Cameron is 71 inches tall, Alan could be 71.4 inches and David 71.49 inches. Because we can always imagine a new value in between two others, height is continuous.
A discrete variable has separate, distinct values with nothing in between. Nominal variables are always discrete, because no species falls “between” a green frog and a brook trout the way 71.4 falls between 71 and 72. Ordinal variables are also discrete. Second place falls between first and third, but nothing can fall between first and second.

Interval and ratio variables can be either. Among ratio variables, height is continuous, but the number of people living in a household is discrete, since you cannot have 4.2 people. Among interval variables, temperature in degrees Celsius is continuous, but the year you started college is discrete, since there is no year between 2022 and 2023.

1.3.6 Treating ordinal scales as interval
These categories are guides, not hard rules. For example, survey responses on a 1–5 “strongly disagree” to “strongly agree” scale are technically ordinal, but researchers often treat them as “quasi-interval” because they assume the steps between responses are roughly equal. Treating the responses as quasi-interval lets researchers average them, which the ordinal scale alone does not allow.

title: 1  Measuring and Describing Data
text:
1.4 Independent and dependent variables
In most studies we have many variables, but when we analyze them, we usually split them into two roles.
The independent variable (IV), \(X\), is the variable used to explain another, and the dependent variable (DV), \(Y\), is the variable being explained. When several variables do the explaining, we number them \(X_1\), \(X_2\), and so on. The logic is that if there’s a relationship, \(Y\) depends on \(X\). These terms can be confusing for two reasons. IVs are rarely “independent of everything else.” Fertilizer amount, for example, may track how much a farmer spends on irrigation. And if there’s no relationship, the DV doesn’t “depend” on the IV at all.
Two alternative vocabularies are often clearer. In experiments, IVs are manipulations and DVs are measured outcomes. When we are using \(X\) to predict \(Y\) rather than manipulating anything, the pair is predictor and outcome.

title: 1  Measuring and Describing Data
text:
1.8 Distribution, central tendency, and variation
Three terms will keep coming up: distribution, central tendency, and variation. Their everyday meanings aren’t far from the statistical ones.

A distribution is the pattern of which values occur in a dataset and how often each occurs. A histogram is one way of showing a distribution. The shape of the distribution tells us where values are concentrated, where they’re rare, and how far the extremes reach. Later we’ll also use distributions to generate theoretical data, which is the basis for sampling distributions (Chapter 3) and tools like \(t\)-tests (Chapter 6).
Central tendency is a single representative value near the center of a distribution, summarizing what most of the data are like. It is about sameness, where values cluster. In the temperature histogram, the tallest bars are in the high 70s and low 80s, so we say the data have a central tendency around 80°F. Central tendency doesn’t mean “everything is the same”, just that many values gather in a common area. Some datasets even have more than one cluster, and therefore more than one central tendency.
Variation is how spread out the values in a dataset are, their differentness. If every day had been 78°F, there would be no variation at all. Instead the days run from 56°F to 97°F, so there is variation to describe. Variation is measured by a family of statistics. This chapter introduces the first of them, the range, and the next chapter builds the variance and the standard deviation.

Variation is one feature of a distribution.
